centre-out-of-the-middle.caption: Your own end, your net at the right: the puck on the centre’s stick in the middle, two opponents closing through it. The instruction is not to beat them — it is to stop being there. The route drawn carries out to the safe ice behind your own net; the outlet from there is the winger on the boards.
centre-out-of-the-middle.describe: The defending half of the rink, your own net at the right. Two opposition forwards come down the middle of the zone from the left. Three of your own: the centre with the puck in the middle of the ice between the faceoff circles; the strong-side winger high on the boards; and the goalie in the crease. Two routes. The first is the centre carrying the puck out of the middle and round behind their own net, curving above the crease rather than across the goalmouth. The second starts where that one finishes and is the outlet pass out to the winger on the boards, ending short of them. Neither a rim nor a reverse is drawn, and your defencemen are not drawn.
centre-out-of-the-middle.title: Out of the middle first

centre-nz-get-it-to-the-outside.caption: The middle of the neutral zone, the end you are attacking at the right, the centre carrying with two opponents closing the middle in front of the carrier. Both drawn routes finish on the outside and only one of them happens: a pass to a winger on the wall, or a chip off the boards, stopping short of the blue line because putting the puck in is a different play. That the middle third is where odd-man rushes against you are made is coaching consensus rather than a tracked figure.
centre-nz-get-it-to-the-outside.describe: The full sheet, your own net at the left, attacking to the right. Your centre has the puck just short of centre ice, in the middle lane. Two opposition forwards are ahead of the centre in the middle, closing. Two of your own forwards are wide, one in each wall lane. Both goalies are in their creases. Two routes, both starting on the centre and both alternatives rather than a sequence: a pass out to the wide forward on the wall at the top of the picture, your left, ending short of that forward, and a chip to those same boards, finishing at the wall inside the neutral zone and well short of the attacking blue line. Your defencemen and theirs are not drawn.
centre-nz-get-it-to-the-outside.title: Get it to the outside

centre-nz-arrive-behind-the-puck.caption: Entering the attacking zone through the middle without the puck, the net you are attacking at the right, drawn the instant before the puck reaches the blue line. The winger carries wide; the centre is in the middle lane level with the puck or slightly behind it, which lets the puck cross first while you keep skating. Which forward carries, and how strictly the wide lanes are held, is a coaching choice rather than a law of hockey, and it varies enormously: some teams hold strict lanes, some are built on crossing and swinging. Find out what your team wants before you decide you know. Nothing here says whether anybody is onside — a glyph has no skates. And do it with your head up: you cannot brace for a hit you cannot see.
centre-nz-arrive-behind-the-puck.describe: The attacking half of the rink, the net being attacked at the right, with the attack coming from the left. Three of your own forwards: a winger wide at the top of the picture, your left, with the puck, a stride short of the blue line; the centre in the middle lane, further from the line than the puck is; and the other winger wide on the far side. Two opposition defencemen stand just inside their blue line, one either side of the middle, and their goalie is in the crease. Two routes, drawn as one instant rather than a sequence: the winger carrying the puck across the line on that side, and the centre skating through the middle and across the line behind it. Neither reaches either defenceman.
centre-nz-arrive-behind-the-puck.title: Arriving behind the puck

centre-oz-slot-options.caption: The centre with the puck in the slot in the attacking zone, the net at the right. This is the free-space case, so no defenders are drawn at all and the picture says nothing about how much time you really have. Four things are drawn and only one of them happens: the shot, a pass to the winger on the half-wall, a pass to the winger in the far circle, or a pass back to the point. With space in front of you, shoot.
centre-oz-slot-options.describe: The attacking half of the rink, the net being attacked at the right, and no opposition skaters drawn — this is the free-space case. Four of your own: the centre with the puck in the slot between the faceoff circles; a winger on the half-wall at the top of the picture, your left; a winger in the far faceoff circle; and a defenceman at the point near the blue line. The opposing goalie is in the crease. Four routes, all starting on the centre and all alternatives — a shot at the net, and three passes, to the winger on the half-wall, to the winger in the far circle, and back to the defenceman at the point. Each pass ends short of the player it is aimed at.
centre-oz-slot-options.title: Options from the slot

centre-nz-deciding-from-the-middle.caption: The middle of the neutral zone with the centre carrying in free space, the end you are attacking at the right. No opponent is drawn at all, which is the case this describes rather than a claim about how much time you really have. The point is the ice the carrier stands on: from the middle lane a winger is a pass away on each side and both of your own defencemen are behind you and in view. Head up — a carrier looking down through the middle cannot brace for contact they have not seen.
centre-nz-deciding-from-the-middle.describe: The full sheet, your own net at the left, attacking to the right. Your centre has the puck in the middle lane of the neutral zone, a little short of centre ice. Two of your own forwards are wide and ahead of the centre, one in each wall lane. Your two defencemen are behind the centre, inside your own blue line, one either side of the middle. Both goalies are in their creases. No opposition skaters are drawn — this is the free-space case. Three routes, all starting on the centre and all alternatives rather than a sequence: the centre carrying the puck straight up the middle, finishing well short of the attacking blue line, and a pass out to each wide forward, each ending short of the player it is aimed at. No route is drawn back to either defenceman.
centre-nz-deciding-from-the-middle.title: Deciding from the middle

notation-key.caption: The drill notation these diagrams use. Shape says the position — a circle is a forward, a triangle a defenceman — while fill says whose team it is, open for your own and solid for the opposition, which is this guide’s own convention rather than either published key’s. A goalie is a bare G, and an X is a pylon and never a player.
notation-key.describe: A two-column key of line styles with their names, then rows showing the two player channels. Shape carries the position: a circle is a forward, a triangle a defenceman, which is the International Drill Symbols axis. Fill carries identity: an open glyph is the reader's own team, a solid one the opposition — that reading is this guide's own, not the key's. A last row shows the puck, a small solid dot about a third the width of a player. So a winger is an open circle whether attacking or backchecking, because the shape follows the player and not the moment. A goalie is a bare letter G, and an X is a pylon and is never a player.
notation-key.title: Drill notation key

puck-on-the-far-side.caption: Keep the puck on the side of you away from the checker, anywhere on the ice. Here the checker is nearer the middle of the ice and the puck is on the other side of you, so your body is the wall between them: nine and a half feet from the checker to you, fifteen to the puck. ⚠️ And at the boards or in open ice, never turn your back to anyone coming at you and never duck, however slowly they come. Head up, chin off your chest, and take any contact on your forearm and hip, never the point of your shoulder.
puck-on-the-far-side.describe: The attacking half of the rink, the opposition net at the right and their goalie in the crease. Two skaters, both in open ice toward the top of the picture, between the blue line and the faceoff circle and well clear of the boards. An own-team forward, an open circle, is the carrier. An opposition forward, a solid circle, stands about nine and a half feet from the carrier, below and slightly ahead of them — that is, on the side nearer the middle of the ice. The puck is a small solid dot drawn just under six feet from the carrier on the opposite side of them from that opponent, toward the boards, so the carrier's glyph lies between the puck and the checker and the puck is about fifteen feet from the checker. No routes are drawn, no region is shaded, and no stick, head or body facing is drawn, because the notation has symbols for none of them.
puck-on-the-far-side.title: Puck on the far side

the-puck-decides-not-you.caption: A loose puck inside the shaded crease beside your goalie; you are outside it. In five of the six books the puck's position decides, not yours: covering a puck inside the crease from outside it, as drawn here, is a penalty shot (under USA Hockey the other team may take a minor instead), and covering one just outside while you stand inside is a minor. Hockey Canada's wording can also be read to count where you are, so under that book treat a cover from inside your crease as the shot too. Every book exempts the goalie. You are drawn as a defenceman; the rule reaches any skater. ⚠️ Wherever you are standing, do not keep hold of the puck. Knock it straight down in one continuous motion and play it with your skate or your blade. With your goalie pulled it can be a goal awarded against you.
the-puck-decides-not-you.describe: Your own defending end, your net at the right. The goal crease is drawn as the rink itself draws it, a shaded blue area in front of the goal with a red outline, eight feet wide and six feet deep. Your goalie stands inside it, pushed off to one side of the goal mouth. The puck is a small solid dot drawn inside the crease on the other side of the mouth from them, clear of its edges, about five feet from the goalie. One of your own skaters, an open triangle and so an own-team defenceman, stands about six feet clear of the nearest corner of the crease, up and to the side of it, with no part of their glyph touching the paint. No opposition players are drawn, no routes are drawn, and no shaded region has been added: the only shaded area in the picture is the crease, which is a real marking on a real rink.
the-puck-decides-not-you.title: In most books the puck decides, not you

you-cannot-beat-two.caption: You have the puck wide, one defenceman is on you and a second opponent is closing from the middle. The dashed routes are the pass to the teammate whose ice the second opponent has left and the chip up the boards behind the first defenceman. The teammate shows what "left open" means, not that they will be there. The third option, protecting the puck outside your own end, is not drawn. It only buys a second: every second you hold the puck under pressure, another checker is arriving. ⚠️ At the boards or in open ice, never turn your back to anyone coming at you and never duck, however slowly they come. At the wall, skates parallel to it, forearm and hip, head up and chin off your chest — and not on the point of your shoulder, and not the whole shoulder if you can help it.
you-cannot-beat-two.describe: The attacking half of the rink, the opposition net at the right and their goalie in the crease. An own-team forward, an open circle, has the puck wide toward the top of the picture, inside the blue line, with the puck drawn as a small solid dot on the boards side of them. An opposition defenceman, a solid triangle, stands about ten feet away, up-ice of the carrier and a couple of feet nearer the middle of the ice. A second opposition player, a solid circle, stands out in the middle of the ice, with a plain route running up toward the carrier that stops about twelve feet short of the carrier and ends in two short bars rather than an arrowhead. A second own-team forward stands in the middle of the ice, about twelve and a half feet from where that opponent is, in the ice the opponent has left. Two dashed puck routes leave the carrier and go different ways: one down and across toward that teammate, ending about six feet short of them, and one curving up and out, round the boards side of the defenceman, finishing in open ice near the wall about ten feet behind the defenceman. The carrier has no route of their own. No third route is drawn, and no region is shaded.
you-cannot-beat-two.title: You cannot beat two

the-last-player-back.caption: You are the last player back, with your own net at the left. You have the puck in the neutral zone, two of their forwards are up on you, and the shaded ice behind you holds only your goalie. Lose it here and both go the other way with only the goalie to beat, so trying a move is off here. Carrying the puck is not. The shading is what is behind you now, not a prediction. None of your four fellow skaters is behind you. Two are drawn up the ice. You are drawn as a defenceman, but it can be anyone. ⚠️ And at the boards or in open ice, never turn your back to anyone coming at you and never duck, however slowly they come. Head up, chin off your chest, and take any contact on your forearm and hip, never the point of your shoulder.
the-last-player-back.describe: The whole sheet. Your own net is at the left with your goalie in the crease, and the net you are attacking is at the right with their goalie in theirs. One of your own defencemen, an open triangle, has the puck in the neutral zone a little to your own side of the centre red line and toward the top of the picture; the puck is a small solid dot about six feet from the defenceman, on the opposite side of them from the pressure. Two opposition forwards, solid circles, stand up-ice of the defenceman toward the middle of the sheet, about sixteen feet apart from each other. The nearer of the two has a plain route running toward the carrier that stops about eight feet short and ends in two short bars rather than an arrowhead. Two of your own forwards, open circles, stand well up the ice inside the attacking zone. Everything behind the defenceman — from a line a few feet behind them back to your own end boards, across most of the width of the ice — is shaded red with a dashed edge and carries no label; the only player standing inside it is your own goalie. The remaining skaters on both teams are not drawn, because the section does not fix where they stand. No other routes are drawn, and the carrier has none of their own.
the-last-player-back.title: The last player back

offside-faceoff-location.caption: Where the draw goes after an offside, under NHL Rule 83.6 — the IIHF and PWHL write it the same way; USA Hockey, Hockey Canada and CARHA word it differently, so check your own book. One attacker has preceded the puck into the zone at the right. The two entries are alternatives, not a sequence. The rule turns on how the puck then came in. Carried in unintentionally, and the draw is the neutral-zone spot nearest that zone; a deliberate offside goes to the offending team’s own end (83.7). Shot or passed in, it goes to the faceoff spot in the zone closest to where the pass came from, drawn as a defenceman firing it in from their own end. That is a faceoff spot, not the patch of ice it left. The far marker is this pass’s answer. Move the pass and the spot moves with it.
offside-faceoff-location.describe: The full sheet. The attacking zone is at the right, the attacking blue line a quarter of the way in from that end, and our own end is at the left. One of our attackers stands well inside the attacking zone, having preceded the puck. Two alternative ways the puck then enters are drawn. First, a teammate in the neutral zone carries it over the blue line near the far boards, and the neutral-zone faceoff spot just outside that blue line on the same side is marked and labelled "if carried". Second, one of our defencemen deep in our own end passes it the length of the ice across the same blue line, and the end-zone faceoff spot beside them is marked and labelled "if shot or passed". Both goalies are drawn. No puck is drawn, because two different offsides are shown side by side rather than one play, and no route is numbered, because neither entry comes before the other.
offside-faceoff-location.title: Faceoff location after an offside

icing-gaining-the-line.caption: Two players in exactly the same place — both bodies on the centre red line, one drawn above the other — and only one of them has iced the puck. NHL Rule 81.1, for a team equal or superior in numerical strength: to nullify a potential icing the puck must make contact with the centre red line while it is on a player’s stick, not on a skate. So the question is not where you were. It is where the puck on your stick was. The shading is the shooting team’s own half: the upper player’s dump-in leaves with the puck still inside it and is iced, while the lower player’s leaves with the puck touching the line — the black dot, which is the whole rule. This notation has no symbol for a stick, so what you can see is only where each dump-in begins.
icing-gaining-the-line.describe: The full sheet, with the attacking end at the right. Two of our players are drawn, one in each half of the width, and both stand on the centre red line at exactly the same point along the ice. Each has dumped the puck the length of the ice into the far corner, drawn as a long dashed line crossing the far goal line. The whole of their own half, from the centre red line back to the end boards, is lightly shaded and labelled. The upper player’s dashed line begins about five feet short of the centre red line, inside the shaded half, and they are labelled as not having gained the line. The lower player’s dashed line begins on the red line itself, where a black puck is drawn, and they are labelled as having gained it. Nothing else is drawn — no goalies, no opponents and no chase — because the picture is about one thing.
icing-gaining-the-line.title: Icing and the centre red line

icing-the-race-and-the-dot.caption: Hybrid icing: the boxed dot is a deadline, not a finish line. By then the linesperson must judge who would touch the puck first, so arriving level settles nothing. A race too close to call is icing. Ask which icing your league plays. The race is no licence to hit. In the NHL, IIHF, PWHL and Hockey Canada, unnecessary contact with the player on the puck on an obvious icing is boarding if they hit the boards, charging if not. USA Hockey penalises any such contact. ⚠️ Whoever wins, in any league, checking or not, never turn your back to anyone coming at you, and never duck. Get your skates parallel to the wall instead, take it on your forearm and hip, head up and chin off your chest — and not on the point of your shoulder, and not the whole shoulder if you can help it.
icing-the-race-and-the-dot.describe: The defending half of the rink, your own net at the right and your goalie in the crease. The puck sits in the right corner, past the goal line. Two skaters are level with each other along the ice, both on the line of the end-zone faceoff dots and about twenty-four feet apart across the ice: your defenceman is out near the boards, and an opposition forward is inside them toward the middle. Each has a plain skating route running toward the puck and stopping short of it, on clearly different bearings; the wall route is the shorter of the two. A small unlabelled box is drawn around the near end-zone faceoff dot, between the two skaters, marking the dot as the cut-off for the decision rather than as a place a draw is taken. Nothing else is drawn: no other skaters, no shot and no chase behind them.
icing-the-race-and-the-dot.title: Hybrid icing: the faceoff dot is the deadline

the-privileged-area.caption: The goalkeeper’s privileged area, shaded: USA Hockey’s term and shape, and the NHL, IIHF, PWHL, Hockey Canada and CARHA books draw no such area. Rule 607(d) Note 2 builds it from the end-zone face-off spots, with a line from each spot straight back to the end boards, so it takes in the net front, the goal line and all the ice directly behind the net, but not the corners. ⚠️ The two red dashed lines behind the net are not part of it. That is the trapezoid, a much smaller shape, drawn because these diagrams use the NHL rink, and USA Hockey marks it nowhere. Read the shading as a boundary, not a licence.
the-privileged-area.describe: The defending half of the rink, the net at the right, and no play in progress. A large shaded region is drawn on the ice: its inner edge is a straight line joining the two end-zone faceoff dots, and from each dot a straight edge runs directly back to the end boards, so the region is a rectangle taking in the net front, the goal line, the crease and all the ice behind the net, and stopping short of both corners. Its far edge follows the curve of the end boards. The two red dashed trapezoid lines the rink itself carries run behind the net inside the shading, splaying out from beside the goal to the end boards, and are a different and much smaller shape. The goalie stands behind their own net, inside the shaded region and off to one side of it, and it is their label that names the region. No other players are drawn.
the-privileged-area.title: The goalkeeper’s privileged area (USA Hockey)

angling-your-route.caption: The defender’s line is aimed at the ice the carrier wants, not at the carrier. It noses at the shaded middle without getting into it and leaves the carrier the wall. That band is a lane, not a marking. The route ends in two bars on a patch of ice, not on a player — no contact is drawn, and where an angle ends depends on whether your league allows checking.
angling-your-route.describe: The defending half of the rink, with the net being defended at the right and our goalie in its crease. Two skaters and nothing else. An opposition forward carries the puck in open ice on the side drawn at the top of the picture, between the centre red line and the blue line and wide of the faceoff-dot line, with the puck a stride ahead of them and outside them. Their route is the skate-and-stickhandle wave: it leaves them heading up the ice and inward toward the middle, runs close along the edge of a shaded band without entering it, then swings up the ice and outward toward the side boards, finishing short of them with an arrowhead. Our defenceman stands inside the carrier and a few feet nearer the defended net. The defenceman’s route is a straight line ending in two short bars rather than an arrowhead: it runs up the ice and outward on a diagonal much more toward the defended net than across the rink, crosses the blue line, and stops inside the shaded band, ahead of where the carrier’s route finishes and well clear of the carrier. The shaded band is the middle lane, drawn between the two faceoff-dot lines from the centre red line down to the tops of the faceoff circles. The two routes start far apart and finish closer together. Nothing in the picture shows contact between the two players.
angling-your-route.title: A defender’s angling route

net-front-walk-out-direction.caption: Your net front; who covers it is your team’s call. Hold the inside, no lean, no push, and lift their stick low on the shaft, well below their bottom hand, as the puck arrives, then let go. ⚠️ Never walk a screener out: it can be called interference wherever you play, and where checking is barred an illegal check as well. Move nobody into or across the shaded goal frame and goalie.
net-front-walk-out-direction.describe: The defending half of the rink, the net being defended at the right with our goalie in its crease. Two skaters and no puck, and nothing moves: no route is drawn. An opposition forward stands in front of the net, about eleven and a half feet out from the goal line and six feet to the side drawn at the top of the picture, clear of the blue crease paint. Our defenceman stands beside them at the same distance from the goal line, on the inside, nearer the middle of the net. A red shaded band covers the goal and the goalie, from the back of the net to a foot and a half in front of the crease and a foot outside each post, labelled goal frame. The puck is at the point, not drawn. Nothing in the picture shows contact between the two skaters.
net-front-walk-out-direction.title: Net-front coverage in your own end

corner-escape-routes.caption: Why a corner is harder to defend than a piece of wall, drawn in your own end with the net you are defending at the right. The carrier’s two ways out are drawn: up the wall, or out behind the net. The third, back toward the slot, is the one you never leave open. You are the player drawn, a defenceman under this guide’s default, arriving on the carrier’s inside, and your body takes that route away, so it is not drawn. The route ends in two bars, meaning arrive and contain, and no contact is drawn. Whether an arrival like that may end in contact at all depends on your age group, your league and the book they play under. ⚠️ Pin the puck and not the player. Never finish into the back of a player who is facing the boards.
corner-escape-routes.describe: The defending half of the rink, the net being defended at the right and our goalie in its crease. An opposition forward stands in the corner at the top of the picture, about seven feet off the side boards, with the puck drawn between them and the wall. Our defenceman is out toward the top of the faceoff circle on the same side; the defenceman’s route curves out toward the side boards and then turns to run toward the end boards, heading past the carrier’s net side, ending in two short bars rather than an arrowhead, about seven feet short of the carrier and on the side of the carrier nearer the middle of the ice. Two skate-and-stickhandle waves leave the carrier. One runs along the side boards away from the goal, finishing with an arrowhead about twenty feet up the wall. The other curves out toward the end boards and then round the back of the goal, passing through the gap between the back of the net and the end boards, and finishing with an arrowhead on the far side of the goal from the corner, pointing across the ice and well clear of the goalie. No route runs toward the middle of the ice, and no shaded region is drawn. Nothing in the picture shows contact between the two players.
corner-escape-routes.title: Escape routes from a corner

angle-into-the-corner.caption: Going back for a puck in your own corner with a checker inside your line; only your line is drawn. It arrives on an angle and finishes running along the boards: the first and best of three cases. Better still, a chip, rim or reverse decided before you arrive moves the puck on, so you are not pinned on the wall with it. The second case: get your skates parallel to the wall and take it on your forearm and hip. The worst, for when you already face the wall, is damage limitation rather than a position to aim for. Turn your skates parallel first if at all possible; failing that, spread the load, with stick and gloves up on the glass, arms out as a shock absorber, and no head contact at all. The cases come from USA Hockey's material; the ordering and ranking do not. ⚠️ Never turn your back to anyone coming at you, and never duck.
angle-into-the-corner.describe: The defending half of the rink, the net being defended at the right and our goalie in its crease. One of our forwards stands well up the ice in the middle of the zone, level with a point about fourteen feet outside the top of the faceoff circle on the side drawn at the top of the picture. A single curved forward-skating route leaves them and runs into the corner: it sets off up the ice and toward that corner, arcs gently outward as it goes, and finishes with an arrowhead in the corner about four feet off the side boards, pointing along them rather than into them. The puck is drawn hard against the boards a few feet before that arrowhead and about three feet outside the line of the route, so the route passes it and continues. An opposition forward stands inside the curve of that route, between it and the middle of the ice and nearer the goal than our forward, with no route drawn at all. Nothing in the picture shows contact between the two players, and nothing in it shows how a player meets the boards.
angle-into-the-corner.title: Skating into your corner at an angle

inside-lane-longer-route.caption: A loose puck in your own end, with the net you are defending at the right; the faint dashed line is the opposition forward’s straight route to it, not a marking on the ice. Your route arcs, so you arrive already turned, inside them and on that line, leaving them the less direct way round. Body position does this work only while you are going for the puck. Change your skating lane or your foot speed to play the opponent’s body rather than the puck and USA Hockey Rule 625(a)(4) makes that a minor for interference. Under Hockey Canada and CARHA, impeding an opponent without the puck is interference, so hold only a lane you already have. ⚠️ Arc for the puck, not their body, and never hold, pull, tug or grab with your free hand.
inside-lane-longer-route.describe: The defending half of the rink, the net being defended at the right and our goalie in its crease. Two skaters. A loose puck is drawn on its own in open ice on the side at the top of the picture, inside the faceoff circle, about twelve feet up-ice of the goal line and well clear of the side boards. An opposition forward stands up-ice of it and wide, out toward the boards. A faint dashed line runs from them straight to the puck. One of our forwards stands level with the opposition forward up the ice and well inside them, nearer the middle of the rink. A single curved forward-skating route leaves our forward: it sets off up the ice, arcs outward as it goes, and finishes with an arrowhead sitting on the dashed line about seven feet short of the puck, pointing across the ice rather than at the puck. No route is drawn for the opposition forward. The two players are never close to one another, and nothing in the picture shows contact between them.
inside-lane-longer-route.title: The inside lane

shot-block-get-close.caption: Where to block a shot from, in your own end with your goalie at the right. An opposition defenceman has the puck at the point, and the faint dashed line is its straight path to the middle of your goal, not a marking on the ice. How much your team blocks at all is a coaching choice, so find out which yours plays and ask your goalie what they want. ⚠️ Where you would be screening your own goalie, do not block. A block there deflects a shot they could not see, so get out of the lane and let them see it. Anywhere else, commit fully or get out. Never stand half in the way with your eyes closed.
shot-block-get-close.describe: The defending half of the rink, the net being defended at the right and our goalie in its crease. Three players and no routes. An opposition defenceman stands at the strong-side point on the side drawn at the top of the picture, with the puck just off the blade toward the middle of the ice. A faint dashed line runs from that puck down the ice toward the middle of the goal, stopping about thirteen feet short of the goal line and well clear of the goalie; extended, it would reach the middle of the goal line. One of our forwards stands squarely on that line about fourteen feet from the shooter, so the forward is at the shooter’s end of it and roughly fifty feet from our own goalie. No shot is drawn, no route is drawn, and no second blocker is drawn anywhere on the line.
shot-block-get-close.title: Blocking close to the shooter

breakout-five-roles.caption: The five jobs on a breakout, frozen at the instant the puck is retrieved, with your own zone at the left. D1 has gone back for the puck in the corner; D2 is on the opposite side of the net, level with the goal line, where a pass behind the net reaches them. The strong-side winger is on the boards between the hash marks and the goal line, the centre is low support inside the faceoff dots rather than out on the wall, and the weak-side winger is the second option. This five-role structure is itself a coaching choice: it is the conventional swing breakout, and under a centre fly the centre leaves early and the weak-side winger takes low support instead — so ask your coach which one you play. No forecheck is drawn: this is the shape, not a play against anybody.
breakout-five-roles.describe: The full 200-foot sheet. The defending zone is at the left, the attacking end at the right. Five own players and a goalie, and no opposition. The defenceman D1 is deep in the top corner with the puck at their stick. The defenceman D2 is on the other side of the net, just above the goal line. The winger W1 is on the top boards between the hash marks and the goal line. The centre C is inside the top faceoff circle, below the hash marks and inside the dot. The winger W2 is on the weak side and higher, near the up-ice edge of the bottom circle. The goalie is in the crease. There are no routes: nothing is moving yet.
breakout-five-roles.title: Five roles on a breakout

breakout-up.caption: The “up”: the defenceman with the puck passes straight up the wall to the strong-side winger. Drawn in your own defensive zone at the left of the picture, moving left to right; the read drawn here is the first forechecker committed behind the net, which leaves the wall lane open. What a still picture cannot show is the risk: that pass travels the lane where a forecheck posts a player to seal the wall, so intercepted at the hash marks it becomes a scoring chance from the top of the circle.
breakout-up.describe: The full sheet, the defending zone at the left. The defenceman D1 has the puck deep in the top corner below the goal line. The winger W1 is on the top boards between the hash marks and the goal line. The centre C is low in the middle, inside the top circle. The defenceman D2 is on the far side of the net near the goal line. One opposition forward is behind the net, the forecheck having committed there. A single dashed route runs from D1 up the wall to the winger’s stick. The winger’s own next move is deliberately not drawn.
breakout-up.title: The up breakout

breakout-wheel.caption: The wheel, drawn in your own zone at the left, moving left to right. D2, standing at the net front, is legal only in some books. The NHL and PWHL allow it: stick in tight and vertical, hands to yourself, no bump. Under USA Hockey even a still screen is a minor when your partner has the puck. Hockey Canada and CARHA give your side no right to it, and make a major and a game misconduct mandatory if it injures. ⚠️ Screen only where your book allows it, and never slide across into the forechecker's path: that is interference everywhere, and two minutes is only the floor.
breakout-wheel.describe: The full sheet, the defending zone at the left. The defenceman D1 has the puck in the top corner. A long smooth wave — skating with control of the puck — runs from them down behind their own net, passing about two feet behind the goal frame, and back up the weak side to the bottom boards below the hash marks. The defenceman D2 stands in front of the net, slightly to the strong side, with no route drawn. The winger W2 is on the bottom boards and the centre C is low inside the bottom circle; both are outlets. One opposition forechecker is up the top wall, behind the play. The goalie is in the crease.
breakout-wheel.title: The wheel breakout

breakout-reverse.caption: The reverse, in your own zone at the left. D1 was working up the wall when the forechecker over-committed and skated past them, so D1 sends the puck back down the boards behind them, against the flow, into the space the forechecker has just left, where D2 is arriving. Read the opponent above D1 as already past them and unable to stop. The puck is a hard backhand banked off the wall, drawn as a plain pass because the notation has no symbol for a bank. Both players here can be hit on the wall, and D2 is arriving onto a puck they have not seen travel. ⚠️ If you are one of them, never turn your back to anyone coming at you, and never duck. Head up, chin off your chest, and take any contact on your forearm and hip, never the point of your shoulder.
breakout-reverse.describe: The full sheet, the defending zone at the left. The defenceman D1 is on the top boards just below the hash marks with the puck. An opposition forward is on the same boards about ten feet further up ice, past D1. Two numbered routes: one, the defenceman D2 skates from the far side of the net, around behind the goal, and up into the strong-side corner below the goal line; two, a dashed pass from D1 back down the top boards behind them, finishing in that same corner space. The two routes finish about nine feet apart. The goalie is in the crease.
breakout-reverse.title: The reverse breakout

breakout-rim.caption: Your own zone is at the left. The rim is a hard pass around the boards behind the net to a teammate further along, usually the far-side winger. The puck travels onward, the way it was already going. The read drawn: a forechecker has sealed D1 against the boards. Keep it low, flat and hard. It concedes possession more often than any option except an outright clear — coaching judgement, not a tracked rate. The trapezoid rules where you play change where to aim it. This is a wall play at both ends: D1 is sealed on the boards and the winger takes it on the far wall. ⚠️ If you are the skater on the wall, never turn your back to anyone coming at you, and never duck. Head up, chin off your chest, and take any contact on your forearm and hip, never the point of your shoulder.
breakout-rim.describe: The full sheet, the defending zone at the left. The defenceman D1 has the puck deep in the top corner with an opposition forward between them and the ice, sealing them against the boards. A single dashed route leaves D1, runs down and around the end boards about two and a half feet off the dasher behind the net, and comes out low on the bottom boards, finishing on the wall four and a half feet off the dasher. The winger W2 stands a few feet up-ice of where it finishes, stepping in to meet it. The goalie is in the crease.
breakout-rim.title: The rim breakout

breakout-d-to-d.caption: D-to-D: the pass across to your partner, which switches sides and makes the forecheck reset. Drawn in your own defensive zone at the left of the picture, with the strong side flooded and the far side free, which is the read the option needs. The route drawn is the default, behind your own net; some teams exchange high, above the circles, instead, so ask which yours plays. Either way, never through the shaded area — the house, or home plate, wider than the slot: across the tops of the two circles, down to the dots and in to the two posts. Intercepted below the goal line it costs little, because there is no shot from there; intercepted in front of the net it is a point-blank chance against. Move it quickly; do not skate it across.
breakout-d-to-d.describe: The full sheet, the defending zone at the left. The defenceman D1 has the puck in the top corner; the defenceman D2 is low in the bottom corner. Two opposition forwards are on the top side, one deep and one on the wall — the flooded side. A shaded region covers the house, the home-plate-shaped area analysts use to define a high-danger chance. Its outline runs square across the top along the tops of the two faceoff circles, straight down the dot lines to the two faceoff dots, then angles in to the two goalposts on the goal line. The single dashed pass runs from D1 down and around behind the goal, staying between four and six feet behind the net the whole way, and up to D2. It never enters the shaded region. The goalie is in the crease.
breakout-d-to-d.title: The D-to-D breakout

breakout-stretch-pass.caption: The stretch pass, which is why this picture is the whole 200-foot sheet: your defensive zone is at the left, the far blue line at the right. The read is the shape drawn: all three of their forwards deep and their defencemen stepped up, which leaves a lane and a winger behind the coverage. Lead the winger so they take it in stride. They are drawn on their own side of the far blue line: a skate blade on the ice, touching the line or behind it until the puck completely crosses, keeps them onside in every book.
breakout-stretch-pass.describe: The full 200-foot sheet. The defenceman D1 has the puck in the top corner of their own zone at the left of the picture. Three opposition forwards are deep in that zone: one on the top wall above them, one low on the bottom side, one in the middle. Two opposition defencemen stand on the blue line of that zone, stepped up. The winger W2 is a long way up ice at the right, just on their own side of the far blue line, alone. A single long dashed pass runs from D1 diagonally across and up the sheet to them, passing under the near forechecker, outside the faceoff dots, and between the two stepped-up defencemen. The goalie is in the crease; no other own player is drawn.
breakout-stretch-pass.title: The stretch pass breakout

breakout-winger-wall.caption: The strong-side winger’s trip, drawn in your own defensive zone at the left of the picture at the instant your team wins the puck. They come down from their high coverage spot to the wall, at or just below the dot line, never above it. ⚠️ Never turn your back to anyone coming at you, and never duck. Puck protection never justifies it. Get your skates parallel to the boards instead, forearm and hip to the wall, head up and chin off your chest — and not on the point of your shoulder, and not the whole shoulder if you can help it.
breakout-winger-wall.describe: The full sheet, the defending zone at the left. The winger W1 is high in their own zone, just inside the blue line and level with an opposition defenceman standing on that line. A skating route curves from W1 out toward the top boards and then down them, finishing on the wall just below the hash-mark line, some forty-eight feet from where it began — inside the range those two spots are apart on an NHL sheet, a little under forty-four to sixty-four feet. The defenceman D1 is deep in the top corner with the puck, which their team has just won. The goalie is in the crease. No pass is drawn: this diagram is the trip, not the exit.
breakout-winger-wall.title: Strong-side winger on a breakout

breakout-centre-swing.caption: The centre’s low support swing, drawn in your own defensive zone at the left of the picture. The shaded box is where the centre is going, inside the strong-side circle. The route curls away from the puck first and then turns back into it, which is how the centre arrives already moving instead of receiving standing still. Centre-low is itself a coaching choice — the alternative is the centre fly, and both are legitimate — but a centre flying in a flat or spread system where the wingers hold high near the blue line leaves nobody underneath the puck at all.
breakout-centre-swing.describe: The full sheet, the defending zone at the left. A shaded box sits in the top faceoff circle, bounded by the hash-mark line above, the faceoff dot line on the boards side, and the middle of the ice — the low support ice. The centre C is above and outside it, higher in the zone. A skating route runs from them, curving first away from the puck toward the middle of the ice and then back toward the boards, finishing inside the shaded box. The defenceman D1 has the puck in the top corner and the winger W1 is on the top boards above the box, on the ice the centre must not drift into. The goalie is in the crease.
breakout-centre-swing.title: Where the centre swings on a breakout

breakout-against-1-3-1.caption: Breaking out against a neutral-zone 1-3-1, your own end at the left. Out from your end: a forward giving token pressure; three flat across by the red line, conventionally two forwards on the walls and a defenceman in the middle; and a defenceman behind them as the last man. Drawn: your defenceman carrying it out with speed, and your winger on the boards at your blue line as the short outlet, with no route. Chipping it past them and racing for it is the other answer, not drawn. Which your team wants is a coaching choice, so ask. A player waiting on the boards is the one who gets hit. ⚠️ Body open to the ice, never turn your back to anyone coming at you and never duck. Head up, chin off your chest, and take any contact on your forearm and hip, never the point of your shoulder.
breakout-against-1-3-1.describe: The full 200-foot sheet. Your defending zone is at the left, the far end at the right. Your goalie is in the crease and the defenceman D1 has the puck deep in the top corner. Five opposition players are drawn in three bands. One forward stands in the middle of the ice about ten feet inside your blue line. Three more are level with each other just beyond the centre red line, spanning the sheet: one near the top boards, a defenceman in the middle of the ice, one near the bottom boards. A second defenceman stands alone behind them, in the middle of their own blue line. Of your own team only two skaters are drawn: D1, and the winger W1 out on the top boards a couple of feet inside your own blue line. A single smooth wave — skating with control of the puck — runs from D1 out of the corner and up the top boards, finishing in open ice about twenty feet short of the winger. The winger has no route. Nothing is drawn arriving at any opposition player.
breakout-against-1-3-1.title: Beating a neutral-zone 1-3-1

rush-gap-and-angle.caption: A 1-on-1 as the carrier crosses the centre red line, attacking right to left toward the defended net at the left. The defender is on the inside — body between the carrier and the middle of the ice — so the carrier’s only visible route is toward the wall. The shaded middle is the ice denied: a lane the length of the rink, cut short only so the shading has an edge; its edges are not painted on the ice. The gap drawn is about nine feet: on any legal stick, nearer one and three-quarter stick lengths than the stick and a half targeted at the red line. That target is a guide, not a law. It varies with your backward speed and the attacker’s skill; the only page found anchoring a distance to the centre red line prints two stick lengths, and one coaching book prints none.
rush-gap-and-angle.describe: The full sheet, the defended net at the left. Two players and a goalie. An opposition forward carries the puck just past the centre red line on the side of the ice at the top of the picture; a defender is about nine feet away from them, both nearer the middle of the ice and nearer the defended net — that is, on the inside and on the defensive side. The carrier’s route curves outward toward the boards and finishes short of them; the defender’s route is backward skating that stays inside the carrier the whole way and finishes slightly tighter than it began. A shaded rectangle between the two faceoff dots, from the top of the circles down to the front of the crease, marks the middle of the ice the angle is denying. The goalie is in the crease. Nothing in the picture shows contact.
rush-gap-and-angle.title: Gap and angle on a 1-on-1

rush-2-on-1.caption: A 2-on-1 — two attackers, one defender — attacking right to left toward the defended net at the left. The defenceman sits in the shaded passing lane, biased slightly toward the middle, on the defensive side of both, and retreats with them rather than stepping toward either: take away the pass and give up the shot. The goalie plays the shooter as though the second attacker did not exist. Ask your goalie before the game: most want it this way, but some will ask you to pressure the puck instead. If a backchecker picks up the second attacker and the shooter walks in unpressured with no realistic pass, it is no longer a 2-on-1. The defenceman should close on the puck.
rush-2-on-1.describe: The full sheet, the defended net at the left. Exactly two opposition forwards and one defender. The carrier is wide at the top of the picture, the second attacker is in the lower half driving toward the far side of the slot, and both are about the same distance from the defended net. The defender is between them and about seven feet nearer their own net than either, inside a shaded band marking the lane a pass between the two attackers would have to travel through; no pass is drawn. The carrier’s route carries the puck down to the faceoff dot and a shot goes from there toward the net, stopping short of the goalie; the defender’s route is backward skating that stays between the two attackers and stops well above the goal line. The goalie is a few feet out of the goal on the line between the net and the puck carrier.
rush-2-on-1.title: Defending a 2-on-1 rush

rush-2-on-2.caption: A 2-on-2 with the two attackers crossing, the attack moving right to left toward the defended net at the left. Drawn man-on-man: each defenceman takes one attacker and holds their gap on the inside of them; zone is the realistic alternative, so find out which your team plays. The gap is drawn wide because the crossing is only beginning; aim for a gap that shrinks the whole way in and never grows. Neither defenceman is drawn with a route, and that is for safety: a crossing rush is exactly where a beginner reaches for a hit instead of holding their position.
rush-2-on-2.describe: The full sheet, the defended net at the left with the goalie in it. Exactly two opposition forwards and two own defencemen, and nobody else. The two forwards are level with each other out in the neutral zone, one on each side of the ice, and each has a skating route running diagonally across to the far side; the two routes cross each other in the middle of the ice just inside the defending blue line. Both routes stop well short of the defencemen. The two defencemen are level with each other inside the defending zone, one either side of the middle, each nearer the middle of the ice than the forward who started on their side. Neither defenceman has a route drawn at all. The puck is with the forward who starts at the top of the picture.
rush-2-on-2.title: 2-on-2 rush with a crossing

rush-3-on-2-default.caption: A 3-on-2 defended "two wide, middle to the backchecker", with the attack moving right to left toward the defended net at the left. The third own player in the picture is the backchecking centre, who has the middle attacker. The two defencemen retreat level with each other, the middle sealed between them — a staggered retreat opens a diagonal seam straight to the slot — and stop above the circles rather than backing all the way to the goal line. This is the two-wide default, a coaching choice rather than a law: the realistic alternative is strong side takes the puck and weak side splits, so ask your coach which you play.
rush-3-on-2-default.describe: The full sheet, the defended net at the left. Three opposition forwards abreast just inside the defending blue line: one wide at the top of the picture carrying the puck, one in the middle, one wide at the bottom. Two own defencemen level with each other about twenty feet nearer the defended net, one in each outside lane just inside the faceoff dots, each with a backward-skating route that ends level with the other and above the circles. One own forward, the backchecking centre, is behind the play up-ice and takes a route that passes inside the middle attacker and finishes slightly nearer the defended net than they are — their inside hip, not their back pocket. The goalie is in the crease.
rush-3-on-2-default.title: Defending a 3-on-2: two wide

rush-3-on-2-alternative.caption: A 3-on-2 defended the realistic alternative way, "strong side takes the puck, weak side splits": the attackers stand as in the two-wide default, and only the defence has changed. The weak-side defenceman is in the shaded lane. The backchecking centre’s route ends in open ice because it takes the third attacker, whichever that turns out to be, rather than the middle. This version never concedes the middle, but the weak-side defenceman covers two people and the far attacker gets more room; the two-wide default keeps three on three if the backcheck arrives and concedes the middle if it does not. Ask your coach which one you are playing.
rush-3-on-2-alternative.describe: The full sheet, the defended net at the left. The same three opposition forwards as the previous diagram: wide at the top of the picture with the puck, in the middle, and wide at the bottom. The strong-side defenceman has stepped up to about ten feet from the carrier, on the inside of them, and retreats backwards steering them toward the boards. The weak-side defenceman is much deeper and toward the middle, inside a shaded band drawn between the middle attacker and the far wide attacker, and drops off further down that band. The backchecking centre comes back through the middle of the ice behind the play, passing inside the middle attacker and finishing in open ice rather than on any one of them. The goalie is in the crease.
rush-3-on-2-alternative.title: Defending a 3-on-2: strong side on the puck

rush-backcheck-lanes.caption: Backchecking lanes, with the attack moving right to left toward the defended net at the left: two outside lanes along the boards and the shaded middle lane between the faceoff dots, each running the length of the rink. In the standard assignment drawn, the centre takes the middle lane and the wingers the outside lanes, and each backchecker’s route bends inside their man: aim for their inside hip, not their back pocket, because you cannot defend anything from behind. The most dangerous player in the picture is the middle-lane driver, skating hard through the middle without the puck, who is missed because eyes go to the puck. The lane assignment is a coaching choice, but under every variant somebody owns the middle and nobody assumes it is somebody else. The defencemen are not drawn.
rush-backcheck-lanes.describe: The full sheet, the defended net at the left, with a shaded band between the two faceoff dots running most of the length of the ice — the middle lane. Three opposition forwards attack, one in each lane: the carrier in the outside lane at the top of the picture, one driving hard through the shaded middle lane without the puck, and one in the outside lane at the bottom. Three own forwards are behind them, up-ice: a winger behind the carrier in the top lane, the centre behind the middle driver, and a winger behind the bottom-lane attacker. All three backcheck routes curve toward the middle of the ice and stop short of the attacker they are chasing, arriving inside them rather than behind them. The goalie is in the crease. No defencemen are drawn.
rush-backcheck-lanes.title: Backchecking lanes on a rush

rush-trailer.caption: The trailer, or late man — the attacker who arrives behind the first wave — with the attack moving right to left toward the defended net at the left. The first wave of two has pulled both defencemen low, and the trailer follows a few metres behind into the high slot with a clean, unopposed look. In the standard system, a low zone collapse behind a 2-1-2 forecheck, the defencemen stay with the first wave, because if either steps up the first wave gets the net, and the backchecking forward arriving from up-ice takes the trailer. That is an assignment rather than a law: some teams give the trailer to the weak-side defenceman and drop the third forward to the net front instead, so ask which your team runs. The defencemen see them before the backcheckers do: "trailer!" or "high!" is the shout.
rush-trailer.describe: The full sheet, the defended net at the left, the play in the defending zone. Three opposition attackers: one wide at the top of the picture with the puck, level with the faceoff dot, one driving the net front on the weak side, and a third — the trailer — well behind them both, skating into the high slot in the middle of the ice. Two own defencemen are low and occupied, one inside the wide carrier and one at the net front beside the weak-side attacker, neither of them near the trailer. One own forward is backchecking from up-ice; its route curves below the trailer and stops short of them rather than finishing at them. The goalie is in the crease. No contact is drawn anywhere in the picture.
rush-trailer.title: The trailer on a rush

dz-the-house.caption: The house, or home plate — the region every defensive-zone system exists to protect: bounded by the two goalposts, widening to the end-zone faceoff dots and up to the tops of the circles. Nothing here is painted on the ice; the circles, dots and crease that fix its corners are.
dz-the-house.describe: The defending half of the rink, the defended net at the right. A shaded six-sided region is drawn on the ice: its two narrow corners are the two goalposts on the goal line, it widens out to the two end-zone faceoff dots, and its far edge runs straight across between the tops of the two faceoff circles. The result is the shape of a baseball home plate lying on its side, pointing at the net. No skaters are drawn; our goalie is in the crease, which is how you know which net this is.
dz-the-house.title: The house in your own zone

dz-collapse-corner.caption: Low zone collapse, the standard coverage here, as the puck goes into the strong-side corner: wingers high on the points, the centre down from the high slot as the second body to make it two on one. Frame one of two. Man-on-man or a hybrid would read bodies, not areas, so ask your coach which your team plays. The second body arrives late and unseen on a carrier facing the boards. In most books a call for checking from behind ends your game every time, in every book it can, and under USA Hockey it must whenever it is forceful at the boards, sends them head first into the boards or net, or is reckless. ⚠️ Take the puck, take the ice or angle them off it. You are there to win it, not to join a pin. Pin the puck, not the player. Never finish into their back.
dz-collapse-corner.describe: The defending half of the rink, the defended net at the right, with the puck in the strong-side corner at the top of the picture. Five opposition players: the puck carrier deep in the strong-side corner with the puck drawn at their stick against the boards, so they are facing the wall with their back to the ice, a forward supporting on the strong-side half-wall, a forward at the net front on the weak side of the crease, and their two defencemen at the two points. Six of our own: the strong-side defenceman on the puck about eight feet goal-side of the carrier, the weak-side defenceman on the doorstep between the net-front forward and the goal, the goalie in the crease, both wingers high and just goal-side of the opposing defencemen at the points, and the centre in the high slot. One route: the centre skating from the high slot out to the corner to make it two on one, finishing inside the carrier and short of them rather than behind them.
dz-collapse-corner.title: Low zone collapse, puck in the corner

dz-collapse-high-slot.caption: A low zone collapse a beat after the corner battle begins — one of several systems — and the weak-side winger’s collapse is where it succeeds or fails. The centre is the second body in the corner, arriving inside the carrier and not behind them, because that carrier is facing the boards and cannot see the centre coming. The weak-side winger has dropped into the high slot; the strong-side winger holds their point, because if both sag the point-to-point pass gives their defenceman a free walk-in. The weak-side point is briefly unmarked on purpose: this system concedes point shots. The rotation is not available if that winger has already followed their own man down off the point.
dz-collapse-high-slot.describe: The defending half of the rink, the defended net at the right, a beat after the corner battle begins. The opposition: the puck carrier deep in the strong-side corner, a forward on the strong-side half-wall, a forward at the net front, and two defencemen at the points. Our own five are drawn mid-collapse. The centre has arrived on the inside edge of the strong-side corner, about nine feet from the carrier and about the same from the strong-side defenceman, so the carrier now has one of ours below them and one inside them — that is the two on one. The weak-side winger has come down from the weak-side point into the high slot in the middle of the ice. The strong-side winger is still high at their own point, and the weak-side defenceman is still on the doorstep. The opposition defenceman at the weak-side point now has nobody near them. No routes are drawn.
dz-collapse-high-slot.title: Low zone collapse, weak-side winger

dz-walk-down-zone.caption: The walk-down from the point, answered by low zone collapse: the winger follows a few feet and does not chase, so their route ends in a stop, not an arrowhead. The opposing defenceman reaches the top of the circle, about 35 feet from the goal line, untouched. A coaching choice — man-on-man and hybrid teams answer it differently, so find out your team’s version before you need it.
dz-walk-down-zone.describe: The defending half of the rink, the defended net at the right. The opposition defenceman at the strong-side point has the puck and carries it down the ice to the top of the strong-side faceoff circle, about 35 feet from the goal line. Our strong-side winger, who started just goal-side of that defenceman at the point, moves about a dozen feet with them and stops, leaving a clear gap between themselves and the defenceman they have released. The rest of our five have climbed a level with the puck: the centre in the high slot, one defenceman at the net front and the other in the low slot, the weak-side winger on the weak-side point. The opposition have a forward in the strong-side corner, one at the net front and one on the weak-side half-wall, and their other defenceman at the far point. Two numbered routes: one, the walk-down; two, the winger following and stopping.
dz-walk-down-zone.title: Walk-down against low zone collapse

dz-walk-down-man.caption: The walk-down from the point under man-on-man: the winger goes with the carrier, wherever the carrier goes, including into the corner — the sharpest practical difference from low zone collapse. Everybody else is on a body too. A hybrid produces nearly this picture, and the difference is only the trigger, usually the faceoff dots, though some teams draw it at the hash marks or the top of the circles, so learn your team’s. What man coverage costs is a winger in a footrace with no help behind them.
dz-walk-down-man.describe: The defending half of the rink, the defended net at the right, and the same walk-down as the previous diagram. The opposition defenceman carries the puck from the strong-side point down to the top of the strong-side faceoff circle. This time our strong-side winger tracks the carrier the whole way, on a route running a few feet goal-side of the carry and finishing just past it, so the winger ends between their man and the net. Our other four are each within a few feet of an opponent rather than in an area: one defenceman on the forward in the strong-side corner, the other on the forward at the net front, the centre on the forward on the weak-side half-wall, and the weak-side winger on the opposition defenceman at the far point. Two numbered routes: one, the walk-down; two, the winger going with the carrier.
dz-walk-down-man.title: Walk-down against man-on-man

dz-box-plus-one.caption: Box+1, one of several defensive-zone systems: coaching material calls it the standard introductory structure for young players and beginner adults, and nobody publishes a count of what teams actually run. The box’s depth is fixed, its width is not, so read the width drawn here as one reasonable version, not a measurement.
dz-box-plus-one.describe: The defending half of the rink, the defended net at the right. Four of our players stand at the corners of a shaded four-sided region drawn around the slot: two low, one either side of the crease near the posts, and two high and wide at the tops of the two faceoff circles. Our fifth player, marked plus one, is out of the box and up in the strong-side corner on the puck carrier; our goalie is in the crease. The opposition have the carrier in the strong-side corner with the puck, a forward at the net front just outside the low box players, a forward on the weak-side half-wall, and both defencemen at the points with nobody near them. No routes are drawn.
dz-box-plus-one.title: Box+1 defensive-zone coverage

dz-collapsing-box.caption: The collapsing box — a state rather than a full system: as the puck goes below the goal line it shrinks until all five defenders are inside the house, sticks in the passing lanes. It concedes the entire outside by design, the points included, and leaves no breakout speed the moment you win the puck. Teams use it in spots — protecting a lead late, six-on-five against a pulled goalie — not to defend a whole game.
dz-collapsing-box.describe: The defending half of the rink, the defended net at the right, with the shaded house region drawn on the ice. All five of our players stand inside it: two defencemen low, one either side of the crease and about nine feet off the posts, and three forwards above them, one in the high slot and one either side of the slot. Our goalie is in the crease. The opposition have the puck carrier behind the net, a forward in the strong-side corner, a forward on the weak-side half-wall, and both defencemen at the points — all five of them outside the shaded region. Only the carrier behind the net is near anybody, about fourteen feet from our low defenceman; the other four have nobody within twenty feet. No routes are drawn.
dz-collapsing-box.title: The collapsing box

dz-strong-side-overload.caption: The strong-side overload: all five defenders on the puck side, and the weak side unoccupied by design. The dashed route is the counter — the cross-ice pass to the attacker alone at the far post. Some teams use it as their base system, others as a situational squeeze; nobody publishes a count of what teams actually run, so neither is offered here as the commoner one. A coaching choice: find out whether yours plays it, and when.
dz-strong-side-overload.describe: The defending half of the rink, the defended net at the right. The opposition puck carrier is on the strong-side half-wall with a teammate supporting in the strong-side corner, and a third forward is alone at the far post on the weak side of the net. All five of our players are on the puck side of the ice: a defenceman squeezing the carrier from below, a defenceman at the strong side of the net front, the centre inside the carrier, one winger above the carrier cutting off the ice up the wall, and the other winger shifted across into the strong-side high slot. The entire weak side of the zone is empty. One route: a dashed cross-ice pass from the carrier to the attacker at the far post, crossing the slot in front of the crease.
dz-strong-side-overload.title: Strong-side overload coverage

faceoff-dzone-alignment.caption: A defensive-zone draw frozen before the drop, at the right-hand circle. Where everyone stands is a coaching choice, not a rule: this alignment goes with a low zone collapse, so find out what your team runs. The boards-side defenceman stands nearer the boards than their winger, which there is no room to draw. The shaded circle is the rule. The NHL, IIHF and PWHL allow a skate on the line and make crossing it the violation; Hockey Canada and CARHA count a skate on the circle as encroachment; USA Hockey’s Casebook requires all sticks and skates completely behind the hash marks. In the NHL, IIHF and PWHL, contact with an opponent before the drop is itself a violation that usually costs your centre the dot; under Hockey Canada and CARHA, contact by anyone but the taker always does. ⚠️ If you are not taking the draw, keep your skates and stick behind your hash mark, your skates off the circle line, and your hands, body and stick off the opponent and their stick: that satisfies every book.
faceoff-dzone-alignment.describe: The defending half of the rink, your own net at the right, the draw at the right-hand end-zone circle. The faceoff circle is shaded to mark the area no player other than the two takers may put a skate inside. Five own players: the centre in the dot on the goal-line side of it; the boards-side winger level with the dot at the outer hash marks, close to the wall; the inside winger level with the dot at the inner hash marks, about five feet off the middle of the ice; the boards-side defenceman about five feet nearer the goal line than their winger, close to the same wall; the second defenceman in the slot in front of the goalie, who is in the crease. One opposition player is drawn, the opposing centre, on the blue-line side of the dot. The rest of the opposing five are drawn in the offensive-zone diagram instead. No routes: this is a still shape at the moment before the drop.
faceoff-dzone-alignment.title: Defensive-zone draw alignment

faceoff-dzone-alignment-other-circle.caption: The defensive-zone draw alignment at the left-hand end-zone circle instead of the right. Every job is unchanged, and the slot defenceman and the goalie stand in the same place at either circle; what changes is which side of the ice each of the others is on. The alignment is a coaching choice, not a rule — find out what your team runs. The shaded circle is the rule rather than the choice: everyone but the two takers stays outside it. ⚠️ What counts as outside differs by book: the NHL, IIHF and PWHL allow a skate on the line; Hockey Canada and CARHA count a skate on the circle as encroachment; USA Hockey’s Casebook requires all sticks and skates completely behind the hash marks.
faceoff-dzone-alignment-other-circle.describe: The defending half of the rink, your own net at the right, the draw at the left-hand end-zone circle — a mirror image of the alignment at the right-hand circle. The faceoff circle is shaded to mark the area no player other than the two takers may put a skate inside. Five own players: the centre in the dot on the goal-line side of it; the boards-side winger level with the dot at the outer hash marks, close to the wall; the inside winger level with the dot at the inner hash marks, about five feet off the middle of the ice; the boards-side defenceman about five feet nearer the goal line than their winger, close to the same wall; the second defenceman in the slot in front of the goalie, who is in the crease. One opposition player is drawn, the opposing centre, on the blue-line side of the dot. No routes: this is a still shape at the moment before the drop.
faceoff-dzone-alignment-other-circle.title: Defensive-zone alignment at the other circle

faceoff-dzone-clean-loss.caption: A defensive-zone draw lost clean. Both wingers release to the opposing points on the drop rather than after they see where the puck went — the boards-side winger to the near point, the inside winger the harder job, all the way to the far one. That is the zone call: under man-to-man each winger instead takes the specific opponent they were assigned before the draw and follows that opponent, which may mean staying low, and a hybrid keeps the wingers releasing while the low defender stays glued to a body — so ask which one your team plays. Nobody else moves yet: the centre picks up the player who beat them, the slot defenceman holds the net front rather than chasing the puck to the point, and the boards-side defenceman takes the strong-side corner or half-wall.
faceoff-dzone-clean-loss.describe: The defensive-zone draw at the right-hand circle, your own net at the right. Two opposition defencemen have been added at the points, just inside the blue line either side of the middle, and the opposing centre is in the dot. Two routes, both beginning on the drop rather than one after the other: the boards-side winger leaves the outer hash marks and goes straight up the ice to the near point; the inside winger leaves the inner hash marks and goes diagonally across to the far point on the other side of the ice. Each route runs at the defenceman it is going to and stops a few feet short of them, ending in two short bars across the line rather than an arrowhead, because the winger is arriving to take that man rather than skating past. The centre, the slot defenceman and the boards-side defenceman are drawn where the draw left them.
faceoff-dzone-clean-loss.title: Defensive-zone draw, lost clean

faceoff-dzone-tie-up.caption: A defensive-zone draw on a tie-up, which is the most likely of the three outcomes — a coaching estimate rather than a counted figure. A tied-up draw is a loose puck in a two-foot area with eight players around it, and it belongs to whoever moves first. The two arrows are the inside winger and the boards-side defenceman, usually the two closest bodies in this alignment — which is a coaching default rather than a rule, so which two are nearest depends on what your team actually runs. Whoever has eyes on the puck calls it: "Loose!"
faceoff-dzone-tie-up.describe: The defensive-zone draw at the right-hand circle, your own net at the right, at the instant the two centres have tied each other up and the puck is loose on the dot. Two forward-skating routes, both beginning on the drop: the inside winger comes up from the inner hash marks toward the dot, and the boards-side defenceman comes down from the wall toward it. Both finish short of the two centres rather than on them. The boards-side winger, the slot defenceman and the goalie hold their positions in the picture; the instruction is that everyone jumps on a tied-up puck, and the two drawn are the two nearest to it.
faceoff-dzone-tie-up.title: Defensive-zone draw, tied up

faceoff-ozone-alignment.caption: An offensive-zone draw, frozen before the drop, at the circle on your left as you attack. Both defencemen are up at the points — the area just inside the blue line, not the line itself. The draw-side one is the shooter, with their feet already set and their stick already loaded; the far one holds the line as the safety against a counterattack. This is the common default and not a rule; every team’s alignment differs, so ask what yours runs.
faceoff-ozone-alignment.describe: The attacking half of the rink, the opposition net at the right, the draw at the upper end-zone circle, on your left as you attack. Five own players: the centre in the dot on the blue-line side of it; the boards-side winger level with the dot at the outer hash marks, close to the wall; the inside winger level with the dot at the inner hash marks; the strong-side defenceman at the point on the draw side, just inside the blue line; the weak-side defenceman at the far point. Two opposition players are drawn, the opposing centre in the dot and the goalie in the crease; the rest of the defending five are drawn in the defensive-zone diagram instead. No routes: this is a still shape at the moment before the drop.
faceoff-ozone-alignment.title: Offensive-zone draw alignment

faceoff-neutral-zone.caption: A neutral-zone alignment, drawn at centre ice so the whole sheet is visible; you attack to the right. Both wingers are wide in their own lanes, level with or just behind the dot, and both defencemen are back toward their own blue line, one either side of the middle. That depth is the argument for taking risks here: a lost neutral-zone draw costs you almost nothing so long as your defencemen are already gapped up to meet the rush. A coaching default rather than a rule, and every team’s differs.
faceoff-neutral-zone.describe: The full sheet, your own net at the left, attacking to the right. The draw is at the centre dot. Five own players: the centre in the dot on their own side of it; the two wingers wide in their lanes, one either side of the middle and well outside the centre circle, level with or a stride behind the dot; the two defencemen well back, just in front of their own blue line, one either side of the middle of the ice. The own goalie is in the crease at the left. One opposition player is drawn, the opposing centre, on the far side of the dot. No routes: this is a still shape at the moment before the drop.
faceoff-neutral-zone.title: Neutral-zone draw alignment

faceoff-goalie-pulled.caption: An offensive-zone draw with your own goalie pulled for an extra attacker: your own net, at the far end of the picture, is empty. The extra attacker is drawn at the net front; the high slot is their other usual place, and both defencemen are at the points. The centre is under maximum pressure to win it back cleanly, because there is no safe outlet and no recovery from a loss. A goalie may not take part in a faceoff in any case: the NHL and IIHF books both say so in the same words, at Rule 76.1. The alignment is a default rather than a rule, so ask what your team runs with six skaters out.
faceoff-goalie-pulled.describe: The full sheet, attacking to the right, the draw at the upper end-zone circle, on your left, in the attacking zone. Your own net, at the left, has no goalie in it. Six own skaters: the centre in the dot on the blue-line side; the boards-side winger at the outer hash marks; the inside winger at the inner hash marks; the extra attacker at the net front, just outside the crease and off to the draw side; and both defencemen at the points, just inside the attacking blue line. Two opposition players are drawn, the opposing centre in the dot and their goalie in the crease. No routes: this is a still shape at the moment before the drop.
faceoff-goalie-pulled.title: Draw with the goalie pulled

faceoff-where-the-draw-goes.caption: Four common stoppages and where each sends the draw — four separate situations, not one play. Your own end is at the left. At centre ice: the start of every period, and after every goal. In your own end: an icing you caused, or a penalty you took. Only one of the two spots there is boxed, because the rule names the END, not the dot; under the NHL and the IIHF the attacking team — your opponents here — picks which. Outside the blue line you were attacking: an unintentional offside where the puck was carried over. In the end you are attacking: a goalie freeze, or another stoppage your team did not cause between the end-zone dots and the end boards, which the NHL and the IIHF draw at the spot on the side it happened. These four are the common ones, not the whole rule.
faceoff-where-the-draw-goes.describe: The full sheet, your own net at the left and the net you are attacking at the right. No players and no puck are drawn. Four spots are marked with boxes and labelled. One is the centre dot, labelled "after a goal". One is the upper end-zone faceoff spot in your own end, labelled "icing or penalty". One is the upper neutral-zone dot just outside the blue line you were attacking, labelled "carried offside". One is the lower end-zone faceoff spot in the end you are attacking, labelled "goalie freeze". Each label sits a few feet to one side of the spot it marks rather than on top of it.
faceoff-where-the-draw-goes.title: Where the draw goes
