faceoff-strong-side-dot.caption: Which of the two circles in your own end is your strong side. The same centre makes the same backhand pull at each circle: at one it sends the puck toward the boards, at the other toward the middle, and a defensive-zone draw won into the slot is barely better than a loss. Only some books give a team the choice of dot: the NHL and the IIHF to the attacking team, USA Hockey none at all, and Hockey Canada only after an icing or a time penalty, only in Junior and Senior divisions, and only to the attacking non-offending team, which loses it unless it tells the referee the dot it wants before the line change procedure starts (Rule 6.4(b)). No handedness is drawn here, so read none into it.
faceoff-strong-side-dot.describe: The defending half of the rink, your own net and goalie at the right, both end-zone circles visible. The same centre is drawn at both dots, each time on the goal-line side of the spot with an opposing centre facing them on the far side of it. From each of the two own centres a dashed line with an arrowhead runs back and across at the same angle, showing the puck pulled backwards. From the upper circle it finishes out toward the side boards; from the lower circle the identical line finishes in open ice toward the middle, in front of the net. No other skaters are drawn.
faceoff-strong-side-dot.title: Your strong-side circle

faceoff-ozone-d-one-timer.caption: The D one-timer, a beat after the drop. The shot’s line to the net runs straight through the inner hash marks, where the inside winger stands for the draw, so on the drop they step out of it, and they are drawn here already out of it. Where they go next is not drawn. All of it is a coaching choice and not a rule of hockey — find out what your team runs, and what the call is, before your first shift.
faceoff-ozone-d-one-timer.describe: The attacking half of the rink, the opposition net and goalie at the right, the draw at the upper end-zone circle, on your left as you attack. Five own players: the centre in the dot on the blue-line side; the boards-side winger at the outer hash marks; the inside winger below the dot line and off to one side of the middle, clear of the shooting lane; and both defencemen at the points just inside the blue line. The opposing centre is on the far side of the dot, and their goalie is in the crease. Two routes. A dashed line runs from the centre in the dot back up the ice to the strong-side defenceman at the near point, stopping short of them. A double line — a shot — runs from that defenceman down to the front of the net, passing about eleven feet clear of the inside winger. No route is drawn for any other player.
faceoff-ozone-d-one-timer.title: Offensive-zone draw back to the point

faceoff-ozone-winger-walkout.caption: The winger walk-out off an offensive-zone draw; whether the winger then shoots or feeds the slot is not drawn, because the picture stops where the choice begins. Both defencemen stay at the points, one of them as the safety against a counterattack. Every part of this is a coaching choice rather than a rule of hockey, and which play is on is a call rather than an individual read — ask what your team’s are.
faceoff-ozone-winger-walkout.describe: The attacking half of the rink, the opposition net and goalie at the right, the draw at the upper end-zone circle, on your left as you attack, and the same five own players as the offensive-zone alignment: the centre in the dot on the blue-line side, the boards-side winger at the outer hash marks, the inside winger at the inner hash marks, and both defencemen at the points. The opposing centre is on the far side of the dot, and their goalie is in the crease. Two numbered routes. First, a dashed line runs from the centre in the dot down to the inside winger, stopping about six feet short of them. Second, a plain line with an arrowhead takes that winger about nine feet toward the middle of the ice, finishing level with the middle. Neither defenceman has a route: they hold the points, and nothing is drawn going to the net.
faceoff-ozone-winger-walkout.title: Offensive-zone draw to the inside winger

forecheck-angling.caption: The skill every forecheck here assumes: skate at the space you want to deny, not at the puck. One forechecker comes in from the weak side, along the goal line toward a carrier retrieving behind their own net, to take that side away and leave the strong-side wall as the carrier’s only route. No contact is drawn, because the aim is to eliminate options rather than land a hit. Which side to take away is a coaching choice, not a rule — the common default takes the middle, some coaches invert it, so find out which your team plays before your first shift.
forecheck-angling.describe: Attacking half of the rink, the opposition net at the right. Three players: the goalie in the crease, their defenceman behind the net with the puck, and one forechecker on the goal line below them, a little nearer centre ice. A short route runs from the forechecker along the goal line toward the net, finishing just below the bottom post, well short of the defenceman. No route is drawn for the defenceman and no contact is shown.
forecheck-angling.title: Angling the retrieval

forecheck-roles-rotate.caption: Drawn just after the opponents pass it defenceman to defenceman. The letter in each glyph is the role just taken; the label beside it is the role held a second earlier. The shape is this guide's default 2-1-2; a lock system pins one winger to the third job instead, so ask which your team runs. The defencemen hold the offensive blue line and do not rotate. Find out first whether you may body check in this game at all — it can change per fixture, not just per division. It is commonly barred at younger ages, in girls' and women's hockey and in non-check adult leagues. Being the new F1 is not a licence to go through the carrier. The new carrier is about to turn their back to you, so the onus is on you. ⚠️ Take the puck, take the ice, or angle them off it, and never finish into their back.
forecheck-roles-rotate.describe: Attacking half of the rink, the opposition net at the right, and the same five opposition players as the forecheck diagrams: the defenceman D1 behind the net, who has just passed; their partner D2 taking that pass in the corner at the bottom of the picture (your right as you attack); the wingers W1 and W2 on the two half-walls; and the goalie in the crease. Five own players. The three forwards are labelled twice over — the letters inside the glyphs are the roles they have just taken and the words beside them are the roles they held before the pass. Deep beside the net toward the top of the picture, the side the pass left from, stands the forward marked F3, labelled "was F1, beaten", with an arrow taking them up ice towards the high middle. Down toward the bottom of the picture, near the new carrier, stands the forward marked F1, labelled "was F2, closest", with a short route ending in two bars up ice of the new carrier and on their inside, toward the middle, short of them and pointed past them rather than at them. In the high middle stands the forward marked F2, labelled "was F3, high", with an arrow taking them down and across toward the bottom of the picture. The two defencemen are on the offensive blue line at the points, with no routes at all. A dashed pass runs from behind the net, round the back of the goal, to the corner at the bottom of the picture.
forecheck-roles-rotate.title: The roles rotate mid-shift

forecheck-212.caption: A 2-1-2 forecheck as the opposing defenceman retrieves the puck behind the net. F1 arrives from the weak side and angles the carrier towards the strong-side wall; F2 attacks the first passing option rather than the puck; F3 stays high in the middle at the top of the circles; both defencemen hold the offensive blue line. It is one system among several, and which way F1 angles and which side F3 sits on are coaching choices, not rules: ask which your team runs. The picture does not show how a forechecker finishes an angle, which is treated separately. Find out first whether you may body check in this game — the answer can change per fixture, not just per division. It is commonly barred at younger ages, in girls' and women's hockey and in non-check adult leagues. ⚠️ Go hard at the carrier, never through them. They are about to turn their back to you, so the onus is on you: take the puck, take the ice, or angle them off it, and never finish into their back.
forecheck-212.describe: Attacking half of the rink, the opposition net at the right. Four opposition players: the defenceman D1 behind the net with the puck; the partner D2 low on the weak side, the reverse option; the winger W1 on the strong-side half-wall, the first passing option; the winger W2 on the weak-side half-wall; and the goalie in the crease. Five own players: F1 deep on the weak side at the goal line, F2 deep inside the strong-side circle, F3 high in the middle at the top of the circles, and two defencemen on the offensive blue line. Four numbered routes: one, F1 takes the weak side away; two, the carrier skates the puck out to the strong-side wall; three, F2 attacks the passing lane; four, the first pass to W1. The opposition centre is not drawn.
forecheck-212.title: The 2-1-2 forecheck

forecheck-212-stacked.caption: The stacked, or strong-side, 2-1-2: F1 and F2 come from the same side to overload one corner, and F3 shades to the puck side too, so all three forwards are on one half of the ice. The cost is drawn too: the far-side breakout, conceded on purpose. Which version your team runs is a coaching call, so find out. Two forwards in one corner is not a licence to go through the player in it. The carrier is behind their own net and about to turn their back to you, so the onus is on you. ⚠️ Take the puck, take the ice, or angle them off it, and never finish into their back.
forecheck-212-stacked.describe: Attacking half of the rink, the opposition net at the right, and the same five opposition players as the other forecheck diagrams: the defenceman D1 behind the net with the puck, the partner D2 low on the far side, the wingers W1 and W2 on the two half-walls, and the goalie in the crease. Five own players, all three forwards on the strong side: F1 deep at the goal line towards the strong-side corner, F2 deep inside the strong-side circle, F3 high but shaded across to the strong side rather than sitting in the middle, and both defencemen on the offensive blue line at the two points. One route: the carrier taking the puck out around the back of the net to the far corner, the escape the shape concedes. The whole weak side of the ice below the net is empty of own players.
forecheck-212-stacked.title: The stacked 2-1-2

forecheck-122.caption: The 1-2-2, same carrier as the 2-1-2: one forward deep, two across the middle, two defencemen high. Dog, fox and hawk on F1, F2 and F3 are a memory hook, not standard terms. The system itself, the side F1 cuts off and where the weak-side defenceman sits are coaching choices, so ask which your team runs. F2 is drawn arriving at the wall, not at the winger. In most books a call for checking from behind ends your game every time, in every book it can, and under USA Hockey it must whenever it is forceful at the boards, sends them head first into the boards or net, or is reckless. ⚠️ If your game allows body checking, the arriving player carries the whole onus: take the puck, take the ice, or angle them off it, and never finish into the back of a player facing away. In IIHF women's hockey, never use the boards on an opponent.
forecheck-122.describe: Attacking half of the rink, the opposition net at the right. The same five opposition players as the 2-1-2 diagram: the defenceman D1 behind the net with the puck, the partner D2 low on the far side as the D-to-D reset, the wingers W1 and W2 on the two half-walls, and the goalie in the crease. Five own players in three bands: F1 alone deep, inside the strong-side faceoff dot; F2 up the strong-side wall and F3 in the high middle, level with each other around the top of the circles; and both defencemen on the offensive blue line, the strong-side one at the point and the weak-side one shaded into the middle. Three numbered routes: one, the carrier picks the puck up unmolested and carries it out to the strong-side wall; two, F2 jumps down the wall onto the outlet; three, the outlet pass to W1. F1 is drawn with no route.
forecheck-122.title: The 1-2-2 forecheck

forecheck-131.caption: The 1-3-1 pushed up into the offensive zone: one forward pressuring, three flat across the ice, one last man behind. F1 steers rather than chases, and the line shifts with the puck, its puck-side player becoming a second attacker. F2 is drawn arriving at the wall, not at the winger. In most books a call for checking from behind ends your game every time, in every book it can, and under USA Hockey it must whenever it is forceful at the boards, sends them head first into the boards or net, or is reckless. ⚠️ If your game allows body checking, the arriving player carries the whole onus: take the puck, take the ice, or angle them off it, and never finish into the back of a player facing away. In IIHF women's hockey, never use the boards on an opponent.
forecheck-131.describe: Attacking half of the rink, the opposition net at the right, and the same five opposition players as the other forecheck diagrams. Five own players in three bands: F1 alone deep, inside the strong-side faceoff dot; then a flat line of three at the top of the circles — F2 on the strong-side wall, a defenceman in the middle of the ice, F3 on the far wall, all three at exactly the same depth; then the second defenceman alone on the offensive blue line in the middle, as the safety behind them. Three unnumbered routes, because they happen together: F2 becomes the immediate second attacker, stepping out to the strong-side wall, and the defenceman in the middle and F3 on the far wall both slide laterally towards the puck side. F1 is drawn with no route.
forecheck-131.title: The 1-3-1 forecheck

forecheck-2-3-lock.caption: The 2-3 lock. The third forward’s arrow stops short of the blue line because they slide into line only if the puck is not won; the lane they fill is a coaching detail. Some teams lock whichever winger is highest rather than always the left. This guide's default is a 2-1-2, so ask which your team plays. ⚠️ Find out first whether you may body check in this game at all — it can change per fixture, not just per division.
forecheck-2-3-lock.describe: Attacking half of the rink, the opposition net at the right, and the same five opposition players as the other forecheck diagrams: the defenceman D1 behind the net with the puck, the partner D2 low in the far corner, the wingers W1 and W2 on the two half-walls, and the goalie in the crease. Five own players in two groups rather than three: F1 deep at the goal line on the puck side and F2 deep inside the puck-side circle, the two who forecheck; and behind them the two defencemen on the offensive blue line at the two points. The third forward, F3, is the odd one out. They stand on the top wall (your left as you attack, and the puck side), nearer the blue line than the opposing winger there, out of the attack, and a single arrow runs from them diagonally back up the ice, finishing short of the blue line between the two defencemen. Nobody else is drawn with a route.
forecheck-2-3-lock.title: The left-wing lock

forecheck-press.caption: The full-ice press: all three forwards deep and both defencemen stepping down from the offensive blue line. Both defencemen going is a called situation, not your own read; the common default is one at a time. In many leagues body checking is not allowed at all, so find out whether you may body check in this game, not just in your division. ⚠️ In every league, checking or not, never turn your back to anyone coming at you on the wall, and never duck. Head up, chin off your chest, and take any contact on your forearm and hip, never the point of your shoulder.
forecheck-press.describe: Attacking half of the rink, the opposition net at the right, and the same five opposition players as the other forecheck diagrams: the defenceman D1 behind the net with the puck, the partner D2 low in the far corner, the wingers W1 and W2 on the two half-walls, and the goalie in the crease. Five own players, all of them below the top of the circles or heading there: F1 deep at the goal line on the puck side, F2 deep inside the puck-side circle, and F3 deep as well on the far side rather than high in the middle. Both defencemen are drawn at the offensive blue line in the act of leaving it, each with an arrow running down its own wall towards the boards. The entire middle of the picture behind them, from the blue line back, is empty of own players.
forecheck-press.title: Forwards deep, both defencemen stepping down

forecheck-pinch.caption: The pinch, inside a 2-1-2: their defenceman rims the puck up the wall, your strong-side defenceman steps down to kill it, and F3 leaves the high middle to cover the point. The test for going is "if you can't arrive on contact, don't go": you and the puck reach the wall together. On a dying rim with nobody to seal, arrive clearly first or hold the line. The weak-side defenceman stays in the middle, so a failed pinch is a two-on-one, not a breakaway. F3 covering is a common choice, not a law; some teams slide the weak-side defenceman across instead, so ask which yours is. Find out whether you may body check in this game, not just in your division. Where it is barred, a pinch is a play on the puck, not a check. ⚠️ In every league, checking or not, never turn your back to anyone coming at you on the wall, and never duck. Head up, chin off your chest, and take any contact on your forearm and hip, never the point of your shoulder.
forecheck-pinch.describe: Attacking half of the rink, the opposition net at the right, with the puck in the strong-side corner. Three opposition players: the defenceman D1 in the corner rimming the puck up the wall, their far winger W2 already high on the weak side heading for the exit, and the goalie. Five own players in a 2-1-2: F1 deep, sealing the strong-side corner; F2 deep inside the strong-side circle; F3 high in the middle at the top of the circles; the strong-side defenceman at the offensive blue line; and the weak-side defenceman at the line but shaded into the middle of the ice. Three numbered routes: one, the rim travelling up the boards outside everybody; two, the strong-side defenceman stepping down the wall to meet it, the two arrows finishing about ten feet apart and pointing at each other; three, F3 leaving the high middle for the vacated point, stopping short of the defenceman who is still drawn on it.
forecheck-pinch.title: The pinch from the point

six-on-five-shape.caption: The most common 6-on-5 shape, your goalie pulled for a sixth attacker. The five defenders are not drawn, and your own net is empty at the far end. Which shape, and who stands where, is your team's choice — an umbrella, an overload, or a net-front body added to your power-play look — so learn yours in practice.
six-on-five-shape.describe: The attacking half of the rink, the opposition net at the right and their goalie in the crease. Six own players and no defenders. Two stand at the points, up at the blue-line end of the zone, one either side of the middle and about forty feet apart: one is drawn as a defenceman, the other as a forward. Two more stand on the boards level with the faceoff dots, one on each side of the zone. One stands at the net front, just outside the crease and a little to one side of it. The sixth stands below the goal line, off the post on the other side of the net from the net-front player. No routes are drawn: this is a shape, not a sequence. Your own goal, empty, is at the far end of the ice and outside this picture.
six-on-five-shape.title: Six-on-five shape

six-on-five-one-point-stays.caption: A 6-on-5 with your goalie pulled, at the moment one point man steps down the wall to keep a puck in and the other does not go with them. The point men do not both pinch. Your own net is empty at the far end, so a puck past both of them is a clear path to it, not a rush against you. Which point man pinches, whether your team pinches at all with the goalie out, and who is standing at the points are coaching choices and not laws of hockey, so find out what your team wants before the goalie leaves. No contact is drawn. The route ends in two bars on a patch of the wall, not on a player. ⚠️ What an arrival like that may end in depends on whether your league allows body checking at all.
six-on-five-one-point-stays.describe: The attacking half of the rink, the opposition net at the right and their goalie in the crease. The six own players stand in the same 6-on-5 shape as the previous diagram: two at the points, two on the half-walls level with the faceoff dots, one at the net front and one below the goal line. One opposition skater has the puck on the wall at the top of the picture, about twenty feet up-ice of the own player on that half-wall. A single route runs from the point man at the top of the picture down and out toward the wall, ending in two bars — arrive and contain — on a patch of boards up-ice of the opposition skater and about nine feet clear of them. The point man at the bottom of the picture has no route at all: they are standing still, and that is the point of the picture. Their other four skaters are not drawn, and your own net, empty, is at the far end of the ice and outside this picture.
six-on-five-one-point-stays.title: One point stays home

five-on-six-clear-three-outcomes.caption: With their net empty, a loose puck reaches you in your end. Every clear is a shot: three endings. On target, it is a goal, not icing. A miss that crosses their goal line untouched from your side of the centre red line is icing. NHL and IIHF Rule 81.4 then lets you change only for an injured player or a penalty that changes the strength (the IIHF's also names a broken skate, which its 82.1 omits, so do not count on it). Rule 81.4's goalie exception lets a team put back its own pulled goalie, and yours is in your net. Hockey Canada bars changes after icing only in U18AAA, Junior and, at the Member’s option, Senior (Rule 6.7(d)), so find out which rules your league runs. A blind clear to their point man hands it straight back. ⚠️ You can be iced against a pulled goalie.
five-on-six-clear-three-outcomes.describe: The full sheet. Your own net is at the left with your goalie in the crease; the opposition net at the right is empty, with no goalie drawn. One own player has the puck deep in your own end, inside the faceoff circle at the top of the picture and up toward the boards. One opposition defenceman stands at the point on the bottom side of the ice, up at the blue-line end of your own zone. Three routes leave the puck carrier, and all three are drawn as shots in the double-line notation. One runs the length of the ice and finishes inside the empty net. The second runs the length of the ice beside it and finishes past the goal line, well wide of the net and out toward the corner. The third is much shorter and goes up-ice and across the zone, finishing just in front of the opposition point man. Their other five skaters and your other four are not drawn.
five-on-six-clear-three-outcomes.title: Clearing at five on six

delayed-penalty-your-own-net.caption: A delayed penalty, drawn in your own defending end — so the net in this picture is yours, and it is empty, because your goalie has already gone to the bench for a sixth attacker. The team to be penalised can only score off your own team's play, so the pass that can beat you is a defenceman-to-defenceman pass across the front of your own goal, and it is deliberately not drawn. The single route drawn is that same pass made the safe way, out and around behind your own net. Only the opponent nearest the puck is drawn. And check before the game rather than in it: not every league allows or practises pulling the goalie on a delayed call, and some officials stop play early. How many is a question about leagues rather than about rulebooks, and no count of it is given here.
delayed-penalty-your-own-net.describe: Your own defending end, your net at the right. The goal crease is empty — no goalie is drawn in it, and the crease itself carries the words "no goalie" across it. One of your defencemen has the puck low in the right-hand corner; your other defenceman is across in the left-hand corner. A single opposition forward is in the right corner as well, inside the puck carrier and toward the middle of the ice. One dashed passing route leaves the puck carrier and runs to the other defenceman. It curves out and around the back of the goal, running four to six feet past the goal line for the whole of its middle third and never entering the crease. No route is drawn across the front of the goal, deliberately: the pass across your own goal mouth is described in words and not drawn. The route is not numbered. No other players are drawn, and no region is shaded.
delayed-penalty-your-own-net.title: Delayed penalty, your own net

ot-3-on-3-regroup.caption: Three-on-three overtime. You are inside their blue line with no high-quality look, so rather than force a shot you turn and take the puck back out through the neutral zone — the long wave running to your own side of centre ice — to reset and come again. All six skaters are drawn, and both goalies are in their creases. Two things this picture is not: Rule 84.1 gives each side three skaters and one goalie and says nothing about who they are, so the two forwards and one defenceman a side drawn here are a team’s choice and not the format; and how the format is played is the account coaches and players give of it rather than a rule of hockey. This is NHL regular-season overtime, and the format you actually play may not be it — in many British fixtures there is no overtime at all.
ot-3-on-3-regroup.describe: The full sheet. Your own net is at the left with your goalie in the crease; the opposition net is at the right with their goalie in theirs. Three own skaters and three opposition skaters are drawn and no more, which is the whole strength of both teams here. Your puck carrier, a forward, is about twelve feet inside the opposition blue line on the upper side of the ice, with the puck drawn just below them on the up-ice side, away from the checker. All three opposition skaters are between the carrier and their own net: a forward inside the carrier and a little deeper, a defenceman in the middle of the ice halfway to the tops of the circles, and a second forward on the far side at the top of the far faceoff circle. Your two supports are spread rather than stacked: a forward wide and low in the neutral zone on the far side, and a defenceman back inside your own blue line. One route is drawn, the long smooth wave with an arrowhead that means skate and stickhandle: it leaves the carrier, curves back out of the offensive zone and across the neutral zone, and finishes past centre ice on your own side and outside the centre circle, pointing back toward your own end. Nobody else has a route.
ot-3-on-3-regroup.title: The three-on-three regroup

goalie-playing-the-angle.caption: An opposition shooter at the top of the faceoff circle on the goalie’s right, with no pass available. The shaded wedge is every straight path from that puck into the net. The goalie is standing on the line from the puck to the exact centre of the goal line, at a depth every goalie coach will adjust — so read it as an example of the read rather than a measured instruction.
goalie-playing-the-angle.describe: The defending half of the rink, the defended net at the right. One opposition forward stands at the top of the faceoff circle on the goalie’s right (the top of the picture), with the puck just off the blade toward the net. A shaded triangle runs from the puck to the two goalposts, narrowing from the width of the net at the goal line to a point at the puck. The goalie stands inside that triangle on its centre line, six feet out from the middle of the goal line, so slightly to the shooter’s side of the middle of the net rather than square in the goalmouth. No other players are drawn: the read this illustrates is the one with no pass available, and drawing a second attacker would change it into a different read.
goalie-playing-the-angle.title: Goalie playing the angle

goalie-front-door-back-door.caption: A strong-side shooter, and a second attacker unmarked on the far side of the net — the back door. With a pass available across the slot the read is to back off rather than challenge, and the goalie has. How far is a judgement made situation by situation: the trade is the front door against the back door, and there is no universally correct answer.
goalie-front-door-back-door.describe: The defending half of the rink, the defended net at the right. An opposition forward has the puck just inside the faceoff dot on the goalie’s right (the top of the picture). A second opposition forward stands unmarked on the far side of the net, five feet out from the goal line and clear of the crease. A dashed line — the notation for a pass — shows the pass available across the slot, running from the puck toward that attacker and stopping well short of them. The goalie stands on the line from the puck to the centre of the goal line, four feet out, nearer the goal line than the top of the crease. No defenders are drawn; the point of the picture is the goalie’s depth decision and the space behind them.
goalie-front-door-back-door.title: Front door and back door

goalie-angle-closes-wide.caption: The puck has gone wide and low, level with the goal line, and the goalie has come back to the near post. Out there the angle closes on its own, so depth buys nothing and only leaves you unable to get back. End the lateral movement at the post rather than a foot short of it — and note that closing the low short side leaves the space over your shoulder still open.
goalie-angle-closes-wide.describe: The defending half of the rink, the defended net at the right. An opposition forward has the puck level with the goal line, about fourteen feet from the net toward the top of the picture, which is the goalie’s right, between the net and the boards. The goalie is at the near post, on the goal line rather than out at the top of the crease, and tight against the post rather than standing a foot off it. No other players are drawn, and no movement is drawn: the picture is one position on the goalie’s arc, not the journey to it.
goalie-angle-closes-wide.title: Goalie on a wide, low puck

goalie-depth-failure-modes.caption: The same goalie drawn twice against one shooter: too deep, with the corners open, and too far out — level with the hash marks, about twenty feet from the goal line. Neither is a position to play from.
goalie-depth-failure-modes.describe: The defending half of the rink, the defended net at the right. One opposition forward stands at the top of the faceoff circle on the goalie’s right (the top of the picture), with the puck. Two goalie glyphs are drawn on the line from that puck to the centre of the goal line, representing the same goalie at two extremes rather than two players. The first is two feet out, effectively in the goalmouth, labelled too deep. The second is twenty feet out, level with the hash marks of that same faceoff circle and out in the slot, labelled too far out. Nothing is drawn between them, because where the goalie should be is a situation-by-situation read rather than a fixed spot.
goalie-depth-failure-modes.title: Goalie too deep, goalie too far out

goalie-safe-outlets.caption: You have the puck behind your own net and three of your five options are drawn, ranked by risk: the short pass to your defenceman on the wall, the rim around the boards to the far winger, and the one to make almost never — the pass into the shaded slot, where a goalie’s turnover is a shot on an empty net you are standing in. Not drawn: leaving it for a defenceman with time, and clearing along the glass rather than over it. Whether you play the puck at all is your team’s convention rather than a law. Ask, and then be consistent.
goalie-safe-outlets.describe: The defending half of the rink, the defended net at the right, with the goalie standing behind their own net and the puck just beside them. Three dashed lines — the notation for a pass — leave the puck. One runs up the boards at the top of the picture to a defenceman of yours standing on the wall level with the goal line, stopping short of them. One curves around the back of the net and down the far boards toward one of your forwards on the far half-wall, again stopping short. The third arcs over the top of the net and into a shaded region labelled "the slot", shaded as a warning rather than as a target. No opponents are drawn, and no route is drawn for the other two of the five options.
goalie-safe-outlets.title: Outlets from behind your net

goalie-rim-stop-or-clear.caption: A puck rimmed hard around the boards is coming behind your net, and the shaded area is the trapezoid that the NHL and IIHF books mark — the area behind the goal line inside which you are allowed to play it. Follow the rim: it crosses the goal line well outside that area, and only then comes into it. Inside, kill it dead and leave it for your defenceman. Out where it crossed the line, get out of the way and let them have it. In Britain, whether England Ice Hockey’s rule suspending the trapezoid still stands, and where, is unsettled. Assume the trapezoid binds, ask your league, and look behind the net to see whether the lines are painted.
goalie-rim-stop-or-clear.describe: The defending half of the rink, the defended net at the right. The area behind the goal line between the two red trapezoid lines is shaded. A dashed line — the notation for a pass — starts high on the boards at the top of the picture, in front of the goal line, and curves around the end boards behind the net, crossing the goal line far out near the boards and outside the shaded area, then running into it and stopping short of the goalie, who stands behind their own net inside the shaded area. One defenceman of yours is coming back on the far side of the net. No opponents are drawn.
goalie-rim-stop-or-clear.title: The rim: stop it or clear it

goalie-breakaway-retreat.caption: A breakaway: the goalie meets the shooter well out and backs in on C-cuts at their speed, keeping the angle closed and staying on their feet. "Well out" is a read rather than a distance. No figure is given for it, so the position drawn is an example.
goalie-breakaway-retreat.describe: The defending half of the rink, the defended net at the right. One opposition forward carries the puck out of the neutral zone toward the net, drawn as a long smooth wave — the notation for skating with the puck — ending well short of the goalie. The goalie is drawn out in front of their net, about eleven feet from the centre of the goal line and on the line from the puck to that centre. A run of flattened arches — the notation for backward skating, the goalie’s C-cuts — leads from them back along that same line to a point three feet out, inside the crease. No other players are drawn: a breakaway is one attacker and you.
goalie-breakaway-retreat.title: Goalie facing a breakaway

goalie-tip-from-the-point.caption: A shot coming from the point with an opposition forward set in the shooting lane, blade on the ice. Two things the picture cannot show. The forward is drawn further out than they would really stand, because two glyphs will not fit in the few feet of real ice between a tipper and a goalie. And the goalie’s depth is a consequence of what fits on the page rather than an instruction, because how deep to play a screened shot from distance is a genuine coaching split — so ask which one your coach teaches.
goalie-tip-from-the-point.describe: The defending half of the rink, the defended net at the right. An opposition defenceman stands at the point on the goalie’s right with the puck. A double line — the notation for a shot — runs from the puck toward the net and stops part of the way there. An opposition forward stands on that line about thirteen feet out from the goal line, in the shooting lane and clear of the crease. The goalie is on the same line, inside the crease, a little under three feet out from the centre of the goal line. No defenders of yours are drawn: the player who would move that forward is not part of what this picture is about.
goalie-tip-from-the-point.title: Point shot with a tip threat

goalie-rebound-corners-not-slot.caption: A shot is on its way from the point, and an opposition forward is standing in the shaded slot waiting for what comes off you. A save that puts a rebound into that area has converted a shot from distance into a shot from six feet. When you cannot absorb the puck you have to aim it, and the target is the corners — wide and low toward the boards, named in words here because only the area to avoid is marked. Know who is where before the shot, and be specific about it.
goalie-rebound-corners-not-slot.describe: The defending half of the rink, the defended net at the right. An opposition defenceman stands at the point on the goalie’s left with the puck, and a double line — the notation for a shot — runs from it toward the net, stopping about nine feet short of the goalie. The goalie is on the line from that puck to the centre of the goal line, six feet out. An opposition forward stands in the slot on the other side of the centre line, inside a shaded region labelled "the slot" and shaded as a warning rather than as a target. No rebound is drawn, and no corner is shaded.
goalie-rebound-corners-not-slot.title: Steering rebounds away from the slot

goalie-fifty-fifty-puck.caption: A loose puck in the corner, you out of your net for it, and the forechecker closer to it than you are — so look at where your net is. That empty net is what losing a fifty-fifty race costs. The puck is in front of the goal line, so the trapezoid is not in play; this picture is only about the race.
goalie-fifty-fifty-puck.describe: The defending half of the rink, the defended net at the right, and the net has nobody in it. A loose puck sits in the corner at the top of the picture, in front of the goal line. The goalie is drawn out of their crease and part of the way to it, about six feet away. An opposition forward is arriving at the same puck from the other side and is slightly closer to it than the goalie is. No routes are drawn, and nothing marks who wins the race: the point of the picture is the distance between the goalie and their own empty net.
goalie-fifty-fifty-puck.title: The fifty-fifty puck

nz-1-2-2-containment.caption: A 1-2-2 neutral zone structure, frozen as the opposing defence starts its breakout: one forward pressuring deep in the opponents’ end, two forwards across the middle third, and both defencemen holding the back layer at your own blue line. The layers are named from the puck outward. F1 takes the middle away and shows the carrier one side rather than hunting the puck, so the first pass is conceded by design. F2 steps up to meet the puck on the wall, stick first, and never into the receiver’s body or back. Whether a hit may follow once they have the puck depends on whether your game allows body checking. Every neutral-zone structure is a coaching choice, not a law — find out which one your team plays.
nz-1-2-2-containment.describe: The full sheet. Our own net is at the left, the opponents’ net at the right, and the opponents are breaking out from right to left. Three opposition players and their goalie: the defenceman D1 behind their net with the puck, D1’s partner D2 in the far corner as the D-to-D option, and the winger W1 on the strong-side wall just inside their blue line. Our five: F1 at the opponents’ goal line on the weak side; F2 and F3 side by side across the middle third just inside the opposing blue line, F2 on the strong-side wall and F3 in the middle; and both defencemen on our own blue line, the strong-side one in the dot lane and the weak-side one nearer the middle. Three numbered routes: one, F1 curves across behind the net taking the middle and the D-to-D away; two, the conceded first pass out to the winger on the wall; three, F2 steps up to meet the puck as it reaches that winger, arriving on the winger’s inside to play the puck rather than the player. The opposition centre, who can beat this structure by supporting low under F2 and F3, is not drawn.
nz-1-2-2-containment.title: 1-2-2 neutral zone containment

nz-1-2-2-trap.caption: The 1-2-2 trap, layers dropped back: F1 just inside their blue line still splits the ice, F2 and F3 sit at the red line on the walls, and the defence holds your own blue line. The carrier is steered to a wall, into F2 stepping up with the strong-side defenceman behind and no lane through the middle. Depth is the tell a still frame can show; whether F1 is closing or gliding is not.
nz-1-2-2-trap.describe: The full sheet, our net at the left and the opponents’ at the right, with the opponents attacking right to left. One opposition defenceman carries the puck out of their zone; both goalies are shown. Our five: F1 alone just inside the opponents’ blue line in the middle of the ice; F2 and F3 level with each other at the centre red line, one on each wall; both defencemen on our own blue line, the strong-side one behind F2. Two routes: the carrier’s way out, curving toward the wall they are being steered to, and F2 stepping up as the carrier reaches the red line, finishing on the carrier’s inside rather than at them. F1 is drawn with no route at all, because in a trap F1 is not closing. Only the carrier is drawn of the opposition’s five skaters; this is not a five-on-one.
nz-1-2-2-trap.title: 1-2-2 neutral zone trap

nz-1-3-1.caption: A 1-3-1 in the neutral zone: F1 pressuring alone, three players spread flat across the width of the ice, and a single defenceman behind them as the last man. Conventionally the three are F2 and F3 on the walls with a defenceman in the middle as the read-maker, and some coaches invert that; what does not happen is three forwards across, because F1 is already one of your three. They slide as a unit toward the puck and their job is to leave no lane through them. This is not the power play 1-3-1, which is a different shape in a different zone.
nz-1-3-1.describe: The full sheet, our net at the left, the opponents’ at the right, opponents attacking right to left. One opposition defenceman carries the puck out on the side at the top of the picture; both goalies are shown. Our five in three rows: F1 alone in the middle of the ice just inside the opponents’ blue line; then F2 on one wall, a defenceman in the middle and F3 on the other wall, all three level with each other just inside the centre red line and spanning the width of the sheet; then a single defenceman alone on our own blue line, in the middle. Three short parallel arrows show the three-player line sliding as a unit toward the side the puck is on. There is deliberately open ice between the three-player line and our own blue line: that is the ice a stretch pass is aimed into. Only the carrier is drawn of the opposition’s five skaters; this is not a five-on-one.
nz-1-3-1.title: 1-3-1 neutral zone structure

nz-1-4.caption: A 1-4, the most conservative structure in hockey: one forechecker, and four skaters in a flat line across your own blue line. The answer drawn is a hard chip past the flat line and a race for the puck, because nobody in a flat line is deeper than anybody else. If the goalie comes out for the puck, pull up rather than finish on them. A stretch pass cannot beat a 1-4: a line held on its own blue line leaves no legal ice behind it, and a receiver already back there is offside the moment the puck crosses. Which skater takes which lane is one arrangement and not a rule.
nz-1-4.describe: The full sheet, our net at the left. Four of our skaters stand in a flat line across our own blue line, evenly spread from wall to wall, with the two defencemen in the middle two lanes and two forwards outside them; the fifth, F1, stands alone near the centre red line. Both goalies are shown. Two opposition forwards have come past F1 and are approaching the flat line, one with the puck and one behind them. Two numbered routes: one, the chip put through the gap between two of the four into the space behind the line; two, the second attacker’s race through the same gap to get to it first, starting from behind the puck so that they are onside when it crosses. There is no opposition receiver drawn waiting behind the line, because there cannot legally be one, and the other three opposition skaters are not drawn either.
nz-1-4.title: 1-4 neutral zone structure

nz-pressure.caption: The neutral zone behind an aggressive forecheck: with two forwards gone hunting the puck in the opponents’ end, F3 is the only layer in front of your defence. F3 holds the middle; the strong-side defenceman closes the gap fast on a pass to the wall; the weak-side defenceman stays back as the last safety. Beat the two forecheckers with one pass and F3 is alone against three — a choice for when you are chasing a goal, not a default. The strong-side defenceman’s step-up goes to the puck, stick first, not the receiver’s body. Whether that may end in a hit once the puck has arrived depends on whether your game allows body checking.
nz-pressure.describe: The full sheet, our net at the left, the opponents’ at the right. Deep in the opponents’ end, two of our forwards pressure their defenceman, who has the puck in the corner; their winger has come up the wall into the neutral zone as the outlet. Our F3 stands alone in the middle of the neutral zone. Our two defencemen are between the red line and our own blue line rather than on it, the strong-side one in the dot lane and the weak-side one deeper and nearer the middle. Two numbered routes: one, the first pass out to the winger on the wall; two, the strong-side defenceman stepping up hard on it, finishing on the inside of the receiver. Both goalies are shown. Two of the opposition’s five skaters are drawn — the other three, the ones who make it a three-on-one if that first pass gets through, are not.
nz-pressure.title: F3 alone in the neutral zone

nz-left-wing-lock.caption: The left-wing lock, frozen the moment possession has been lost: two forwards are still forechecking and the left wing has dropped back into line with the two defencemen, making a three-player line across the back. Conventionally the centre and the right wing are the two who forecheck, but that is a coaching choice rather than a law, and many teams now lock whichever winger is highest in the zone instead. The cost is real: it takes one player out of the counterattack and asks them to do a job most wingers are not trained for.
nz-left-wing-lock.describe: The full sheet, our net at the left, the opponents’ at the right. Two of our forwards, marked C and RW, are deep in the opponents’ end forechecking their defenceman, who has the puck behind their own net. Three of our players stand in a line across the ice just inside the centre red line: the left wing LW in one outside third, a defenceman in the middle third, and the second defenceman in the other outside third, evenly spaced so each covers about 28 feet of width. Both goalies are shown. No routes are drawn: the drop back into the line has already happened at the instant shown, and the forecheck’s own routes are not the subject here. Only the puck carrier is drawn of the opposition’s five skaters.
nz-left-wing-lock.title: Left-wing lock in the neutral zone

nz-regroup-d-to-d.caption: A D-to-D regroup, drawn at the instant the pass across is made, our team attacking left to right. The pass across makes the opposing structure slide. The three forwards sit at three different depths rather than all curling to the same place: short outlet, outside lane, stretch. You are declining a bad entry to buy a better one, not retreating.
nz-regroup-d-to-d.describe: The full sheet, with our own net at the left and our team attacking to the right. Two of our defencemen are just inside our own blue line, one on each side of the ice, with a clean lane between them. Our three forwards are at three clearly different depths in the neutral zone: one high on the puck’s wall (the top of the picture) who has just turned the puck back, one swinging wide and low on the far wall, and one high in the middle near the opponents’ blue line as the stretch option. Two opposition players hold the middle third, one of them pressuring the forward who turned the puck back; neither is in the lane between our defencemen. Two numbered routes, both passes: one, the forward’s pass back; two, the flat D-to-D across. Both goalies are shown; the opponents’ end is otherwise empty because the play has not gone there, and their other three skaters are not drawn.
nz-regroup-d-to-d.title: D-to-D neutral zone regroup

nz-hinge.caption: The hinge, with our team in possession attacking left to right. The numbers are the order. One, the D-to-D; two, the passer sinks back into mid-ice; three, the partner carries it up into coverage; four, the return to a player behind the play, in the middle, facing up ice. The only mark at that spot is their own arrowhead, because each player is drawn once.
nz-hinge.describe: The full sheet, with our own net at the left and our team attacking to the right. Two of our defencemen stand in the neutral zone, one on the upper side of the ice and one on the lower, with a clean lane between them and the puck beside the upper one. One of our forwards is drawn: a winger swung wide on the upper wall. Two opposition skaters are drawn, one low on the same side as the lower defenceman, and one in the middle of the neutral zone sitting in the lane from the lower defenceman to that winger. Neither is between our two defencemen, and neither is behind them. Four numbered routes. One, a flat pass from the upper defenceman straight across to the lower. Two, the upper defenceman’s own skating route, curling back and then down into the middle of the ice behind their partner. Three, the lower defenceman carrying the puck up ice and toward the middle, drawn as a wave. Four, a pass from there back to a point just short of where route two’s arrowhead finishes. No glyph is drawn at the place the upper defenceman ends up. Route two’s arrowhead is the only mark for it. Both goalies are shown. The centre and the third forward are not drawn, and neither are the opponents’ other three skaters.
nz-hinge.title: The hinge regroup

nz-stand-up-at-the-line.caption: Standing up at your own blue line: the defenceman meets the attacker at it with their feet stopped, refuses to give ground and tries to turn the carry into a dump, a pass or a turnover — a carried entry is worth roughly twice a dumped one in shot terms, on NHL tracking more than a decade old. Drawn with it is what beats it, the chip-and-chase past the defenceman’s hip: stopped feet cannot win that race. Beaten standing up is beaten completely. Nothing in the picture finishes into the carrier. That is deliberate: this is exactly where a beginner reaches for a hit. It is a bet that your forwards got back, which no still frame can show. Backing off is the other answer to this moment, not the next frame. Standing up or backing off is a coaching choice, so find out which your team wants.
nz-stand-up-at-the-line.describe: The full sheet. Our own net is at the left with our goalie in it, our own blue line a quarter of the way in from that end, and an opposition puck carrier is coming the other way through the neutral zone on the puck’s side (the top of the picture), about twenty feet short of that line. One of our defencemen stands just inside the blue line in front of the carrier, in the dot lane, with no route drawn at all: their feet are stopped. Two routes come from the carrier and both pass outside the defenceman on the boards side rather than into them — a dashed line, the puck chipped past their hip into the zone behind, and a curved skating route round the outside of them. No backchecker is drawn, no defence partner is drawn, and the opposition’s other four skaters are not drawn. The opposing goalie is shown at the far end.
nz-stand-up-at-the-line.title: Standing up at your blue line

nz-back-off-at-the-line.caption: Backing off at your own blue line: the defenceman gives up the line and skates backwards at the attacker’s speed, keeping them in front and funnelling them outside, where the shot is low-percentage. You cannot be beaten wide by pure speed, and a catastrophic error is very hard to make. The shaded band is the middle, between two unpainted lines through the faceoff dots. Concede the blue line, never the middle or your body position. The cost is drawn too: they enter with speed and possession, and you defend skating backwards toward your own net. It is the play against a clear speed advantage, on a two-on-one or worse, when you are the last defender, or with no backpressure.
nz-back-off-at-the-line.describe: The full sheet, and the same arrangement as the diagram beside it: our own net at the left with our goalie, our own blue line a quarter of the way in, and an opposition puck carrier coming the other way on the puck’s side (the top of the picture), about twenty feet short of that line. Our defenceman is in exactly the same place as in that diagram, just inside the blue line, but here they have a backward skating route retreating into our zone and drifting toward the middle of the ice as they go. The carrier’s route curves away from the defenceman toward the boards on that side and deeper into the zone: the carrier has been let in and steered outside. A shaded band down the centre of the ice, its long edges on the faceoff-dot lines, running from the blue line back to the level of our end-zone faceoff dots, is labelled "the middle" — the ice the defenceman is not conceding. No backchecker, no defence partner and none of the opposition’s other four skaters are drawn. The opposing goalie is shown at the far end.
nz-back-off-at-the-line.title: Backing off at your blue line

oz-home-plate.caption: The home-plate area, also called the house — the shape analysts use to mark the dangerous part of the offensive zone. It runs across the tops of the two faceoff circles, straight down the dot lines to the two faceoff dots, and then angles in to the two goalposts. The inner, high-danger boundary is deliberately not drawn: no description of it is precise enough to place on the ice. Nothing shaded here is painted on a real rink — it is a counting convention.
oz-home-plate.describe: The attacking half of the rink, the opposition net at the right. A single shaded six-sided region is drawn over the end zone: its up-ice edge runs across the ice at the tops of the two faceoff circles, its two long sides run down-ice from the top of each circle to that circle's faceoff dot, and from each dot an angled edge runs in to the nearer goalpost. The goalie is in the crease. No skaters are drawn — this diagram is geography, not a play.
oz-home-plate.title: Home plate in the offensive zone

oz-royal-road.caption: The royal road — an imaginary line down the centre of the ice, net to net — and a pass crossing it in the offensive zone, which drags the goalie across before the shot arrives. Defenders are not drawn. Passes across it finished at 15.50% — volunteer-tracked Passing Project data, 51,308 shots at 5-on-5, counting all attempts rather than shots on goal, so it is not comparable with a plain shooting percentage. ⚠️ Published descriptions of where the line runs do not agree: the net-to-net version drawn here is the more conservative instruction, not the better supported one.
oz-royal-road.describe: The attacking half of the rink, the opposition net at the right. A dashed line runs down the middle of the ice from the centre of the goal line out through centre ice, labelled "the royal road". A forward has the puck on the strong-side half-wall, level with the faceoff dot. A dashed pass route runs from there straight across the zone, crossing the road between the faceoff dots, and finishes short of a second forward standing at the weak-side faceoff dot. The goalie is in the crease. No defenders are drawn.
oz-royal-road.title: The royal road

oz-cross-the-road-yourself.caption: Two carries across the royal road. The 15.50% this document quotes measures passes, and no figure here measures the carry. Only one of the two happens, so no puck is drawn. ⚠️ And both of these carries take you through the middle: head up, chin off your chest — you cannot brace for a hit you have not seen, and coming out past the post you can be driven into the goal frame.
oz-cross-the-road-yourself.describe: The attacking half of the rink, the opposition net at the right. A dashed line runs down the middle of the ice from the centre of the goal line out through centre ice, labelled "the royal road". Two own forwards and no puck. One stands on the strong-side half-wall, level with the faceoff dot; a wavy route ending in an arrowhead — the notation for skating with the puck — leaves them, bows toward the net and finishes on the weak side of the high slot, having crossed the dashed line. The second forward stands behind the goal line, ten feet to the strong side of the middle of the net; a second wavy route leaves them, swings out past the side of the net well clear of the crease, and finishes in the slot on the weak side of the dashed line. The goalie is in the crease. No defenders are drawn.
oz-cross-the-road-yourself.title: Crossing the road yourself

oz-five-man-shape.caption: The five-player offensive-zone shape with the puck on the strong-side half-wall: one forward below in the corner, one above at the top of the circles, both defencemen on the blue line. That below-level-above attack triangle is a default, not a law of hockey — overload, a five-player rotation and a 1-3-1 are real alternatives, so find out which one your team plays. Defenders other than the goalie are not drawn.
oz-five-man-shape.describe: The attacking half of the rink, the opposition net at the right. Five own players. F1 has the puck on the strong-side half-wall. F2 is below them in the strong-side corner, nearer the goal line. F3 is above them and toward the middle, at the top of the circles and inside the home-plate area. Two defencemen stand on the offensive blue line, one each side. The opposing goalie is in the crease; no other defenders are drawn. Two numbered routes: one, the pass from the half-wall down to the corner, finishing short of F2; two, F1 rotating up off the wall. F3 has no route, because the high player holds.
oz-five-man-shape.title: Five attackers, puck on the half-wall

oz-rotation-one-pass-later.caption: The same offensive-zone shift one pass later, the puck now in the strong-side corner: the triangle has moved but the shape has not. F-numbers are roles set by order of arrival, not people, so the corner player is now F1, the old carrier has rotated up off the wall to F2, and the high forward holds as F3. One default structure, not a law of hockey. No routes are drawn: this frame is the result, not the movement.
oz-rotation-one-pass-later.describe: The attacking half of the rink, the opposition net at the right, one pass after the previous diagram. F1 now has the puck in the strong-side corner — this is the player who was labelled F2 a moment ago. F2 is the player who was carrying on the half-wall, now eight feet up-ice of it and five feet inside it, nine feet off the boards. F3 is unchanged at the top of the circles, inside the home-plate area. The two defencemen are unchanged on the blue line. The goalie is in the crease. No routes are drawn.
oz-rotation-one-pass-later.title: Offensive-zone rotation, one pass later

oz-half-wall-options.caption: The four options from the strong-side half-wall on one frame: low to the corner or behind the net, high to the point, the seam across the middle, or taking it yourself off the wall to the inside. The routes carry no numbers, because only one of them happens and which one is a read. The failure is arriving on the wall with only one in mind. Expect the seam to be defended and to open only briefly.
oz-half-wall-options.describe: The attacking half of the rink, the opposition net at the right. A forward has the puck on the strong-side half-wall. Four routes leave them and none is numbered. A dashed pass runs down and back to a teammate deep in the strong-side corner. A second dashed pass runs up the ice to a defenceman at the strong-side point. A third dashed pass runs across the zone, crossing the centre line of the ice, to a forward on the weak side of the high slot. And a wavy carrying route cuts off the wall toward the middle of the ice, inside the home-plate area. A second defenceman is on the blue line on the weak side, and the goalie is in the crease. No opposition skaters are drawn.
oz-half-wall-options.title: Options from the half-wall

oz-cycle-rim.caption: The rim, in an offensive-zone cycle. The checker is inside the carrier and still in front of them, sealing the carrier to the boards. The puck goes onward around the boards to a teammate arriving behind the net, in the direction the play was already going. Only the checker and the goalie are drawn on the other team. ⚠️ Rim or reverse, this is a wall battle: never turn your back to anyone coming at you and never duck. Skates parallel to the wall, forearm and hip to it, head up and chin off your chest — and not on the point of your shoulder, and not the whole shoulder if you can help it.
oz-cycle-rim.describe: The attacking half of the rink, the opposition net at the right. Own players are drawn open, the opposition solid. An own forward has the puck deep in the strong-side corner, with the puck on the boards side of their body. An opposition forward stands about eight feet inside them and two feet nearer the goal line, between them and the middle of the ice. A dashed pass route leaves the carrier and bows out toward the boards, running around the curve of the corner about five feet off the dasher, past the outside of the checker, and finishing short of a second own forward who stands behind the goal line to the strong side of the net. The goalie is in the crease. No other opposition players are drawn, and no route is drawn for the passer.
oz-cycle-rim.title: The rim in the cycle

oz-cycle-reverse.caption: The reverse, in a deep offensive-zone cycle: the checker has skated past the carrier and on toward the end boards. The puck goes back up the wall, against the flow, into the ice they just left, to a teammate arriving on the half-wall. A still picture cannot draw momentum. Only the checker and the goalie are drawn on the other team. Read the checker as past and unable to stop, and reverse it when the teammate arriving behind you calls for it. Without that call, do not reverse on hope. ⚠️ Rim or reverse, this is a wall battle: never turn your back to anyone coming at you and never duck. Skates parallel to the wall, forearm and hip to it, head up and chin off your chest — and not on the point of your shoulder, and not the whole shoulder if you can help it.
oz-cycle-reverse.describe: The attacking half of the rink, the opposition net at the right, the same corner as the previous diagram. Own players are drawn open, the opposition solid. An own forward has the puck deep in the strong-side corner, in the same place as before and with the puck on the far side of their body from the pressure. The opposition forward is now past them, about five feet nearer the goal line and five feet inside, level with the goal line. A dashed pass route leaves the carrier and runs back up the wall, away from the checker, finishing about six feet short of a second own forward standing on the strong-side half-wall. The goalie is in the crease. No other opposition players are drawn, and no route is drawn for the passer.
oz-cycle-reverse.title: The reverse in the cycle

oz-low-to-high.caption: Low-to-high, numbered in order: the puck from the half-wall up to the point (1); the passer supports toward the strong-side hash marks (2); the defenceman walks it toward the middle before releasing (3); the shot goes low through the screen (4). The play is only worth doing when the net front is occupied. The shot-blockers this play is trying to beat are not drawn. ⚠️ At even strength a point shot is among the lowest-percentage and most-blocked shots on the ice — but that caution is an even-strength one, and on the power play the same map puts roughly the whole zone at or above it, so it is no argument against a point shot there.
oz-low-to-high.describe: The attacking half of the rink, the opposition net at the right. Four numbered routes. One: a dashed pass from a forward on the strong-side half-wall up the ice to a defenceman at the strong-side point. Two: the same forward then skates in off the wall toward the hash marks on the inside edge of the strong-side faceoff circle. Three: the defenceman carries the puck in along the blue line, stopping short of the middle of the ice. Four: from there a shot, drawn as a double line, runs down the ice and finishes short of the net, passing to the weak side of a forward who is standing at the net front, eight feet out from the goal line and just outside the strong-side post. A second forward stands in the high slot on the strong side. The weak-side defenceman stays on the blue line. The goalie is in the crease; no other defenders are drawn.
oz-low-to-high.title: The low-to-high play

oz-net-front-screen.caption: Stand inside the dots, about eight feet off the goal line, because the crease is six feet deep. Get on the line from the goalie's eyes to the puck, not from the goalie to the net. Slide as the point man walks the line. The marker is drawn at nine and a half feet only because it is wider than a player. A screen from outside the crease without contact is normally legal under NHL and IIHF rules, so do it constantly, and both add that Rule 69 is "enforced exclusively in accordance with the on-ice judgement of the Referee(s)". Under USA Hockey 625(b) and IIHF 69.1 a foot in the paint can cost you the zone as well as the goal. A rec league may be stricter; read your league's rule. ⚠️ Keep your feet out of the blue paint, and off the crease line at its edge.
oz-net-front-screen.describe: The attacking half of the rink, the opposition net at the right. A defenceman has the puck at the strong-side point, wide, eight feet toward the boards of the point itself. A forward stands at the net front, nine and a half feet out from the goal line and clear of the shaded goal crease, offset to the puck side of the middle of the net so that they sit on the straight line between the goalie's position and the puck rather than in front of the net. The goalie is in the crease. A shot, drawn as a double line, runs from the point and finishes short of the screener; extended, it would pass through them and arrive inside the far post. No other players are drawn.
oz-net-front-screen.title: Net-front screen position

oz-behind-the-net.caption: Attacking from behind the net, a place to go on purpose rather than one you end up in. The pass out to the slot is the primary play, not the last resort: it crosses the royal road almost by definition and reaches a player already inside home plate. Passes from below the goal line finished at 6.73%, second only to royal road passes — volunteer-tracked Passing Project data, 51,308 shots at 5-on-5, counting all attempts rather than shots on goal. The other arrow is the reverse to the corner to restart the cycle. ⚠️ Nobody can come at you from directly behind here, but that is geometry and not immunity: checking from behind is a penalty anywhere on the playing surface and players do get driven into the goal frame, so keep your head up and know who is arriving.
oz-behind-the-net.describe: The attacking half of the rink, the opposition net at the right. A forward has the puck behind the goal line, ten feet to one side of the middle of the net. Two unnumbered routes leave them. A dashed pass runs out past the side of the net, clear of the crease, and across the centre line of the ice, finishing short of a forward standing on the weak side of the high slot. A second dashed pass runs back up to a teammate deep in the strong-side corner — the reverse that restarts the cycle. The goalie is in the crease. No defenders are drawn.
oz-behind-the-net.title: Attacking from behind the net

oz-post-shot-shape.caption: The shape in the seconds after a shot: F3 high as the safety, two forwards at the net, both defencemen on the blue line. That is the standard five-player setup, not a law: who covers a pinching defenceman’s point is a coaching choice this picture does not draw. Find out which your team plays.
oz-post-shot-shape.describe: The attacking half of the rink, the opposition net at the right, in the moments right after a shot. Three own forwards. F3 is high, at the top of the strong-side circle and just inside the home-plate area, drawn as the safety. A second forward stands at the net front, just outside the blue paint, for the screen and tip. A third stands closer to the strong-side faceoff dot, also inside the home-plate area, hunting the rebound. Both defencemen remain on the blue line, one each side. The opposing goalie is in the crease. No routes are drawn: this is the shape at a moment, not a sequence.
oz-post-shot-shape.title: Shape after a shot

the-call-and-who-can-see-it.caption: In this picture the defenceman going for the puck cannot see the forechecker closing from behind; the two who can, partner and goalie, cannot reach the puck, so all they can do is tell the defenceman. Where two can see it, both call it, because the failure is silence, not duplication. With nobody arriving, the call is "time" — and a false "time" sends a teammate into contact unbraced. Turning your back or ducking is what turns contact with the boards into a neck injury. ⚠️ At the wall, whether or not anyone calls "man on", take the contact with your skates parallel to it, on your forearm and hip — not on the point of your shoulder, and not the whole shoulder if you can help it — head up and chin off your chest. Never turn your back to anyone coming at you, not even to protect the puck, and never duck.
the-call-and-who-can-see-it.describe: Your own end, your net at the right and your goalie in the crease. A loose puck sits in the right corner. One of your defencemen, an open triangle, is between the right faceoff dot and the corner; a plain arrowed route runs from them out toward the corner and stops about six feet short of the puck. An opposition forward, a solid circle, stands about twenty feet behind them, just outside the top of the same faceoff circle and a little toward the middle of the ice, on the line the retriever has just skated along; their route runs after the retriever and ends in two short bars across the line, about eight feet short, on their inside, rather than in an arrowhead. Your second defenceman, an open triangle, stands on the far side of the net level with the goal line, and neither that defenceman nor the goalie has a route: nobody else in the picture moves. Both of them are labelled "calls it", the retriever is labelled "cannot see F" and the forechecker "closing in behind". No contact is drawn, and nothing in the picture shows where anybody is looking.
the-call-and-who-can-see-it.title: Who sees the danger and calls it

area-pass-into-space.caption: An area pass at the attacking blue line, and the one thing a picture can show and a sentence cannot: there is nobody at the target. The carrier chips the puck into the shaded patch behind the defender who stood them up, a place rather than a person. The winger is drawn short of the blue line on purpose: a receiver whose skates both cross the leading edge before the puck does is offside, and under USA Hockey Rule 630(a) and Hockey Canada Rule 6.11 a lifted trail skate is offside too — so keep it down.
area-pass-into-space.describe: The attacking half of the rink, attacking to the right, with the blue line running down the picture about a quarter of the way across and the opposition net at the far right, their goalie in the crease. Three skaters. Your puck carrier stands in the neutral zone, eleven feet outside the blue line and in the top half of the picture, with the puck beside them. An opposition defenceman, drawn as a solid triangle, stands one foot inside the blue line and about six feet closer to the middle, between the carrier and the ice beyond. Your winger is wider still and further back, about ten feet from the carrier; a plain skating arrow runs from them straight up the ice and stops four feet short of the blue line. A shaded rectangle of ice, fourteen feet by twelve, sits inside the attacking zone beginning eight feet beyond the defenceman. A dashed passing route leaves the carrier, passes about seven feet clear of the defenceman, and its arrowhead finishes inside that shaded patch. No player is drawn at the end of the pass. The carrier is drawn as a circle only because this notation has no glyph without a position in it, and the section does not say who they are.
area-pass-into-space.title: Area pass into space

lead-the-receiver.caption: Passing into space rather than onto the tape: the pass is aimed at the spot where the receiver’s stick will be when the puck arrives, and the gap between the end of their skating arrow and the end of the pass is the lead. This is not the area pass, which aims at ice nobody owns yet and turns the play into a race.
lead-the-receiver.describe: The attacking half of the rink, attacking to the right, the opposition net at the right with their goalie in the crease. Two of your players and no other opponents. Your passer stands just inside the attacking blue line, a little above the middle of the ice, with the puck beside them. Your receiver stands eighteen feet away, also just inside the blue line but below the middle. A plain skating arrow runs from the receiver about twelve feet up-ice, angled slightly towards the middle. A dashed passing route runs from the passer diagonally up-ice and across, staying about fifteen feet clear of the receiver, and its arrowhead finishes twelve feet beyond the end of the receiver’s arrow and on the straight continuation of it, in the middle of the ice between the two faceoff circles. The two arrowheads point in similar directions, about forty degrees apart, and no player is drawn at either of them. Neither player’s facing is drawn, and the notation cannot show which side of the receiver is their forehand.
lead-the-receiver.title: Leading the receiver

bank-pass-angle.caption: A bank pass off the boards, drawn in your own end: your own net is at the right of this picture and up-ice is to the left. A forechecker sits in the direct lane, so the puck is sent at a spot on the wall instead, chosen so it comes off at roughly the mirror of the angle it went in at. The bounce is not fully predictable, which is why you call it.
bank-pass-angle.describe: One end zone, drawn with your own net at the right of the picture and up-ice to the left, so the play runs from right to left. Your goalie is in the crease. You stand along the right-hand boards, out towards the corner and about nine feet off the wall, with the puck between you and the boards. An opposition forward, drawn as a solid circle, stands about thirteen feet up-ice of you and towards the middle, exactly on the straight line between you and your teammate; the forward’s stick is not drawn. Your teammate stands further up-ice again, roughly level with the top of the faceoff circle and about twenty-two feet off the boards, thirty-eight feet from you. The puck’s route is two straight dashed legs meeting at a point on the boards up-ice of you: the first runs from you out into the wall and its arrowhead points at the wall itself, and the second leaves that point at the mirror of the same angle, passes about ten feet outside the forechecker, and finishes four and a half feet short of your teammate. The straight line from you to your teammate, the one the forechecker is standing in, is not drawn.
bank-pass-angle.title: Bank pass around a forechecker

stick-in-lane-body-net-side.caption: Your own end, your net at the right: an opponent has the puck on the half-wall, and the shaded band is the passing lane to the player you are covering. Your body is not in it — you are on the goal side of them, between them and your net. Blade in the lane and body net-side are two tools, not one; this notation has no stick symbol, so only the body is drawn. Read it as one instant, not a spot on the ice. Where you cannot do both, net-side wins in the defensive zone.
stick-in-lane-body-net-side.describe: One end zone, the net at the right, defended by your own goalie in the crease. Two opposition players: one with the puck on the right half-wall, level with the faceoff dot, and one in the low slot, the player you are covering. You are drawn as a defender roughly eight feet from them, on the goal side, between them and the net, and about eight feet clear of the shaded band. The shaded band runs from the puck down to the player in the low slot and is labelled "the lane". No routes are drawn: nobody moves in this picture. Sticks are not drawn, because the notation has no symbol for one.
stick-in-lane-body-net-side.title: Stick in the lane, body goal side

loose-puck-who-goes.caption: A loose puck in your own corner, your net at the right, drawn under a low zone collapse: the closest player goes hard to it, one teammate supports on the boards side, one covers the net front, and nobody else joins. Find out which coverage your team plays. The other two skaters are not drawn. Two postures carry two different dangers. A chin dropped to the chest is the one USA Hockey ties to almost all on-ice cervical spine injuries, on head-on contact. A back turned to anyone coming at you makes the contact a hit from behind, and USA Hockey warns the checker delivering one: "Even a light hit from behind could inflict a severe head or neck injury." Neither warning depends on the angle you arrive at. ⚠️ Never turn your back to anyone coming at you, and never duck.
loose-puck-who-goes.describe: Your own end zone, the net at the right, your goalie in the crease. A loose puck sits in the right corner with no player on it. Three of your players: one starting near the faceoff dot with an arrow into the corner that stops about five feet short of the puck; one holding the right half-wall as boards-side support; and one defender in front of the net, outside the crease. No opposition player is drawn, and neither are your other two skaters.
loose-puck-who-goes.title: Who goes to a loose puck

unmarked-but-unavailable.caption: The attacking zone, a teammate carrying the puck on the half-wall and you alone in the high slot: the nearest defender is a good ten feet away, and you are still not available. The shaded band is the only line the puck can travel to your blade, and a defenceman has laid their stick flat across it — the requirement your own position cannot tell you about. The stick is not drawn; this notation has no symbol for one. The fix is three or four feet sideways until the angle opens, a change too small to draw as a second band.
