unmarked-but-unavailable.describe: The attacking end zone, the opposition net at the right. Your teammate has the puck on the half-wall at the top of the picture. You stand in the high slot, level with the faceoff dots, with nobody marking you. A shaded band runs straight down the ice between the two of you: it is the passing lane. An opposition defenceman stands about six feet to one side of it and about ten feet from you; their stick, which is not drawn, is what lies across the lane. No routes are drawn.
unmarked-but-unavailable.title: Unmarked but not available

screen-the-goalie-sightline.caption: The shaded wedge is the sightline between the puck at the point and the goalie, with the screen inside it, outside the crease. The wedge swings as the puck moves: stand where the goalie’s eyes are, not where the puck is going. Keep your stick on the ice for tips and rebounds, and move late. Outside the crease and touching nobody, a screen is normally legal, but contact, a position that stops the goalie moving freely in their crease, or a screen held inside it, can still cost the goal (NHL and IIHF 69.1 and 69.3). So stay off the paint and its red line, and touch nobody. A head-down, head-first hit on a goal post is the same injury as one on the boards, and can happen at walking speed. ⚠️ Never meet a goal post head first, and never duck. Head up, chin off your chest instead.
screen-the-goalie-sightline.describe: The attacking end zone, the opposition net at the right with its goalie in the crease, positioned on their angle. One of your players stands at the point at the top of the picture, with the puck. A narrow shaded wedge, labelled "the sightline", runs from the puck down to the goalie, widening as it goes. A second player of yours stands inside that wedge about eight feet in front of the goalie and clear of the crease. No routes are drawn: no shot, and no movement.
screen-the-goalie-sightline.title: Screening the goalie’s sightline

width-makes-the-middle-lane.caption: A three-on-two just inside the attacking blue line, drawn for what the two players without the puck are doing: each winger holds their width near the boards, which keeps a defenceman out on each side, and the middle drive goes through the gap that opens between them. Neither wide forward touches the puck on this rush, and their width is what made that lane exist. How much width a team wants once the puck is settled in the offensive zone is a coaching choice, so ask — some coaches want the far winger high and wide against the counter-attack, others want them crashing the back post on every shot. This is one instant of a rush, not a system.
width-makes-the-middle-lane.describe: The attacking half of the sheet, the opposition net and goalie at the right. Three of your forwards have just crossed the blue line: one carrying the puck up the middle with a route driving further into the zone, and one on each side near the boards, each behind the puck and each with a short route straight up the wall that keeps their width. Two opposition defenders are drawn ahead of them, one on each side, held out toward their wingers, with a wide gap between them that the middle carrier is driving into. Your defencemen are not drawn.
width-makes-the-middle-lane.title: Width and the middle lane

drive-the-net-before.caption: The first of two frames a beat apart, in the attacking end with the opposition net at the right. You are skating hard at the net without the puck, and the defender you are about to pull is still high, in the high slot, which is not shaded because it is not open yet. Read the arrow as effort rather than as a path. It stops more than twenty feet short of the goalmouth and off the defender’s line on purpose, because the last few feet of a net drive are contact in front of a goalie, which this picture does not teach. ⚠️ Never arrive into the goal frame head first. Know where the posts are, and take a post or the boards with an arm or a leg instead. Head up, chin off your chest, and never duck.
drive-the-net-before.describe: The attacking half of the rink, the opposition net and goalie at the right. One of your forwards starts wide, at the top of the near faceoff circle, with a curved route driving in toward the net front that stops well short of it and to one side. One opposition defenceman stands in the high slot, level with the faceoff dots and just off the middle of the ice, between the driver and the net. A second forward of yours stands at the far point with no route, not yet involved. Nothing is shaded. No puck is drawn, and neither are the rest of either team.
drive-the-net-before.title: Driving the net, first frame

drive-the-net-after.caption: A net drive a beat later: a before and an after, not two alternatives. This second frame is the reason for the first. The defender has bent low with the driver, and the high slot they were standing in is now shaded and empty. That ice, and the point behind it, is what the drive opens, and a teammate arriving into it late is how it gets cashed. The shaded band names a piece of ice, not a marking on a real rink. Of the defence, only the pulled defender is drawn, and no puck is drawn. Read the arriving route as one instance of the play, not as a place to stand.
drive-the-net-after.describe: The attacking half of the rink, the opposition net and goalie at the right, a beat after the previous diagram. The driver has arrived, standing more than twenty feet out from the goalmouth and to one side, where the previous frame’s route ended, and has no route now. The opposition defenceman who was in the high slot has come down with the driver and now stands between them and the net and well outside the crease. The high slot — the band between the two faceoff circles, from the dots up to the tops of them — is shaded, labelled, and contains nobody. Your second forward, who was at the far point, is halfway down with a route finishing inside that shaded region and running across it rather than on toward the net. No puck is drawn.
drive-the-net-after.title: Driving the net, second frame

legal-route-through-traffic.caption: Your own legal route past a teammate, in the attacking end with the opposition net at the right. Your route goes round the outside of your teammate, who is standing still, and finishes in open ice, while the straight line your check would take to that same ice runs through them. No arrow in this picture ends at a body. The section around the picture says when this route is legal. The drawing cannot show it. A chaser arriving at the back of a player standing still is not drawn. No puck is drawn. The collision you are engineering is your check at chase speed into a teammate who is facing away and cannot see them. ⚠️ Shout as you come, and run past your teammate rather than into the space they are standing in. That is a coaching caution, not a rulebook requirement.
legal-route-through-traffic.describe: The attacking end zone, the opposition net and goalie at the right. Three skaters, all on the weak side of the ice and none of them near the net front. One of your forwards stands low, about ten feet off the boards and below the faceoff dot, with a curved route running up the ice and in toward the middle: it passes outside a second forward of yours and finishes in open ice just above the top of the faceoff circle, pointing away from everybody. That second forward stands still a few feet inside the route, level with and just above the faceoff dot, with no route of their own. An opposition skater, labelled as your check, stands between you and the middle of the ice, ten feet from your teammate and eleven from you, and they carry no route at all. No puck is drawn and nothing is shaded.
legal-route-through-traffic.title: Your route past a teammate

centre-low-zone-collapse.caption: Your own defensive zone with the puck in the strong-side corner, at the moment the centre has left the slot to help win it. The strong-side defenceman plays the puck and the centre joins that defenceman, because two of you on the puck usually wins it; the weak-side winger collapses from their own point to cover the high slot the centre has vacated, while the weak-side defenceman stays at the goalmouth — two layers with two owners. This is a low zone collapse, a coaching choice rather than a rule of hockey: under man-on-man the wingers follow their check into the corner instead, so find out which one your team plays.
centre-low-zone-collapse.describe: The defending half of the rink, your own net at the right. Three opposition players: the puck carrier deep in the right corner, and the two opposing defencemen at their points near the blue line. Six of your own: the goalie in the crease; the strong-side defenceman in the corner between the carrier and the net; the centre low in the strong-side circle supporting that defenceman; the weak-side defenceman at the goalmouth on the far side of the net; the strong-side winger high on the right, goal-side of the opposing defenceman they are covering; and the weak-side winger, who has left their point on the left and is skating to the high slot. The high slot is shaded. One route: the weak-side winger’s collapse. The opposition forwards other than the carrier are not drawn.
centre-low-zone-collapse.title: Centre in a low zone collapse

centre-swing-low.caption: Your defenceman has the puck behind their own net and the centre is swinging low to be the outlet — inside the faceoff dots and below the hash marks, which in practice means inside the strong-side faceoff circle rather than out on the boards, which are the winger’s ice. Having received it, the centre carries out through the middle if that lane is clearly open; if it is not, the puck goes to the winger on the boards instead. Low support like this belongs to the conventional swing breakout, a coaching choice and not a rule: under a centre fly the weak-side winger drops in to take this job instead, so find out which one your team plays.
centre-swing-low.describe: The defending half of the rink, your own net at the right, and no opposition drawn — this is the free-space case. Three of your own players: the defenceman behind their own net with the puck; the centre low in the strong-side faceoff circle, inside the dot and below the hash marks; and the strong-side winger out on the boards above the centre. Two numbered routes: one, the pass from the defenceman to the centre, passing above the goal frame rather than across the goalmouth; two, the centre carrying out through the middle of the ice toward the blue line.
centre-swing-low.title: Centre swinging low for the outlet

centre-backcheck-middle-lane.caption: A rush coming back at you, and the centre’s backcheck. The centre comes back on the defensive side of the middle-lane driver, and does not swing wide to help on the carrier, because the defencemen have the carrier and the middle is the ice they are protecting. They are drawn retreating together with that middle sealed. Which backchecker takes which lane is a coaching choice and not a law: some teams give the middle to the first man back, whoever that is, and others pick up man-on-man from the puck outward — so find out which yours plays.
centre-backcheck-middle-lane.describe: The defending half of the rink, your own net at the right, with three opposition forwards attacking from the left. The puck carrier is wide along the top wall; a second forward comes up the middle of the ice behind the carrier, with a route showing that forward crossing the blue line late, behind the play; a third is wide along the bottom wall. Coming back: the centre in the middle lane, already goal-side of the middle driver and between that driver and your own net; a winger in each outside lane, goal-side of the attacker in that lane; the two defencemen retreating together in front of them, keeping the middle of the ice sealed; and the goalie in the crease.
centre-backcheck-middle-lane.title: Centre’s backcheck on a rush

winger-high-then-down-the-wall.caption: A winger’s defensive-zone job, drawn at both ends of one move. While the other team has the puck you are high on your side, level with the opposing defenceman you cover and between them and the slot. Staying high out of the corner is the low zone collapse job, a coaching choice: under man-on-man you follow your man wherever they go, corner included, so find out which your team plays. Stay high until your team actually wins the battle below you; then come down the wall to between the hash marks and the goal line, stick on the ice and feet already moving. That trip belongs to the conventional swing breakout: a flat or spread structure holds you higher toward the blue line, and a stretch sends one winger up ice instead, so find out which one you are in.
winger-high-then-down-the-wall.describe: The defending half of the rink, your own net at the right. Two opposition players: a defenceman at their point just inside the blue line on the right side, and a forechecking forward in the right corner. Three of your own: the goalie in the crease; a defenceman in the corner contesting the puck; and the right winger high on the right side, goal-side of the opposing defenceman they are covering. One route runs from the winger down the wall, hugging the boards, to the outlet position on the boards between the hash marks and the goal line, arriving above the corner battle rather than in it. The centre and the weak-side players are not drawn.
winger-high-then-down-the-wall.title: Winger high, then down the wall

winger-offensive-zone-patches.caption: Where a winger works in the offensive zone: the half-wall level with the faceoff dot, your own circle and the side of the net. Driving in from your circle or the wall, as drawn, arrive as the shot is taken rather than well before it; if the net front is your assignment, be planted there before the release. Stay out of the shaded high slot unless your team sends you there. From the wall, lean toward the shot: "shoot first" is a bias, not a rule. At the net front, screen with no contact, and keep your feet out of the blue paint and off its red edge. ⚠️ Know where the near post is before the shot, arrive head up with your chin off your chest, and never meet a goal post head first or duck. A defender can walk you sideways into the frame: take it with an arm, a leg, anything but your head first, in every league, checking or not.
winger-offensive-zone-patches.describe: The attacking half of the rink, the opposition net at the right, with only the opposition goalie drawn. Two of your own players: the left winger on the half-wall at the top of the picture with the puck, and the right winger in the bottom faceoff circle. Two routes: a shot from the half-wall toward the net, stopping short of the crease, and the right winger’s skate to the side of the net, arriving beside it rather than in the blue paint. The high slot, between the faceoff dots and the top of the circles, is shaded and empty — it is the layer a winger stays out of unless their team’s structure sends them there. The opposition defence is not drawn.
winger-offensive-zone-patches.title: Winger’s offensive-zone areas

winger-dz-rim.caption: Beating a checker who has sealed you against the boards, in your own end. Keep the puck on the far side of your body from them, as drawn, and keep your feet wide and low and still moving: a stationary player on the wall gets pinned. The checker is inside you, taking away the middle, so a RIM beats them because it goes where they are not. Decide where the puck is going while you are still skating to it. Skates parallel to the boards, forearm and hip to the wall, head up and chin off your chest — and not on the point of your shoulder, and not the whole shoulder if you can help it. ⚠️ Rim or reverse, never turn your back to anyone coming at you and never duck. Those are two different injuries — a hit from behind you cannot brace for, and a chin tucked to the chest, which does not need speed to do it.
winger-dz-rim.describe: The defending half of the rink, your own net at the right. Your goalie is in the crease. Your right winger is on the wall, level with the faceoff dot, holding the puck on the boards side of their body. An opposition forward is a little inside the winger and a little up-ice, between the winger and the middle of the ice, sealing them to the wall. A second player of yours waits on the same boards up at the blue line. A passing route runs from the winger along the boards, bowed into the wall so it hugs it, past the checker and up to that teammate.
winger-dz-rim.title: Rimming past a sealing checker

winger-dz-reverse.caption: Beating a checker who has over-committed and skated past you up the wall, in your own end. The ice they have just left is behind you, so the play that beats them is a REVERSE to a teammate arriving there, and that teammate calls it — "reverse!" — because you cannot see them behind you; without the call, do not reverse on hope.
winger-dz-reverse.describe: The defending half of the rink, your own net at the right. Your goalie is in the crease. Your right winger is on the wall, level with the faceoff dot, with the puck on the boards side of their body. An opposition forward has skated past the winger and is now up-ice of the winger and slightly inside, the forward’s momentum carrying them away from the puck. Your defenceman is arriving behind the winger, deeper toward the corner. A passing route runs from the winger back down the boards to that defenceman, in the opposite direction to the checker.
winger-dz-reverse.title: Reversing past an over-committed checker

off-wing-open-to-the-ice.caption: Receiving a breakout pass up the wall on your off wing, in your own end: it arrives on your backhand with a forechecker coming. Taken open to the ice, hips turned out and a step or two off the boards, it leaves three options, drawn as alternatives rather than a sequence: skate, pass to the centre or pass back to your defenceman. ⚠️ Never turn your back to anyone coming at you as you receive it, and never duck. If contact comes, skates parallel to the wall, forearm and hip to it, head up and chin off your chest — and not on the point of your shoulder, and not the whole shoulder if you can help it.
off-wing-open-to-the-ice.describe: The defending half of the rink, your own net at the right. Your goalie is in the crease and your defenceman is in the right corner with the puck already moved. Your winger stands on the right side a step or two off the boards rather than flush against them, level with the faceoff dot, with the puck on the inside of their body. An opposition forechecker is up-ice of the winger and hard against the boards, arriving. Three routes leave the winger at once, and they are alternatives rather than a sequence: one route carrying the puck inside and up the ice, one pass into the middle to the centre, and one pass back down to the defenceman in the corner. The section lists four options and the picture draws three routes, without mapping them one to one onto that list.
off-wing-open-to-the-ice.title: Receiving a pass on your off wing

defender-two-on-one.caption: A two-on-one: the defenceman sits in the passing lane between the attackers, stick flat on the passing side, backing up under control — taking the pass away and leaving the shot to the goalie. One of two systems; the other is a timed slide. No backchecker is drawn, because one would make this a different situation.
defender-two-on-one.describe: The defending half of the rink, your own net at the right. Two opposition forwards attack from the left, one wide on each side of the ice, with the puck on the one drawn nearer the top of the picture; a route shows that forward carrying toward the top of the faceoff circle on that side. Between and ahead of them is a single defenceman, sitting in the passing lane that joins the two attackers, with a backward skating route showing the defenceman retreating under control rather than stepping up. The goalie is in the crease. Nobody is backchecking.
defender-two-on-one.title: Defending a 2-on-1

defender-three-depths.caption: The three depths a defenceman plays at in the offensive zone. Just inside the blue line is the default. The top of the faceoff circle is the activated position: the strong-side defenceman may step down to it to support a cycle or create a shot, but only when there is no immediate threat of a turnover, and from there they can still recover. Below the circles you are a fourth forward and cannot recover if it turns over, which is why that band is drawn empty. Only one defenceman steps in at a time and the other holds the line as the safety — a near-universal coaching convention rather than a rule, and coaches do call exceptions. When in doubt, stay at the line.
defender-three-depths.describe: The attacking half of the rink, the opposition net at the right. Three shaded bands run across the ice, marking the three depths: one just inside the blue line, one at the top of the faceoff circles, and one below the circles near the goal line. Both of your defencemen are in the first band, just inside the blue line. A route runs from the strong-side defenceman down to the second band at the top of the circle. The third band is empty. One of your forwards is on the strong-side half-wall with the puck, the cycle the strong-side defenceman is stepping down to support. The rest of the forwards and the opposition are not drawn.
defender-three-depths.title: Defenceman’s three offensive-zone depths

defender-d-to-d-behind-the-net.caption: A defence-to-defence pass in your own end goes behind your own net, below the goal line, and never across the slot — the shaded area, where most goals are scored from. One intercepted in front of the net is a point-blank chance against, and among the most punished mistakes in the game — coaching emphasis, not a counted ranking. The same holds if you are carrying rather than passing: if no pass is on, skate behind the net to the other side instead of going through the middle. What varies between teams is the route rather than the prohibition — some exchange high in the zone instead, above the tops of the circles, so ask your coach which yours uses.
defender-d-to-d-behind-the-net.describe: The defending half of the rink, your own net at the right. Two of your defencemen stand low in the zone, one on each side, level with the faceoff dots and toward the goal line, with the puck on the right-hand one. A passing route runs from that defenceman around behind their own net, dipping below the goal line and passing behind the goal frame, to their partner on the far side. The goalie is in the crease and an opposition forward stands in front of the net in the lane the pass is deliberately not taking. The slot is shaded: a narrow band down the middle of the ice between the inner edges of the two faceoff circles, running from the top of the circles to the front of the crease. It is not a marking on the ice.
defender-d-to-d-behind-the-net.title: D-to-D pass behind your net

defender-step-up.caption: A step-up at your own blue line, your net at the right: you move forward to meet the carrier early. The cost is the ice behind you: nobody is between you and your goalie, so a miss leaves your partner, on the far side, alone in a two-on-one. Step up only when you are sure you can win the puck or force a turnover, with your forwards tracking back; how aggressive to be is a coaching choice, so ask. Finished as a hit, a step-up runs into the charging rules, and a head-down carrier tells you only that they cannot change direction. Two strides is a safe harbour in no book. USA Hockey calls accelerating through a check charging, and leaving your feet to hit is charging in all six. ⚠️ A step-up closes space; it is not a hit, so the route ends in two bars: arrive and contain.
defender-step-up.describe: The defending half of the rink, your own net at the right, your goalie in the crease. Your own blue line runs across the picture near the left-hand edge. One of your defencemen is a few feet inside that line on the puck’s side (the top of the picture), labelled "you", and their route runs forward and out across the line toward an oncoming opposition forward, ending in two short bars rather than an arrowhead. That forward is out in the neutral zone on the same side with the puck beside them, and their own route carries them toward the line. A second opposition forward is wide on the far side of the ice, level with the neutral-zone faceoff dot there, with no route. Your other defenceman, labelled "partner", is well back on that far side, between the blue line and the top of the faceoff circle. The whole of the ice between the stepping-up defenceman and their own goalie is empty: no third defender and nobody else. Any of your forwards tracking back would be behind the carrier, beyond the left-hand edge of the picture.
defender-step-up.title: Stepping up at your own line

defender-holding-the-line.caption: Holding your own blue line as the safety valve, your own goal at the left. Your two defencemen stand on that line either side of the middle, inside the width the neutral-zone faceoff dots mark out: the last line before your zone. Your forwards are up ice and the nearest has a forechecker closing, so the dashed pass back to the near defenceman is the job: be the option they can find, with your stick in the passing lane. Where a pair holds in the neutral zone is part of your team’s system rather than a fixed spot, so find out what yours wants. Nothing here is contact. The forechecker’s route ends in two bars, meaning arrive and contain.
defender-holding-the-line.describe: The full two-hundred-foot sheet, your own goal at the left with your goalie in the crease, and your team attacking to the right. Two of your defencemen stand on your own blue line, one on each side of the middle of the ice, each about eleven feet off the centre of the sheet and so well inside the two neutral-zone faceoff dots. Neither has a route: they are holding. Three of your forwards are up ice. Two are in the attacking zone, one of them labelled "up ice"; the third is out in the neutral zone just past the centre red line with the puck beside them, and a single opposition forward is closing on them from the attacking side, that forechecker’s route ending in two short bars rather than an arrowhead. One dashed passing route runs from the forward with the puck back down the ice toward the nearer of the two defencemen, stopping just short of that defenceman. No other opposition players are drawn.
defender-holding-the-line.title: Defencemen as the safety valve

defender-pair-overview.caption: Two defencemen working as a pair, shown in your own end, contesting a loose puck in the corner. One of you plays the puck; the other holds the goalmouth — the ice at the mouth of your own goal — and you swap those jobs the moment the puck crosses the middle of the ice. That net-front assignment is a low zone collapse — the coverage assumed throughout this guide, and a coaching choice rather than a rule: under man-on-man the net front belongs to whoever's man is standing there, so find out which your team plays.
defender-pair-overview.describe: The defending half of the rink, your own net at the right, your goalie in the crease. One opposition forward is deep in the right corner with a loose puck between them. Your strong-side defenceman is beside that forward, contesting the puck. Your weak-side defenceman is on the opposite side of the net from the corner, at the goalmouth, labelled "goalmouth", between the net front and where an unmarked opponent would stand. No route is drawn: the picture is the shape the pair forms, not a movement.
defender-pair-overview.title: The defence pair

drill-execution-no-opponent.caption: The first of two frames: nobody defending. The dashed pass was the answer before the rep started, because no opposing skater in the picture could take it away. This is not a bad drill; what it cannot train is the choice. Which drills your team runs is your coach’s decision rather than a rule of hockey — so if a drill’s purpose is not obvious, ask.
drill-execution-no-opponent.describe: The attacking half of the rink, the net at the right with the opposing goalie in the crease. Two own players and no opposition skaters. One stands inside the faceoff circle at the top of the picture, above the dot with the puck drawn beside them, and a dashed passing route runs from them across the ice and down to the second, who stands in front of the net a little to the far side and about six feet clear of the crease. Nothing else is drawn: no defender, no other route, and no cone.
drill-execution-no-opponent.title: Drill rep with no defender

drill-decision-one-defender.caption: The second frame: the same instant, with exactly one player added, standing in the lane the pass was going to travel down. No route is drawn in this picture at all. That is the point of it: the answer has left the frame. Adding a defender is a coaching approach, not a rule of hockey. Shrinking the space, shortening the clock or playing a small-area game do similar work. Ask your coach which one a drill is using. The defender drawn here is an opposition forward playing passively, allowed to take away a single option and nothing else. ⚠️ How hard a defender may compete in a drill, and whether body checking is permitted at all, depends on your age group, your league and the book they play under, and no picture can tell you that.
drill-decision-one-defender.describe: The same attacking half and the same instant as the previous diagram, with everything unchanged except that one opposition player has been added and the pass route has gone. Your own two players are where they were — one inside the faceoff circle at the top of the picture with the puck beside them, one in front of the net — and the opposing goalie is in the crease. The opposition forward stands squarely on the line between the two of them, about twenty-three feet from the puck carrier and about fourteen from the teammate. No routes are drawn anywhere in this frame.
drill-decision-one-defender.title: Drill rep with one defender added

practice-the-line-and-one-rep.caption: A full-ice drill at one instant: six skaters, one carrying the puck up the ice and five standing in a line against the boards waiting their turn. No goalie and no opponent are drawn, so nothing can surprise the player taking the rep. It teaches a pattern; this is not a badly run practice, but it is expensive in time. How a practice is built is your coach’s call; what is yours is what you do while you wait. Keep your feet moving: coaches warn that going flat out after standing still in a cold rink is how people pull something. ⚠️ Above all, keep your head up, because a practice has loose pucks flying and a line against the boards is exactly where they arrive.
practice-the-line-and-one-rep.describe: The full two-hundred-foot sheet, with no opposition and no goalie drawn. Five own skaters stand in a row along the upper boards at the far end, evenly spaced about eight feet apart, from level with the far faceoff dot up toward the far blue line. A sixth own skater is out in the neutral zone above the middle with the puck beside them, and a wavy route — the mark for skating with the puck — runs from them about fifty feet up the ice, finishing just inside the attacking blue line and toward the middle. Nobody else is drawn and nothing else is moving.
practice-the-line-and-one-rep.title: Line drill: one skater, five waiting

practice-small-area-in-one-zone.caption: The same six skaters, now three against three in one end zone: your three attack the net a goalie defends. All six are in the play, none more than about forty-five feet from the puck. Everything about this setup is a coaching choice, not a law of hockey: the numbers, the area, whether there is a goalie, what each team scores on and what constraint is added. One of the six is closing on the carrier on the wall, and their route ends in two short bars, not an arrowhead: they arrive and contain rather than skating through. That is all the picture says about how they arrive, on purpose. They close on the puck with the stick, not on the carrier’s body. ⚠️ How hard anyone may compete for a puck, and whether body checking is allowed at all, depends on your age group, your league and the book it plays under, and no diagram can tell you that.
practice-small-area-in-one-zone.describe: The full two-hundred-foot sheet again, with the whole picture in the right-hand end zone below the blue line and the rest of the ice empty. Three own skaters, three opposition skaters and one goalie. One of yours has the puck on the half-wall along the top of the picture, level with the faceoff dot, with the puck drawn just below them; one is low in the slot on the far side of the middle; one is high, just inside the blue line. An opposition player is about nine feet out from the top of the faceoff circle on that side, toward the blue line, with a route running out toward the puck below the carrier: it stops about six feet short of the puck and about nine feet short of the carrier, and ends in two short bars rather than an arrowhead. A second opposition player stands in front of the net, about nine feet clear of the crease, and a third stands high near the blue line beside your own high player. The opposing goalie is in the crease. That is the only route in the picture; nothing else is drawn.
practice-small-area-in-one-zone.title: Small-area 3-on-3 in one zone

support-in-a-line.caption: Three teammates in a straight line up the boards, the puck on the deepest of them. One opponent standing in that line is between the carrier and both receivers, so a single stick blade in a single lane kills two options at once — a line is the cheapest shape in hockey to defend. What is wrong is the shape, and it is just as cheap to defend wherever on the ice the three of them happen to be.
support-in-a-line.describe: The attacking half of the rink, the opposition net at the right. Three own-team forwards stand in a straight line along the boards at the top of the picture, fifteen feet apart: the puck carrier deepest, in the corner; a second at the half-wall; a third further up the wall towards the blue line. A single opposition forward stands on that same line, between the carrier and the other two. No routes are drawn — the point of the picture is the shape, not any movement.
support-in-a-line.title: Three teammates in a line

support-triangle.caption: Three teammates with one of them pulled off the boards into the middle, so the lanes out of the carrier now diverge. The opponent has not moved: they are still in the lane up the boards, and covering it means turning their body away from the middle option.
support-triangle.describe: The attacking half of the rink, the opposition net at the right. The puck carrier is deep in the top corner, on the boards, and one teammate remains high on the same boards, but the third has moved off the wall into the middle of the zone, level with and just below the faceoff dot, so the three form a triangle. The opposition forward stands where they stood in the previous diagram, on the line between the carrier and the high wall option. A single dashed passing route runs from the carrier into the middle, stopping short of the receiver — the lane that forward cannot also be in.
support-triangle.title: Three teammates in a triangle

support-distance-range.caption: Support has a working range, drawn here as a band of ice around a carrier on the half-wall rather than as a spot, because it travels with the puck. The range is eight to ten feet when the carrier is pressured, stretching to about fifteen when they have time — the tighter end is the one figure here with a source behind it, and the ten-to-fifteen default is a widely-taught coaching rule of thumb rather than a rule of hockey, because no governing body has been found to set a support distance as a standard and coaches differ — read that as none found, not as none existing. One teammate inside the band is an option; the other, inside its inner edge, is supporting too close. The self-test is time, not distance — if your teammate released the puck now, would it reach you before a defender does?
support-distance-range.describe: The attacking half of the rink, the opposition net at the right. A puck carrier stands on the boards at the top of the picture, level with the faceoff dot. A shaded band of ice curves around them on the open-ice side, its inner edge eight feet away and its outer edge fifteen. One teammate stands inside the band, below and inside the carrier, with a short dashed passing route drawn to them. A second teammate stands inside the inner edge, about seven feet from the carrier, too close to be an option. No opposition players are drawn.
support-distance-range.title: Support distance range

support-angles.caption: The three support angles, drawn once around a carrier in the neutral zone attacking to the right: one teammate behind the puck, one level with it across the ice, one ahead of it. Behind is the outlet, a low-risk reset that still exists when the other two are covered. Level changes the side of the ice, a normal, high-value play in the neutral and offensive zones; in your own zone the lateral option goes behind your net, not across the slot, where an interception is a point-blank chance. Ahead gains ground and is the most interceptable; at the blue line, time your entry rather than parking in the zone. Until the puck is completely across, keep the trail skate on the ice on or behind the line, which is onside under every book. A team needs all three at once.
support-angles.describe: The full sheet, attacking to the right. A puck carrier stands on the centre line towards the boards at the top of the picture. Three teammates: one behind the puck and nearer the defensive end, one level with the carrier but across on the far side of the ice, and one ahead of the puck and wide, still well short of the attacking blue line. Three dashed passing routes run from the carrier to each, stopping short of the receiver, at clearly different angles. No opposition players are drawn.
support-angles.title: Behind, level and ahead

defensive-zone-support.caption: The defensive-zone support structure, drawn with your own net at the right and up-ice to the left, at the moment your defenceman retrieves the puck behind the net and before they turn. The standard set of options is three: the strong-side winger on the wall roughly level with the faceoff dot; the centre swinging low through the middle and curling toward the same side; and the defence partner on the far side, reached behind the net and below the goal line, never through the slot. Your goalie has the best view on the ice and no puck to look at, so they are part of this structure as a voice whatever your league does about the trapezoid.
defensive-zone-support.describe: One end zone, which here is your own end: your net at the right, up-ice to the left. Your defenceman stands behind your own net with the puck. Three dashed passing routes leave them, each stopping short of its receiver: one up to the winger on the right-hand boards level with the faceoff dot, one to the centre low in the middle of the zone, and one back across behind the net and below the goal line to the defence partner. A solid route shows the centre swinging low through the middle and curling back toward the strong side. The weak-side winger stands high and wide on the far boards, above the faceoff dots. The goalie is in the crease. No opposition players are drawn.
defensive-zone-support.title: Defensive-zone breakout support

neutral-zone-lanes.caption: The neutral zone organised as three lanes — strong-side boards, middle, weak-side boards — with one player in each, attacking to the right. One player per lane is the usual default and a coaching choice rather than a law: two players in the same lane can be covered by one defender, but the realistic alternative is a 1-3-1 regroup that deliberately stacks the middle lane with a low centre and a high middle support, accepting that one checker can see both. Find out whether your team spreads or stacks, because the two look identical for the first stride and then require opposite decisions. The lane boundaries are drawn here on the faceoff-dot lines so that the shading has an edge; they are not marked on the ice.
neutral-zone-lanes.describe: The full sheet, attacking to the right. The neutral zone between the two blue lines is shaded in three bands: a boards lane on each side and a middle lane between the faceoff-dot lines. One own player is in each band, at three different depths, none of them level with another. The player in the strong-side boards lane has the puck and carries it up ice on a curved route; the other two skate curved routes of their own, all three stopping well short of the attacking blue line. No opposition players are drawn.
neutral-zone-lanes.title: Three neutral zone lanes

support-a-battle-from-outside.caption: Your teammate is pinned on the boards with the puck. The support player stays out in open ice about five metres away, stick down for an exit, and keeps their checker out with them. Two exceptions send you in: a genuine fifty-fifty scramble nobody has, and a team that assigns a second player to the wall — find out if that is you. If you go in, how you arrive outranks winning the puck. Skates parallel to the wall, forearm and hip to it, head up and chin off your chest — and not on the point of your shoulder, and not the whole shoulder if you can help it. ⚠️ Never turn your back to anyone coming at you, and never duck. Never push or hit the opponent on the wall from behind. Even in non-checking hockey, that is checking from behind. Play the puck at their feet.
support-a-battle-from-outside.describe: The attacking half of the rink, the opposition net at the right. An own-team forward is on the boards at the top of the picture with the puck, level with the faceoff dot, with an opposition forward tight to their inside shoulder, pinning them against the wall. A second own forward stands about sixteen feet away in open ice, inside and up-ice of the battle, near the faceoff dot. An opposition forward stands between that support player and the net, marking them. No routes are drawn.
support-a-battle-from-outside.title: Supporting a wall battle from open ice

layer-not-converge.caption: Two players defending one puck carrier, forechecking towards the net on the right: the first pressures, and the second layers behind and to the side of them instead of converging on the same puck. First and second here are the order they arrive in, not two particular players. The layer is offset diagonally rather than directly behind, at two or three stick lengths — close enough to take over the coverage, far enough that a single move does not beat both of you. Converging instead puts two of you on one puck, both beaten by the same pass. A deliberate double-team — commonly allowed below your own goal line, where a turnover is contained by the net and the boards — is a coaching decision rather than something to freelance, so ask your coach where and when your team doubles. Whether the first player’s arrival may end in a hit depends on whether your game allows body checking. ⚠️ Arrive on the carrier’s inside, stick on the ice inside them, and never into the back of a player facing the boards.
layer-not-converge.describe: The attacking half of the rink, the opposition net at the right. An opposition defenceman has the puck in the top corner. One own forward closes from up-ice and inside, with a pressure route that finishes short of the carrier and aimed at the ice inside them rather than at the puck. A second own forward stands about fifteen feet behind and to the boards side of the first, up the wall and a stick’s reach off the lane to the opposition winger who waits higher up the same boards. No pass is drawn.
layer-not-converge.title: Layering behind the first forechecker

the-slot.caption: The slot: the ice in front of the net, between the faceoff circles, from the top of the circles down to the goalmouth — shaded here; not painted.
the-slot.describe: One half of the rink, a net at the right. A shaded rectangle runs down the middle of the end zone from the top of the two faceoff circles to the front edge of the goal crease, its sides on the inner edges of the two circles. No players are drawn.
the-slot.title: The slot

the-high-slot.caption: The high slot: from the faceoff dots up to the top of the circles, between the two circles — shaded here; not painted, though the dots and circles are.
the-high-slot.describe: One half of the rink, a net at the right. A shaded rectangle occupies the middle of the zone between the two faceoff circles, running from the top of the circles down to the depth of the two faceoff dots — the upper part of the slot. No players are drawn.
the-high-slot.title: The high slot

the-low-slot.caption: The low slot: from the faceoff dots down to the goalmouth, outside the crease — shaded here; not painted, but its edges follow real markings.
the-low-slot.describe: One half of the rink, a net at the right. A shaded rectangle occupies the middle of the zone between the two faceoff circles, running from the depth of the faceoff dots down to the front edge of the light blue goal crease — the lower part of the slot. No players are drawn.
the-low-slot.title: The low slot

the-goalmouth.caption: The goalmouth: the immediate front of the net, at the edge of the crease — a small shaded box here, much smaller than the low slot.
the-goalmouth.describe: One half of the rink, a net at the right. A small shaded box sits directly in front of the goal, the width of the goal crease and running from the goal line out to the front edge of the crease. It is drawn over the light blue crease. No players are drawn.
the-goalmouth.title: The goalmouth

the-point-and-the-half-wall.caption: The point and the half-wall: two spots beginners conflate. Defencemen stand at the point, wingers at the half-wall — placed only to mark the spots, not as a formation.
the-point-and-the-half-wall.describe: The attacking half of the rink, the opposition net at the right. Two defencemen stand just inside the blue line, one toward each side, at the point. Two wingers stand against the side boards level with the faceoff dots, at the half-wall. The defenceman and the winger at the top of the picture are labelled "the point" and "the half-wall". No puck and no routes are drawn.
the-point-and-the-half-wall.title: The point and the half-wall

the-trapezoid.caption: The trapezoid: the goaltender’s restricted area behind the net, shaded here at NHL dimensions. Playing the puck behind the goal line outside it is a delay-of-game minor. The rule text’s one exception, a goalie keeping skate contact with the crease, excuses playing the puck, never freezing it. The IIHF’s Situation Handbook adds two more: a puck stopped on the goal line, and one that only deflects into you. USA Hockey, Hockey Canada and CARHA mark no trapezoid, but all three still stop the goalie at the centre red line and limit where the puck may be frozen. England Ice Hockey’s suspension of the trapezoid, whatever its standing, never touched where a goalie may freeze the puck. Cover the puck straight off your own save: coming out to cut the angle, saving and covering stays legal (IIHF 63.2(VI)). Being checked excuses a freeze only inside the crease (63.2(VII)); out of it, falling on a loose puck as an attacker bears down is still a minor.
the-trapezoid.describe: One half of the rink, a net at the right. The area behind the goal line is shaded between the two red trapezoid lines, which begin either side of the goal and splay outward to the end boards: narrower at the goal line, wider at the boards. No players are drawn.
the-trapezoid.title: The trapezoid

strong-side-and-weak-side.caption: Strong-side and weak-side: whichever half of the ice the puck is on right now, and the other half — not painted; the boundary moves with the puck.
strong-side-and-weak-side.describe: One half of the rink, a net at the right, tinted in two different shades lengthways down the middle. The puck is in the top half of the picture, just inside the strong-side faceoff dot. The half of the ice containing the puck is labelled "strong side" and the other half "weak side". No line is drawn between them and no players are drawn.
strong-side-and-weak-side.title: Strong side and weak side

the-goal-crease.caption: The goal crease — the blue paint — shaded here: 8 ft wide at the goal line, 6 ft deep, extending 4 ft up as a volume, not a floor. The red boundary line itself counts as crease in the rule text or glossary of the IIHF, USA Hockey, Hockey Canada and CARHA; the NHL and the PWHL leave it unsaid. The books’ reference tables answer the other way, the IIHF’s own among them — a contradiction inside one book that nothing here resolves. So keep your skates off the red line, not merely out of the blue paint. No shading can draw an edge that fine.
the-goal-crease.describe: One half of the rink, a net at the right. The goal crease is shaded: it is eight feet wide where it meets the goal line, a short straight side runs out from each end of that width, and the two are joined by an arc that reaches six feet out from the goal line at its deepest point, so the shape bulges into the zone rather than back toward the end boards. The goal stands on the goal line behind it, and is narrower than the crease. No players are drawn.
the-goal-crease.title: The goal crease

home-plate-the-house.caption: Home plate — the high-danger area, also "the house": tops of the circles down the dot lines to the dots, angling in to the goalposts. Not a painted marking.
home-plate-the-house.describe: One half of the rink, a net at the right. A shaded six-sided region is drawn on the ice: its up-ice edge runs straight across between the tops of the two faceoff circles, its two long sides run down-ice from the top of each circle to that circle's faceoff dot, and from each dot an angled edge runs in to the nearer goalpost, so the shape narrows to the width of the goal at the goal line. No players are drawn.
home-plate-the-house.title: Home plate, or the house

above-and-below-the-dots.caption: Above and below the dots: the split coaches use to divide the zone at the end-zone faceoff dots — unequal halves, tinted here.
above-and-below-the-dots.describe: One half of the rink, a net at the right, tinted in two shades either side of an unmarked line drawn across the zone through the two faceoff dots. The part from that line out to the blue line is labelled "above the dots"; the part from it in to the end boards, containing the net, the crease and the ice behind the net, is labelled "below the dots". No line is painted between them and no players are drawn.
above-and-below-the-dots.title: Above and below the dots

the-three-zones.caption: The whole sheet, split by the two blue lines into defending, neutral and attacking zones — attacking drawn on the right here, the picture’s choice, not a fixed fact.
the-three-zones.describe: The whole two-hundred by eighty-five foot rink seen from above, tinted in three bands across its length. The band from the left-hand end boards to the near blue line is labelled "defending zone"; the band between the two blue lines, containing the centre red line and the centre faceoff circle, is labelled "neutral zone"; the band from the far blue line to the right-hand end boards is labelled "attacking zone". Each band runs the full width of the ice and follows the rounded corners to the boards. No players are drawn.
the-three-zones.title: The three zones

rink-map-neutral-zone.caption: The whole sheet, with the neutral zone — the middle third between the two blue lines — shaded, showing the centre line, centre dot and four neutral-zone spots.
rink-map-neutral-zone.describe: The full two hundred by eighty-five foot rink seen from above. The band between the two blue lines is shaded and labelled "neutral zone". In it are the centre red line, the centre faceoff dot inside its blue circle, and four red faceoff spots without circles, two just outside each blue line. The two end zones either side are unshaded, each with its goal, crease, trapezoid and pair of faceoff circles. No players are drawn.
rink-map-neutral-zone.title: The neutral zone

rink-map-end-zone-markings.caption: One half of the sheet at twice the scale: the blue line, faceoff circles, goal line, crease, trapezoid, and the shaded strip of ice behind the net.
rink-map-end-zone-markings.describe: One half of the rink seen from above, from the centre red line at the left to the end boards at the right. A blue line crosses a quarter of the way in; then two faceoff circles with their hash marks; then the goal line, with the net standing on it, the light blue crease in front of it and two dashed red trapezoid lines behind it. The strip of ice between the goal line and the end boards is shaded, running the full width of the sheet and following the curve of the corners round to the end boards. No players are drawn.
rink-map-end-zone-markings.title: The end-zone markings

rink-map-end-zone.caption: One end zone at twice the scale, labelled with the standard position vocabulary: the point, half-wall, crease and corners, with the high and low slot shaded as regions. Left and right are as the attacking team sees them, skating toward the net on the right of the picture.
rink-map-end-zone.describe: One half of the rink seen from above, from the centre red line at the left to the end boards at the right, with the blue line about a quarter of the way in: two faceoff circles, the net on the goal line with the crease in front of it and the trapezoid behind. Most named areas — the point, the half-wall, the top of the circle, the crease and the corners among them — are marked with a dot and a plain-English label; the high slot and the low slot are shown instead as two shaded regions in front of the net.
rink-map-end-zone.title: End zone position vocabulary

the-risk-map.caption: A map of turnover cost by location, by coaching consensus rather than measurement. Own net left, attack left to right; darker red costs more. Your own slot is worst; your own end and the middle of the neutral zone share a shade — both dangerous, the middle also disorganised; their end, in blue, is cheapest.
the-risk-map.describe: The full 200-foot sheet, seen from above, with no players and no routes. Your own end is at the left and the opposition end at the right. Four regions are shaded in red and one in blue, and the four reds carry three different strengths, because two of them are deliberately the same. Your whole defensive zone, from the end boards at the left to your own blue line and following the two board arcs into the corners, carries a medium red. Inside it, a much darker red rectangle runs down the middle of that zone from the tops of the two faceoff circles to the front edge of the goal crease, its sides on the inner edges of the circles: it is labelled "your slot". A band of the same medium red as your defensive zone spans the neutral zone from blue line to blue line, its sides on the two faceoff-dot lines, labelled "the middle". A narrow, much fainter red band runs across the full width of the ice from the opposition blue line about eight feet into their zone. The deep end of their zone, from the boards level with their faceoff dots back around both corner arcs to the end boards, is shaded blue and labelled "their end". The ice between the faint band at their blue line and their faceoff dots is left unshaded.
the-risk-map.title: Turnover risk map

pinch-centre-high.caption: A pinch at the offensive blue line with the centre high in the zone behind it, which is an arrangement that makes a pinch defensible. What makes a pinch good is not whether it works but what is behind it if it does not: here the pinching defenceman’s partner has held the middle at the line and the centre is high rather than deep, so the worst a miss can produce is two of their forwards against those two teammates — a rush a team can defend. No contact is drawn: the pinching defenceman’s route ends in two bars. ⚠️ Arrive and contain on the wall, stick on the puck, not on a player, and whether that arrival may end in a hit depends on whether your league allows body checking at all.
pinch-centre-high.describe: The attacking half of the rink, the opposition net at the right, the attack having been moving left to right. Three opposition players are drawn as solid glyphs: a forward on the upper half-wall, about eleven feet up-ice of the faceoff dot, with the puck at that forward’s stick; a second forward on the lower, weak side of the ice, just up-ice of the lower faceoff circle, with a plain arrowed route heading back out toward the blue line; and their goalie in the crease. Own players are open glyphs: a defenceman at the upper point whose route runs in a shallow arc toward the upper boards and ends in two short bars across the line, about eight feet short of the puck carrier, and a second defenceman at the blue line on the lower side, shaded into the middle of the ice. A centre is drawn on the upper side of the middle of the ice, about seventeen feet inside the blue line and higher up the zone than the point where the pinching defenceman’s route ends, with a plain arrowed route running back toward the point the pinching defenceman has vacated and stopping about nine feet short of that defenceman’s glyph. So the pinching defenceman has committed themselves to the wall, and the two own players left to defend a rush the other way are the defenceman’s partner and the centre — against the carrier and the one forward climbing with the carrier.
pinch-centre-high.title: A pinch with the centre high

pinch-centre-below-the-goal-line.caption: A pinch at the offensive blue line with the centre below their goal line, which makes it a bad decision even when it works. In front of the pinching defenceman it looks like a good pinch; behind them, their partner is the only player between two of the opposition forwards and your own end. Beat the pinch and it is a two-on-one the other way, waiting to happen whether the pinch came off or not. So before you jump a lane, pinch or activate, ask not only "am I right?" but "what happens if I am right and I still miss it?" No contact is drawn: the pinching defenceman’s route ends in two bars. ⚠️ Arrive and contain on the wall, stick on the puck, not on a player, and whether that arrival may end in a hit depends on whether your league allows body checking at all.
pinch-centre-below-the-goal-line.describe: The attacking half of the rink, the opposition net at the right, the attack having been moving left to right. Three opposition players are drawn as solid glyphs: a forward on the upper half-wall, about eleven feet up-ice of the faceoff dot, with the puck at that forward’s stick; a second forward on the lower, weak side of the ice, just up-ice of the lower faceoff circle, with a plain arrowed route heading back out toward the blue line; and their goalie in the crease. Own players are open glyphs: a defenceman at the upper point whose route runs in a shallow arc toward the upper boards and ends in two short bars across the line, about eight feet short of the puck carrier, and a second defenceman at the blue line on the lower side, shaded into the middle of the ice. A centre is drawn below their goal line and past the back of their net, five feet below the line and eight feet out to the weak side of it, with no route: the centre is at the far end of the picture from the play and from the centre’s own end. So the pinching defenceman has committed themselves to the wall and the defenceman’s partner is the only own player left to defend a rush the other way — one player against the carrier and the one forward climbing with the carrier.
pinch-centre-below-the-goal-line.title: A pinch with the centre below the goal line

cross-ice-in-your-own-end.caption: Never pass across the front of your own net. A defenceman sealed in the corner passes below the tops of the circles, across the slot. Their middle forward stands beside the lane, stick reach not drawn. Their third forward slides across. A designed cross-ice breakout is a different play, made only when the middle is empty. The far outlet could be your weak-side defenceman; their defencemen are not drawn, so do not count bodies. No contact is drawn, and whether a hit may follow depends on whether your league allows body checking. ⚠️ If you collect a puck on that wall, never turn your back to anyone coming at you, and never duck. Skates parallel to the wall, head up, chin off your chest, and take any contact on your forearm and hip, never the point of your shoulder.
cross-ice-in-your-own-end.describe: The defending half of the rink, your own net at the right. Three own players are drawn as open glyphs: a defenceman in the upper corner about five feet up-ice of the goal line with the puck at the defenceman’s stick; a forward low on the opposite boards, level with the far faceoff dot; and the goalie in the crease. Three opposition players are solid glyphs: a forward inside and below the puck carrier, sealing them toward the corner; a second forward in the middle of the zone, a few feet above the passing lane and about seven feet off it; and a third forward on the lower, weak side, level with the tops of the faceoff circles and just clear of the lower one, with a route running down toward the lower boards that ends in two short bars across the line, about ten feet short of the forward waiting there. A shaded band runs down the middle of the zone from the tops of the two faceoff circles to the front edge of the goal crease, its sides on the inner edges of the two circles. One dashed pass leaves the defenceman in the corner, runs straight across the width of the ice through that shaded band in front of the net — it is the play this section tells you not to make, and finishes about six feet short of the forward on the far boards.
cross-ice-in-your-own-end.title: Cross-ice in your own end

never-both-defencemen-to-the-puck.caption: Never both defencemen to the same puck — the formation itself, not what happens after. Your own defensive zone, own net at the right. Both have gone to a puck battle in the corner, and the ice in front of your own net, shaded here, is left completely empty. A coaching convention, not a law — and it has a real exception: under a defensive strong-side overload some coaches send both defencemen low and give the slot to a forward instead, so somebody is still home. Find out what your team plays. No contact and no route are drawn: this is a shape, not a play.
never-both-defencemen-to-the-puck.describe: Your own defensive zone, the net at the right. An opposition forward, a solid circle, is deep in the strong-side corner with a loose puck near them. Two open triangles — both defencemen — are with that forward in the same corner: one about level with the faceoff-dot line and a stride up-ice of it, closer to the middle of the ice; the other higher, on the boards below the hash marks. All three are converged on one puck, drawn between them rather than at any one stick. A shaded rectangle, labelled "your slot", runs down the middle of the zone from the tops of the two faceoff circles to the front edge of the crease, and it is completely empty — no player stands in it. The goalie is alone in the crease. No routes are drawn: this is a frozen shape, not a play in progress.
never-both-defencemen-to-the-puck.title: Both defencemen and one puck

scan-before-a-wall-reception.caption: One instant, everything visible before the pass: the puck is coming to you on the half-wall and a forechecker is closing. No look is drawn. The notation has no head. Pressure could come from the middle too, so check both shoulders. The retriever could be any teammate. Looking does not protect you; position does. Whether the forechecker may hit you depends on whether your game allows body checking. A reception on the wall can end with you against the boards, checking league or not. Get your skates parallel to the wall and take any contact on your forearm and hip, head up and chin off your chest — not on the point of your shoulder, and not the whole shoulder if you can help it. If you are already facing the wall and cannot turn, get your stick and gloves up and spread out on the glass, with no head contact at all. ⚠️ Never turn your back to anyone coming at you, and never duck.
scan-before-a-wall-reception.describe: Your own end zone, your net at the right with your goalie in the crease. A teammate stands behind the net, off the near post, and a dashed pass line runs from them up to the right half-wall, level with the faceoff dot, where you stand waiting to receive; the puck is drawn on that line, about forty per cent of the way across, so the pass is in flight. A second teammate stands inside and below you, between you and your own net, as the support option. An opposition forward is up ice on the same wall with a route running down the wall and easing off it toward the ice side of you, stopping about eight feet short and ending in two short bars rather than an arrowhead, meaning they arrive and contain rather than skating through. Nobody else is drawn, and no head turn is drawn, because the notation has no symbol for one.
scan-before-a-wall-reception.title: Scanning before a wall reception

scan-the-danger-in-your-own-end.caption: A puck battle in the corner of your own end. The question is not where the puck is but who scores if it comes out now: the net front, whose weak side is called the back door, and the shaded high slot — the ice between the circles, from the dots up to the top of them. Your other four skaters are deliberately not drawn, so whether either of these opponents is really unmarked depends on the coverage your team plays: a low zone collapse, a strict man-to-man or a hybrid. Find out which one your team plays, because it decides where your eyes belong. Neither region is painted on a rink.
scan-the-danger-in-your-own-end.describe: Your own end zone, your net at the right with your goalie in the crease. A loose puck sits in the right corner with two players contesting it, one of yours below it and an opposition player above it nearer the boards. Two further opposition players are drawn and no more of yours: one just outside the crease on the far side of the net, at the back door, and one inside a shaded band in the middle of the zone. That band runs between the inner edges of the two faceoff circles, from the level of the faceoff dots up to the top of the circles: it is the high slot. No routes are drawn — nobody moves in this picture — and your other four skaters are not drawn at all.
scan-the-danger-in-your-own-end.title: Where the danger is during a corner battle

lane-jump-anticipation.caption: The first of two frames of the same moment: this one is the anticipating position, the next one is the guess. You are standing inside the shaded band — the ice between the puck and your own net, a name for a piece of ice rather than a marking — on the side of it nearer the carrier’s option. If the pass never comes, you are still in front of your own net and still doing a job. The cue itself cannot be drawn: this notation has no facing and no stick. You are drawn as a forward because a shape had to be chosen, and who is standing here depends on the coverage your team plays.
lane-jump-anticipation.describe: Your own end zone, your net at the right with your goalie in the crease, and no routes drawn. An opposition forward has the puck inside the right faceoff circle, above the dot. A second opposition forward stands far across the ice on the left half-wall, level with the far faceoff dot. A shaded band runs from just in front of the puck carrier down to the front edge of the crease, narrow at the carrier’s end and about seven feet wide where it meets the crease: it is the ice between the puck and your net. You are drawn as a forward standing inside that band, about eighteen feet from the carrier and offset within the band toward the far-side opponent. No routes are drawn in either frame of this pair: the whole comparison is where you are standing. Your other four skaters are not drawn.
lane-jump-anticipation.title: Lane jump: the anticipating position

lane-jump-guess.caption: The second of the two frames: the same moment, the same read, and the other choice. You have left the band, which now has nobody in it, and committed to the passing lane. If the pass does not come, or you miss it by a foot, the carrier has a clean lane at your goalie. Here the place makes it a gamble: in the middle of your own zone a miss is a point-blank chance, so stay in the band unless the read is near-certain. If you are the last player back, there is no version of this jump worth making.
lane-jump-guess.describe: The same end zone and the same instant as the previous diagram, with everything unchanged except where you are. The opposition carrier is still inside the right faceoff circle with the puck, their teammate is still on the left half-wall, your goalie is still in the crease, and the shaded band still runs from the puck down to the front of the crease — but the band is now empty. You are drawn out in the left faceoff circle, roughly halfway along the line between the two opponents and about twenty-eight feet from each of them, where in the previous frame you stood inside the band. No routes are drawn in either frame: the pair is a comparison of two positions. Your other four skaters are not drawn.
lane-jump-guess.title: Lane jump: the guess

shooting-lane-and-the-step.caption: Getting a point shot through: find the lane first, then shoot. The faint dashed line is the lane the shooter had a second ago, with an opponent standing squarely in it — not a marking on the ice, and nothing travels along it. Take how far from the words and not from the picture: go until the blocker has to move their feet, and the ten feet drawn here is only what makes the change of lane visible at this scale. No other opposition skaters are drawn, and nothing here shows whether the blocker adjusts. ⚠️ Keep it low and say out loud who you are shooting at — it passes your own winger at the net front, and they need a blade on the ice for the tip.
shooting-lane-and-the-step.describe: The attacking half of the rink, the opposition net at the right. Own players are drawn open, the opposition solid. A defenceman, drawn as a triangle, stands at the strong-side point at the blue-line end of the point area, with the puck just off the blade toward the middle. An opposition forward stands about fourteen feet down-ice of them, directly on the straight line from that point to the middle of the goal line. That line is drawn, faintly and dashed and labelled "old lane", running from the defenceman past the forward and stopping thirteen feet short of the goal line. Two numbered routes. One: a wave ending in an arrowhead — the notation for skating with the puck — running ten feet along the blue line from the defenceman toward the middle of the ice. Two: from the end of that move, a double line ending in an arrowhead, which is the notation for a shot, running down the ice and stopping sixteen feet short of the goal line; it passes about eight feet clear of the opposition forward’s marker, and extended it would cross the goal line one foot inside the far post. An own forward stands at the net front, eight feet out from the goal line and six feet to the strong side of its centre, outside the crease. The opposition goalie is in the crease. No other players are drawn.
shooting-lane-and-the-step.title: Finding a point-shot lane

shooting-rush-wide-and-the-trailer.caption: A wide rush at the moment the decision is made: the goalie has come across to the near post, which leaves them exposed far side and low. Two plays are on and only one happens. Your own shot is not drawn, because a plan view cannot show height and "far side and low" is half a height instruction. The feed to the trailer is. The picture cannot say when the defender’s stick arrives, and it cannot draw the delay, which is a beat of time rather than a movement backwards. The trailer is a forward only because a marker has to be a forward or a defenceman — you are told a trailer is coming, not who it is.
shooting-rush-wide-and-the-trailer.describe: The attacking half of the rink, the opposition net at the right. Own players are drawn open, the opposition solid. An own forward has the puck wide on the upper side of the ice, nine feet up-ice of the upper faceoff dot and eleven feet outside it toward the boards, about nine feet off the side wall, with the puck off the blade toward the net. An opposition defenceman, drawn as a triangle, stands sixteen feet away on the straight line between that carrier and the middle of the goal line, just inside and below the faceoff dot; no route is drawn for them. The opposition goalie stands five feet out from the middle of the goal line, on the line from the puck to the centre of the goal, which puts the letter just outside the near post rather than square in the goalmouth. A second own forward — the trailer — stands in the high slot on the far side of the middle, four feet further out from the goal line than the carrier. A dashed line ending in an arrowhead, which is the notation for a pass, runs from the puck straight back down the ice and stops eight feet short of them. No shot is drawn, no route is drawn for the trailer, and there are no other players.
shooting-rush-wide-and-the-trailer.title: Wide rush: shot or trailer

shooting-breakaway-approach.caption: The breakaway approach, numbered in order. The tops of the circles are thirty-five feet out from the goal line, so easing off there still leaves most of a zone to accelerate through. The last arrow deliberately does not say which move you make. The goalie is drawn out at the top of the crease because that is the well-coached one; at rec level they are far more likely to be deep, flat-footed and square, which is a coaching observation rather than a counted one. Nobody else is on the ice.
shooting-breakaway-approach.describe: The attacking half of the rink, the opposition net at the right. Own players are drawn open, the opposition solid. One own forward, alone, is in the neutral zone fourteen feet short of the blue line in the middle of the ice, with the puck just ahead of the blade. Three numbered routes run up the middle of the ice, each a wave ending in an arrowhead, which is the notation for skating with the puck. One: from the forward to the blue line. Two: from the blue line to a point level with the tops of the two faceoff circles, thirty-five feet out from the goal line. Three: from there, thirteen feet further in and three feet off the middle, finishing sixteen feet short of the goalie and pointing past them rather than at them. The opposition goalie stands at the top of the crease, six feet out from the goal line. No other players are on the ice, and nothing is drawn between the end of the third route and the net.
shooting-breakaway-approach.title: Breakaway approach speed

skating-pivot-toward-the-boards.caption: If you are beaten in the pivot, this shows where each failure leaves you; the turn itself is not drawn. Beaten toward the wall leaves you past the faceoff dot, heading for the corner. Beaten into the shaded ice in the middle — the slot — is a scoring chance, and that shading is a warning rather than a target. The distance drawn between the two players is not a gap figure. ⚠️ And being beaten toward the wall is not an invitation to ride them into it: driving an opponent into the boards is a separate act, and every rulebook has a boarding rule that reaches it — they do not grade it the same way. Nothing in this picture shows contact.
skating-pivot-toward-the-boards.describe: The defending half of the rink, the net being defended at the right with our goalie in its crease. Two skaters. An opposition forward, a solid circle, is in the neutral zone three feet outside the blue line and wide, toward the side drawn at the top of the picture, with the puck a small solid dot about seven and a half feet from the forward, ahead of them and nearer the boards. Our defenceman, an open triangle, stands about nine and a half feet from the forward, inside the blue line and nearer both the middle of the ice and the defended net. A run of backward-skating arches leaves the defenceman and runs up the ice and slightly wider, ending with no arrowhead. A single skate-and-stickhandle wave leaves the carrier, bows outward toward the side boards, passes outside the faceoff circle and finishes with an arrowhead against the boards past the end-zone faceoff dot, about four feet off the wall and short of the corner. A rectangle down the middle of the end zone, from the top of the two faceoff circles to the front edge of the crease, is shaded as a warning and labelled "the slot"; no route enters it. Nothing in the picture shows contact between the two players, and no turn or pivot is drawn.
skating-pivot-toward-the-boards.title: Pivot toward the boards

pp-131.caption: Five attackers on a 5-on-4, the four penalty killers not drawn so the shape reads on its own: one player at the point, three across the middle — two on the half-walls with a bumper between them in the slot — and one at the net front, just outside the blue paint and off the crease line: under the IIHF book the marked line belongs to the crease. The dashed lines are the four options a half-wall player has at once, drawn as alternatives rather than a sequence; the solid line is the point walking the line laterally. Which formation your team runs, and who stands where inside it, is a coaching choice and not a rule of hockey — and no published count of how many teams run a 1-3-1 rather than an umbrella or an overload was found.
pp-131.describe: Attacking half of the rink, the opposition net at the right, the opposition goalie in the crease. Five own players: one at the point, in the middle and just inside the blue line, two on the half-walls level with the faceoff dots, one bumper in the middle of the slot between them, and one at the net front just outside the crease. The puck is on the top half-wall. Four dashed passing options run from that player: back to the point, inside to the bumper, down to the net front, and across the seam to the far half-wall. A short solid route runs sideways along the blue line from the point. No penalty killers are drawn.
pp-131.title: 1-3-1 power play

pp-umbrella.caption: Five attackers on a 5-on-4, the killers not drawn. This is the modern umbrella: the lone defenceman takes the apex just inside the blue line and two forwards drop to the tops of the circles, so the three high players sit on a deep arc, with two low. There is no bumper: the middle of the slot is vacated on purpose. The two numbered routes are one option among many. In the classic version a forward takes the apex with both defencemen on the flanks near the line, a far shallower arc, so find out which your team runs.
pp-umbrella.describe: Attacking half of the rink, the opposition net at the right. Five own players in an arc and a pair: a defenceman at the apex in the middle just inside the blue line, two forwards lower than them at the tops of the left and right faceoff circles, one forward at the net front outside the crease and one at the side of the net below the goal line.
