The middle of the slot is empty. Two numbered routes: one, a pass from the top flank up to the apex; two, a shot from the apex past the low side of the screen. No penalty killers are drawn.
pp-umbrella.title: Umbrella power play

pp-overload.caption: Five attackers on a 5-on-4, the killers not drawn: four loaded onto one side — below the goal line, in the corner, on the half-wall and at the point — with the fifth alone on the weak side as a release valve. The numbered passes are one cycle among many, not a set play, and who stands where inside it is a coaching choice.
pp-overload.describe: Attacking half of the rink, the opposition net at the right. Four own players stacked on the top side of the picture: one below the goal line beside the net, one in the top corner, one on the top half-wall and one at the top point, just inside the blue line. A fifth own player stands alone on the far side, on the edge of the bottom faceoff circle nearer the blue line. Three numbered passes: one, from below the goal line out to the corner; two, up the wall to the half-wall; three, cross-ice to the weak-side player. No penalty killers are drawn.
pp-overload.title: Overload power play

pp-spread-5on3.caption: Drawn at 5-on-3, where it is the standard shape: two attackers low either side of the net, two high and wide at the tops of the circles though the points are the other option, one in the slot. What is fixed is the spacing, not who plays which spot. The numbered passes cross the royal road rather than going round the perimeter.
pp-spread-5on3.describe: Attacking half of the rink, the opposition net at the right. Five own players spread wide: two low on the goal line just outside each post, two high and wide at the tops of the left and right faceoff circles, and one in the middle of the slot. Three opposition players form a tight triangle: two just in front of the net either side, one high in the slot. The opposition goalie is in the crease. Two numbered passes: one, straight across from the circle at the top of the picture to the one at the bottom, crossing the middle of the ice; two, from there inside to the player in the middle of the slot.
pp-spread-5on3.title: 5-on-3 spread power play

pp-2-3.caption: Five attackers on a 5-on-4, the killers not drawn. Two at the points with three low and nobody in the middle of the slot is this shape; a spread has two high, one in the middle of the slot and two low beside the posts; a 1-3-1 has one point player and a bumper in the slot; an umbrella has three high in an arc; an overload puts four on one side. Which your team runs is a coaching choice, and that it stays common in rec and youth hockey is an impression rather than a measured share.
pp-2-3.describe: Attacking half of the rink, the opposition net at the right. Five own players: two defencemen at the left and right points, just inside the blue line, and three forwards low — one in the right faceoff circle, one in the left faceoff circle and one at the net front outside the crease. The middle of the slot is empty. Two numbered routes: one, a pass from the circle at the top of the picture up to the point on that side; two, a shot from the point to the low side of the net front. No penalty killers are drawn.
pp-2-3.title: 2-3 power play

pp-backdoor.caption: The weak-side post, away from the puck. When the kill's low defender commits to the strong side or to the net-front player, drawn here occupying that defender, nobody is covering it. Arrive late: a player camped at the back post is marked, one arriving as the pass is released is not. A read off any formation, not a shape of its own.
pp-backdoor.describe: Attacking half of the rink, the opposition net at the right, the opposition goalie in the crease. Three own players: one up top near the point on the top side of the picture, holding the puck; one at the net front just outside the crease, on the top side; and one at the weak-side post outside the crease on the bottom side, arriving late. One opposition defenceman stands low on the top side, close to the net-front attacker rather than the one on the bottom side. A dashed pass runs from the point across the middle of the ice, stopping just short of the weak-side attacker. The other two power-play attackers and the other three penalty killers are not drawn.
pp-backdoor.title: The back door on a power play

pp-walk-down.caption: The half-wall player skates the puck down toward the goal line and inside rather than passing, forcing a decision: if the low defender steps out, the net front is open; if they hold, the shot comes from the top of the circle with a moving goalie. Neither is drawn. Walk toward the dot, not the corner.
pp-walk-down.describe: Attacking half of the rink, the opposition net at the right, the opposition goalie in the crease. One own player carries the puck from the top half-wall, drawn with the long smooth wave that means skate and stickhandle, angling down and in toward the goal line and stopping short of the slot. One own player stands at the net front just outside the crease. One opposition defenceman guards low on the same side, between the carrier's route and the net-front attacker. The pass that opens to the net front if the defenceman steps out to challenge is not drawn. The other three power-play attackers and the other three penalty killers are not drawn.
pp-walk-down.title: Half-wall walk-down on a power play

pk-box.caption: Four killers, shorthanded 4-on-5, drawn against the power-play 1-3-1 that counters it: two forwards high, one each side in the shooting lanes, and two defencemen low — the strong-side one on the puck when it comes low, the weak-side one on the goalmouth and the backdoor. When the puck moves, all four slide together as one unit — as usually taught, a box kill does not rotate. The 1-3-1's letters: P at the point, H on the half-walls, B the bumper, N at the net front. A box has no single top — describing one means you are describing a diamond. Nobody is assigned to the middle, by design, so the bumper stands uncovered. Which shape a team runs is a coaching choice, and no public count of bases exists.
pk-box.describe: Defending half of the rink, our net at the right and our goalie in the crease. Four own players in a rectangle around the slot: two forwards high, level with the tops of the circles and inside them, and two defencemen low, either side of the net front. Five opposition players in a 1-3-1: one at the point just inside the blue line, two on the half-walls, one bumper in the middle of the slot inside the rectangle with no killer near them, and one at the net front. The puck is on the top half-wall. No routes are drawn.
pk-box.title: Box penalty kill

pk-diamond.caption: Four killers, shorthanded 4-on-5, drawn against the power-play 1-3-1 it exists to answer, with the puck at the point: one high at the apex, two in the middle either side, one low. Exactly one player at the top is what makes it a diamond and not a box. Both middle killers collapse onto the bumper. What it concedes is the low player alone against the net front and a backdoor arriver. Which shape you run is a coaching choice.
pk-diamond.describe: Defending half of the rink, our net at the right and our goalie in the crease. Four own players in a diamond: one high in the middle between the blue line and the tops of the circles, two in the middle of the zone either side of the slot, and one alone in front of the net. Five opposition players in a 1-3-1: one at the point with the puck, two on the half-walls, a bumper in the middle of the slot between the two middle killers, and one at the net front. One route: the apex applying pressure out toward the point player, finishing short of them and inside them, on the middle shooting lane.
pk-diamond.title: Diamond penalty kill

pk-wedge-plus-1.caption: The wedge+1 penalty kill, 4-on-5, against a power-play 1-3-1 with the puck on the half-wall. Three killers hold a tight triangle around the net and do not chase: two defencemen just off the crease edges, drawn wider apart than they really stand, and one forward at the mid-to-high slot. All three are marked W, for wedge rather than winger. The +1 hurries whoever has the puck, stick on the puck, here straight out from the goal toward the carrier: one of three published routes, and a coaching choice. Whether that pressure may end in a hit depends on whether your game allows body checking. Blocking shots is a technique, not an act of courage. Be in the lane before the shot, not sliding into it, and never block from a screening position. Half-deflecting a shot your goalie could not see is worse than letting it through cleanly. ⚠️ Block from close and on your feet, head out of the lane, hands behind your body with the backs of the gloves out.
pk-wedge-plus-1.describe: Defending half of the rink, our net at the right and our goalie in the crease. Three own players form a tight triangle around the net: two defencemen just outside the crease edges either side, and one forward in the slot in front of them. A fourth own player, the +1, is out on the puck side, the top of the picture, between the net and the puck, with a pressure route running outward toward the puck on the half-wall and finishing short of it. Five opposition players in a 1-3-1: one at the point, two on the half-walls with the puck on the top one, a bumper in the middle of the slot shaded to the puck side, and one at the net front.
pk-wedge-plus-1.title: Wedge+1 penalty kill

pk-nz-1-3.caption: Four killers, shorthanded 4-on-5, defending the net on the right against a power play attacking from the left. This is the passive 1-3. The 1-3's same-side press, the 1-1-2, the retreating box and tandem pressure are the alternatives, so ask which your team plays. Only the power play's puck carrier is drawn.
pk-nz-1-3.describe: The full sheet. We defend the net at the right; the opposition power play attacks from the left. One opposition player carries the puck in the neutral zone on the upper side. Four own players: F1 ahead of the carrier, giving token pressure back toward the puck on the carrier’s inside and finishing short of it; and behind F1 a line of three across the ice — a forward in the middle and a defenceman near each side — each backing up toward our blue line, drawn with the row of separate overlapping arches that means backward skating. Our goalie is in the crease at the right. The other four power-play attackers are not drawn.
pk-nz-1-3.title: 1-3 neutral zone penalty kill

pk-nz-1-1-2.caption: Four killers, shorthanded 4-on-5, defending the net on the right against a power play attacking from the left. This is the 1-1-2. Some coaching material calls this a common NHL choice for neutral-zone pressure; no count of NHL teams was found to confirm it. The 1-3, the retreating box and tandem pressure are the alternatives. Only the power play's puck carrier is drawn.
pk-nz-1-1-2.describe: The full sheet. We defend the net at the right; the opposition power play attacks from the left. One opposition player carries the puck up the upper side of the neutral zone. Four own players: F1 ahead of the carrier on the same side of the ice with a pressure route running back toward the puck on the carrier’s inside and finishing short of it; F2 stacked behind F1 on that same side, level with F1 along the boards; and two defencemen abreast just in front of our blue line, one either side of the middle. Our goalie is in the crease at the right. The other four power-play attackers are not drawn.
pk-nz-1-1-2.title: 1-1-2 neutral zone penalty kill

forcing-them-outside.caption: Forcing a carrier outside, your net at the right. Read the defenceman, not the route: inside the carrier and nearer your goal at the instant drawn — the whole difference from getting beaten wide. No gap distance and no retreat are drawn. Steering with the route you skate is legal. Riding the carrier into the wall with your body is a body check — barred outright in many classifications by USA Hockey 604 and Hockey Canada 7.3; in women's hockey IIHF 101.1 bars using the boards to push, pin or eliminate an opponent, and makes any step or glide into one an illegal hit. ⚠️ Find out which book you are under. Nothing here ends in contact.
forcing-them-outside.describe: The defending half of the rink, your own net at the right, your blue line at the left. Two skaters and a goalie. An opposition forward carries the puck about fifteen feet inside your blue line, wide on the right-hand side, with the puck on the boards side of their body. Your defenceman stands about nine feet from the carrier, both nearer the middle of the ice and nearer your own net — that is, on the inside and on the defensive side. One route is drawn, the carrier’s: a wave bowing gently outward toward the boards and finishing out on the wall a few feet short of the faceoff dot line and about four feet short of the boards themselves, finishing just outside the painted faceoff circle and just short of the nearer hash mark — close to both, crossing neither. The defenceman has no route drawn. Your goalie is in the crease. Nothing in the picture shows contact.
forcing-them-outside.title: Defenceman inside the carrier

getting-beaten-wide.caption: Getting beaten wide, your net at the right: the carrier is past the defenceman’s outside shoulder with nobody between them and the net. The route is not redrawn to the net on purpose: a still picture cannot draw "whenever they choose". ⚠️ Chasing from behind, your stick goes on the puck and nothing else — a hook, trip, hold or slash that denies the chance is a penalty shot under the NHL and IIHF, and USA Hockey 616(a) and Hockey Canada 4.11(a) are narrower. All four carry conditions.
getting-beaten-wide.describe: The defending half of the rink, your own net at the right, your blue line at the left. The same two skaters and goalie as the diagram before, and the opposition carrier stands in exactly the same place, wide on the right-hand side about fifteen feet inside your blue line, with the puck on the boards side of their body. They skate the same route as in that diagram, and it is the only route drawn: a wave bowing gently outward toward the boards and finishing out on the wall a few feet short of the faceoff dot line. Your defenceman has moved, and is the only player who has: the defenceman is now eighteen feet further up the ice, back toward your blue line, so the carrier is about eleven feet past them toward the net and six feet outside them, with the whole end of the rink behind them empty. The defenceman has no route drawn. Your goalie is in the crease. Nothing in the picture shows contact.
getting-beaten-wide.title: Carrier past the defenceman

attack-the-seam.caption: The seam is the gap two defenders have both left unclaimed — space by ambiguity rather than by distance, and it moves as they move. They are drawn staggered because two defencemen retreating level seal the middle and leave nothing to attack. Where a defence chooses to meet a rush is a coaching choice and not a law, so read this as one arrangement, and the shaded band as one instant rather than a marking. No contact is drawn.
attack-the-seam.describe: The attacking half of the rink, the opposition net at the right, the attack moving left to right. Two opposition defencemen are drawn as solid triangles near their own blue line, staggered rather than level: one is stepped up to the line on the upper side of the ice, the other is about ten feet deeper into the zone on the lower side. A shaded band, labelled "the seam", runs from the gap between the two of them toward the net, ending level with the tops of the faceoff circles. Three own players are drawn as open circles: the puck carrier coming up the middle from near centre ice, with the puck on their stick and a skate-and-stickhandle route that ends inside the mouth of the shaded band, and two teammates wide on either side, a little ahead of the carrier, with no routes drawn. The opposition goalie is in the crease.
attack-the-seam.title: Attacking the seam

deny-the-reception.caption: Deny the reception, not the pass. Drawn here as one instance: a pass from the wall into the middle of your own end. The read is the same wherever the pass goes. The pass and the covering run are one instant, not a sequence. Your stick is not drawn. The route ends in two bars rather than an arrowhead because it finishes on ice, not on a person. No contact is drawn. What an arrival like this may end in depends on whether your league allows body checking. Come from where the receiver can see you, and never finish into the back of a player turned away from you. Who takes this job depends on the coverage your team plays; the read is the same for a defenceman.
deny-the-reception.describe: Your own end, your net at the right and your goalie in the crease. Two opposition players are drawn as solid circles: one on the boards level with the faceoff dot with the puck, and one in the middle of the ice level with the faceoff dots, in the high slot. A dashed passing route runs from the first to the second, stopping just short of the receiver. One own player, an open circle, stands between the receiver and your net and a little to the puck side; their route curves out toward the receiver and ends in two short bars across the line, about six feet short of the receiver, on the net side. It does not cross the passing lane at any point. The two routes are drawn as one instant rather than as a sequence, and neither is numbered.
deny-the-reception.title: Denying the reception

show-one-shoulder-open-the-other.caption: The carrier’s line is aimed at the inside shoulder, the one toward the middle of the ice; the defenceman closes the middle — the shaded band — and the ice between them and the boards is what opens. The mirror is not drawn here. The line stops well short of the defenceman and no contact is drawn. A defender who does not bite gives you nothing, so read this as a defender who moved and not as a promise that they will. The band is not painted on the ice. Its sides are the two faceoff-dot lines, and its ends are drawn only so the shading has an edge: the middle is a lane running the length of the rink, and nothing gives it a depth.
show-one-shoulder-open-the-other.describe: The attacking half of the rink, the opposition net at the right, the attack moving left to right. One own player, an open circle, carries the puck wide on the upper side of the ice near centre ice. One opposition defenceman, a solid triangle, is between them and the blue line, out toward the same side and a few feet outside the faceoff-dot line. The carrier’s skate-and-stickhandle route runs toward the defenceman’s inside shoulder — the side nearer the middle of the ice — and stops on the blue line, about eleven feet short of them. A shaded band labelled "the middle" fills the centre of the zone, its sides on the two faceoff-dot lines and its ends at the blue line and the tops of the faceoff circles. A second route runs from the defenceman inward, about eleven feet, ending inside that band. The opposition goalie is in the crease.
show-one-shoulder-open-the-other.title: Skating at one shoulder to open the other

winger-wall-depth-by-system.caption: Where a winger stands on the wall in their own end, your goal at the left, at the moment your defenceman has the puck behind your net. Three wingers are drawn and only one is on the ice at a time: the same player under three breakout structures. In the conventional swing breakout you come down between the hash marks and the goal line, roughly level with the faceoff dot. Under a flat or spread structure you hold higher up the same wall. Under a stretch or flying-winger structure one winger leaves the zone altogether, drawn past the centre red line. None of the three is more correct, so find out which one you are in. Where you stood a second earlier belongs to your team’s defensive-zone system, a separate coaching choice; this guide assumes a low zone collapse there.
winger-wall-depth-by-system.describe: The full two-hundred-foot sheet, your own goal at the left and the attacking end at the right. Your goalie is in the crease and one of your defencemen is behind the net with the puck. Three of your own forwards are drawn, all along the boards at the top of the picture, which is your left as you face up the ice, and they are three alternative positions for one player rather than three players: the first is deep in your own end on the boards just below the faceoff dot, between the hash marks and the goal line; the second is on the same boards about twenty feet inside your own blue line; the third is out in the neutral zone past the centre red line, short of the far blue line and well off the boards. No opposition players are drawn, and no routes.
winger-wall-depth-by-system.title: Winger’s wall depth by system

winger-leaves-the-point.caption: What it costs a winger to leave the point, drawn in your own end with your net at the right. You went down into the corner to help, and the puck has come out to the opposing defenceman you were covering, who is walking in with nobody near them. ⚠️ This is a mistake under low zone collapse, a coaching choice rather than a rule of hockey: under man-on-man, following your check into the corner is the job, and under a hybrid it is the job only below the line your team sets. Find out which one your team plays.
winger-leaves-the-point.describe: The defending half of the rink, your own net at the right. Your goalie is in the crease and one of your defencemen is just in front of it, off the blue paint. Your right winger is down in the right-hand corner with an opposition forward. An opposition defenceman is up at their point, a few feet inside the blue line on that side, with the puck beside them. Two routes are drawn: a dashed pass running from the corner up the length of the zone to them, bowed away from the corner battle, and the defenceman’s own skating route curving down off the point toward the middle of the ice and the top of the faceoff circle. The only players of yours in the picture are the one in the corner and the one at the net front. Nobody is near the opposing defenceman, and nobody is on the boards between the hash marks and the goal line.
winger-leaves-the-point.title: Winger leaving the point

winger-arriving-at-the-line.caption: Arriving at the attacking blue line as a winger, with the zone you are entering at the right. The defenceman meeting you is stood up on their own line, defending the ice your body, your hands and your stick reach before your trailing skate does. The trail skate is not drawn. Drag it with the blade touching the blue line or the ice on your side of it, which keeps you onside wherever you play. ⚠️ Keep your head up — it is the condition of the technique, because you cannot brace for a hit you cannot see — and never turn your back to anyone coming at you and never duck. Those are two different injuries — a hit from behind you cannot brace for, and a chin tucked to the chest, which does not need speed to do it.
winger-arriving-at-the-line.describe: The attacking half of the rink, the attacking net at the right and the attacking blue line running across the picture near the left-hand edge. Two opposition defencemen stand at that line, one near the top of the picture squarely on it and one on the far side of the ice from the first, with their goalie in the crease. Two of your own forwards are in the neutral zone on the near side of the line: the carrier towards the middle with the puck beside them, and the winger out wide toward the top boards. Two routes: the winger’s skating route taking them across the line and on into the zone, still wide, and a dashed pass from the carrier that curves over and lands just inside the line ahead of the winger. No stick, no skate and no contact is drawn.
winger-arriving-at-the-line.title: Winger arriving at the attacking blue line

winger-corner-and-the-empty-point.caption: A winger with the puck in the offensive corner. The opposition net is at the right and their defenceman is on you from the inside, so your body is the wall between them and the puck. Two outlets are drawn: your own defenceman, and your centre. What the picture is actually about is where that defenceman is. They have stepped down off the blue line to the top of the faceoff circle to support the cycle, which is normal and legitimate — so the point behind them, exactly where a blind pass up the wall goes, is empty. Look up before you throw it there. Your defenceman may equally be holding the line. ⚠️ Never turn your back to anyone coming at you and never duck. Nothing in this picture is contact, and nothing in it is a licence to hit.
winger-corner-and-the-empty-point.describe: The attacking half of the rink, the opposition net at the right. Your left winger has the puck in the corner at the top of the picture, which is your left as you attack, the puck drawn on the boards side of their body, away from an opposition defenceman who is inside them and nearer the net. Three more of your own players are drawn: a defenceman at the top of the faceoff circle on that side rather than up at the blue line, your centre in the slot in front of the net, and your second defenceman across at the far-side point. The point on the winger’s own side, just inside the blue line at the top of the picture, has nobody in it. Two dashed passing routes leave the winger, one to the defenceman at the top of the circle and one to the centre; neither is numbered, because only one of them happens. The opposition goalie is in the crease.
winger-corner-and-the-empty-point.title: Winger in the corner and the empty point

entry-three-lanes.caption: Drawn at the instant the two wide players are already on the blue line at speed and the puck is still a stride short of the line — that order is the point. They are onside because a skate is still on the line. Both the skates and the puck are in the test, and they do different jobs: the skates decide, and the puck completely crossing fixes the instant at which they are read. So a player with both skates fully over the line when the puck crosses is offside however far behind them the puck was, and a skate on or behind the line keeps you onside whatever the puck does — which is what the trail-skate drag is for. Which of the three carries, and whether the lanes cross at all, is a coaching choice.
entry-three-lanes.describe: The attacking half of the rink, opposition net at the right. Three own forwards approach the blue line in three lanes: one wide near each side wall, level with the line, and one in the middle seven feet short of it with the puck. Two opposition defencemen are inside the zone, backing in, roughly between the faceoff dots, with their goalie in the crease. Three routes: each wide player continues into the zone down their own lane, and the carrier carries the puck across the line through the middle.
entry-three-lanes.title: Three lanes at the line

entry-wide.caption: A wide entry; no contact is drawn. The net drive stops at the edge of the blue paint, off its red line: screen from there. The drive is not a licence to hit the goalie: it is where the goalie is, not where you are, that decides. Contact you start with a goalie in the crease voids the goal, incidental or not, though the NHL, IIHF and PWHL allow incidental contact in a rebound scramble. A goalie out of the crease is not fair game either. A head-first hit on a post is the same neck injury as one on the boards, and can happen at walking speed, checking or not. ⚠️ At every level, arrive head up, chin off your chest: never meet a goal post head first, and never duck.
entry-wide.describe: The attacking half of the rink, opposition net at the right. An own forward has just crossed the blue line wide on the top wall with the puck, outside an opposition defenceman who is inside the carrier. A curved route carries the puck down the boards to the goal line. A second own forward drives from the high slot to the front of the net, stopping short of the crease. A third own forward waits high on the far side for the back-door or point option. A second opposition defenceman stands in front of their own net and the goalie is in the crease. The beaten defenceman is drawn with no route, because the route they would have to skate finishes at a player travelling along the wall and that is a shape that is not drawn here.
entry-wide.title: The wide entry

entry-delay-curl.caption: Alone at the line against two defenders, the carrier curls back toward the neutral zone before either can reach them, buying late support time. The re-attack is not drawn. The curl is drawn out in open ice because one safety point outranks the play, and two different postures injure a neck at the boards: a turned back makes the contact a hit from behind, and a chin tucked to the chest straightens the cervical spine. ⚠️ Curl away from the wall, and never turn your back to anyone coming at you. If you cannot get off the boards, take the contact rather than turning away into them: skates parallel to the wall, forearm and hip into it — not on the point of your shoulder, and not the whole shoulder if you can help it — head up and chin off your chest, and never duck.
entry-delay-curl.describe: The attacking half of the rink, opposition net at the right. An own forward with the puck is just short of the blue line in the middle of the ice, alone against two opposition defencemen who are standing up inside the line. The carrier's route turns away from them and curls back toward the neutral zone in open ice, well clear of both side walls. The puck is drawn on the far side of the carrier from the nearest defender, which is what protecting it with your body means. A second own forward arrives late from behind on the other side of the ice, skating toward the line. The opposition goalie is in the crease.
entry-delay-curl.title: The delay and curl-back

dump-hard-rim.caption: Rimmed round behind the net and on in the direction of play, arriving on the far side before the defence can rotate.
dump-hard-rim.describe: The attacking half of the rink, opposition net at the right. An own forward with the puck is on the top wall near the blue line, with an opposition defenceman inside them and slightly up-ice, stepping up. Two numbered segments trace one puck path: first along the top wall into the top corner, then round behind the net and out to the far corner. A third numbered route is an own forward skating down the far wall into that corner to meet it. The opposition weak-side defenceman stands in the middle of the zone, the partner who has to rotate, and the goalie is in the crease. No route ends on a player.
dump-hard-rim.title: The hard rim

dump-soft-area.caption: Placed, not fired, so it stops in the corner — which is why the chaser is drawn already most of the way there. A soft dump is only worth it if your chaser wins the race.
dump-soft-area.describe: The attacking half of the rink, opposition net at the right. An own forward with the puck is just outside the blue line on the bottom side of the ice. A dashed route places the puck into the bottom corner. A second own forward, already well inside the zone along the bottom wall, skates toward that corner and their route stops short of the puck and up-wall of it. An opposition defenceman is turning back from in front of their own net toward the same corner, their route also stopping short. The goalie is in the crease. The two arriving routes finish apart from one another and neither finishes behind the other player.
dump-soft-area.title: The soft area dump

dump-chip-past.caption: The defenceman is stepping up to meet you at or before the line with space behind them on the wall, so the puck is lifted past them down the wall while you go around the other side to collect it yourself. A possession play rather than a surrender.
dump-chip-past.describe: The attacking half of the rink, opposition net at the right. An own forward with the puck comes up the wing lane along the top wall toward the blue line. An opposition defenceman is standing on the line in front of the carrier. Route one is the carrier changing their line, swinging inside the defenceman and back out to the wall behind them. Route two is the puck, chipped past the defenceman on the boards side and landing on the wall inside the zone, where the carrier is heading. The two routes separate before the defenceman and rejoin behind the defenceman. The defenceman is drawn with no route of their own, because every route from them finishes pointing at the carrier, and an arrow that reads as a collision is not drawn here. The opposition goalie is in the crease.
dump-chip-past.title: The chip past a defenceman

dump-cross-corner.caption: Shot hard diagonally into the far corner, leaving the weak-side defenceman the long backhand retrieval drawn here. It only works if your far-side winger is already going there. ⚠️ A defenceman facing their own boards has their back to you, which is the picture the checking-from-behind rules are written about. Arrive on the puck, never on their back.
dump-cross-corner.describe: The attacking half of the rink, opposition net at the right. An own forward with the puck is just outside the blue line on the top side of the ice; a dashed route carries the puck diagonally across the zone into the far, bottom corner. An opposition defenceman stands on the top side, the one the puck is being taken away from. Their partner, on the bottom side, has a long route across and down toward that far corner. A second own forward is driving down the bottom wall and their route finishes on the wall side, up-ice of where the puck lands and clear of the retrieving defenceman. The goalie is in the crease.
dump-cross-corner.title: The cross-corner dump

dump-flip-over-trap.caption: The structure drawn is a neutral-zone 1-3-1, and skating into the three is the trap working. So the puck is lifted high, blade opened under it, to land behind their defence and short of the goal line. A flat diagram cannot show the height, and the height is the whole play: it goes over the three-player wall rather than through it.
dump-flip-over-trap.describe: The full sheet, own end at the left, attacking end at the right. An own forward with the puck is at their own blue line. One opposition forechecker pressures them. Three opposition players are spread across the middle of the ice at the centre red line, one near each side and one in the centre, and a fifth opposition player is back near their own blue line. A long dashed route runs from the carrier, between the players of the three-player layer, and lands high in the attacking zone short of the goal line. Two own forwards skate from the neutral zone toward that area, their routes stopping short of it. Both goalies are in their creases.
dump-flip-over-trap.title: The flip over a trap

dump-and-the-trapezoid.caption: Dump to the corners, not to the goalie: where a trapezoid applies, the marked area is the only ice behind the goal line on which they may play the puck. The NHL and the IIHF book mark one, with the KHL commonly said to have one too though no KHL rulebook was available to check that; the USA Hockey, Hockey Canada and CARHA books mark none, and the PWHL switches its off though one rule still writes the minor, so plan for a PWHL goalie to come out. In any British competition, plan for them to come out too: England Ice Hockey calls it "not currently enforced", but that rule’s scope and standing are unsettled. Look behind the net, ask your league, and where there is none, rim it hard and low instead.
dump-and-the-trapezoid.describe: The attacking half of the rink, opposition net at the right, with the goalkeeper’s restricted area marked behind the net by two dashed lines running from the goal line out to the end boards. The opposition goalie stands behind their net, inside those lines. An own forward with the puck is just outside the blue line on the top side of the ice; a dashed route sends the puck into the top corner, outside the marked area and behind the goal line. A second own forward skates down the top wall toward it, their route stopping short. An opposition defenceman is between the net and the corner, the skater who now has to go and get it. The goalie is drawn with no route: the diagram is about where the puck may legally be played, not about where they skate.
dump-and-the-trapezoid.title: Dumping and the trapezoid

entry-outside-shoulder.caption: You threaten the lane the defender is least worried about, because covering it means opening their hips toward the boards — and the moment they open outward, the inside lane is available. That lane is shaded here; nothing marks it on the rink. The carrier's line stops short of the defender on purpose, and no contact is drawn.
entry-outside-shoulder.describe: The attacking half of the rink, the opposition net at the right, the attack moving left to right. One own player, an open circle, carries the puck up the upper side of the ice from near the centre line. One opposition defenceman, a solid triangle, is between the carrier and the blue line and about ten feet nearer the middle of the ice than the carrier is. The carrier’s skate-and-stickhandle route runs at that defenceman’s outer shoulder, the side nearer the boards, and stops about twelve feet short of the defenceman. A short plain route runs from the defenceman outward toward the boards, showing their hips opening that way. A shaded band labelled "the inside lane" fills the ice on the middle side of the defenceman, running from the blue line toward the tops of the faceoff circles. The opposition goalie is in their crease.
entry-outside-shoulder.title: Attacking the outside shoulder

entry-middle-drive.caption: A teammate without the puck skating hard through the seam between the two defencemen, at the net, while the carrier comes in wide, so neither defenceman can step up on the carrier. A still picture cannot show effort — read that arrow as full speed. Where the two defencemen are drawn is one instance and not a system: how a defence meets a rush is a coaching choice. The drive stops well short of the goalmouth here, because what happens in the last few feet of a net drive is contact in front of a goalie, which this picture does not teach. ⚠️ Your head is up: this is the one route where two defencemen can both stand you up in open ice, and looking down at the puck as you arrive is what turns that into an injury.
entry-middle-drive.describe: The attacking half of the rink, the opposition net and goalie at the right, the attack moving left to right. Two opposition defencemen are drawn as solid triangles just inside their own blue line, level with each other and about twelve feet either side of the middle of the ice. Two own players are drawn as open circles. One carries the puck wide on the upper side, just short of the blue line, with a skate-and-stickhandle route continuing down the wall into the zone. The other, without the puck, is in the middle of the ice behind the line, with a long plain route running between the two defencemen and on toward the net, finishing more than twenty feet short of the goalmouth. No puck is drawn on the driver and nothing in the picture shows contact.
entry-middle-drive.title: The middle drive

entry-trail-skate-drag.caption: The winger's body, hands and stick are already in the attacking zone; only the trailing blade is on the painted line, which keeps them onside, because a skate touching any part of the twelve-inch blue line counts as contact with it. Under NHL Rule 83.1, IIHF Rule 83.1 and PWHL Rule 85.1 that skate could instead be held in the air and still be legal, but only while the blade has not broken the vertical plane rising from the leading edge of the line: swing it forward over the line and you are offside in those books too. Under USA Hockey Rule 630(a) and Hockey Canada Rule 6.11 an airborne skate is offside outright, and CARHA Rule 72(c) settles it neither way. So keep the blade on the ice, which is onside under every book.
entry-trail-skate-drag.describe: The attacking half of the rink, opposition net at the right. An own forward — the far-side winger — is on the blue line, body, stick and hands already inside the attacking zone, with a short route continuing on into the zone at speed. A second own forward, the puck carrier, is a stride behind, still short of the line, with the puck. An opposition defenceman stands up at the blue line, well clear of the winger, and the opposition goalie is in the crease.
entry-trail-skate-drag.title: The trail-skate drag

entry-drop-pass.caption: The carrier has already left the puck rolling short of the line and drives on alone as a decoy; the trailer arrives with speed the defence has not matched. The drop is to a space, not to a stick — dropped blind it leaves a stationary puck facing your own net.
entry-drop-pass.describe: The attacking half of the rink, opposition net at the right. A puck sits alone in the neutral zone, short of the blue line. An own forward who has just released it is already past it, angling on toward the blue line and into the zone as though they still carry it. A second own forward is well back and to the far side, with a long route arriving from behind toward the loose puck, stopping just short of it. Two opposition defencemen are positioned toward the side the first forward is driving into, and the goalie is in the crease.
entry-drop-pass.title: The drop pass

entry-high-triangle.caption: The carrier driving wide, a second attacker driving wide on the far side with no puck, and the third trailing into the high slot. The read is which wide driver a defenceman takes — here the near one slides to the puck carrier, which leaves the far one responsible for two of you. Which named pattern your team runs is a coaching choice.
entry-high-triangle.describe: The attacking half of the rink, opposition net at the right. Three own forwards approach the blue line: the puck carrier drives wide at the top of the picture (your left as you attack), a second forward without the puck drives wide at the bottom, and a third trails through the middle toward the high slot. Two opposition defencemen are inside the zone; the one nearer the puck carrier, toward the top, has a short route sliding toward the side the puck carrier is driving into, and the farther one holds a central position. The goalie is in the crease.
entry-high-triangle.title: The high triangle

entry-vs-standing-up.caption: A defence holding the line level rather than backing in, taking away the middle — one structure among several. Two answers at once: the wide attacker chips past a stationary defenceman with no backward momentum to recover, while a fourth attacker arrives late and unmarked behind the play.
entry-vs-standing-up.describe: The attacking half of the rink, opposition net at the right. Two opposition defencemen stand at the blue line without backing in: the one toward the top of the picture (your left as you attack) is positioned in the wide attacker's own lane, out toward the boards, and their partner holds centrally, denying the middle. An own forward with the puck is near the blue line on that same side, the top; a dashed route chips the puck past that defenceman, staying wide toward the boards, and the forward's own route curls in front of the defenceman and back out to the boards to collect it. A fourth own forward, well back in the neutral zone toward the bottom of the picture, has a long route arriving unmarked at the blue-line edge of the faceoff circle at the bottom of the picture. The goalie is in the crease.
entry-vs-standing-up.title: Against a standing-up defence

defend-squash-and-slide.caption: You are defending: squash-and-slide. The puck is wide, so the puck-side defenceman forces the carrier outside and their partner slides across at the same depth; the first forward back holds the slot. One team's system, not a universal one.
defend-squash-and-slide.describe: The attacking half of the rink from the defending team’s point of view, their own net and goalie at the right. An opposition forward carries the puck in on one side, the top of the picture, with a route continuing into the zone along that side. Two own defencemen, level with each other well inside their own blue line, each have a short route sliding sideways toward the puck side, the same distance and the same direction, so the pair moves as one unit. An own forward arrives from behind into the high slot in front of their own net, rather than joining the pressure on the puck carrier.
defend-squash-and-slide.title: Squash-and-slide
